title: The Fathers on John
rules: Larry Sanger's rules for Deep Dive Bible commentary editions (email of 8 Nov 2026): comments of at most 6 adjacent verses (Selected at most 3); cuts marked with an ellipsis; square brackets for editorial additions only; paragraphs added; one-sentence capsule no longer than 40% of the comment. Every word outside brackets is Via Patrum's published translation, checked by script.
scope: Church Fathers (all died by 749) in works published on viapatrum.org as of 8 Nov 2026.

comments.capsule: John's “In the beginning was” leaves no room for the claim that the Son once did not exist.
comments.comment:
“In the beginning was the Word.” Who can think worthily about the beginning? What power of words can be found that is able to present the thought with equal worth? When John was about to hand down to us the teaching about the divinity of the Son of God, he gave the Word no other beginning than the beginning of all things. The Holy Spirit knew those who would spring up against the glory of the only Son. He foreknew those who would bring forward against us their sophisms, contrived for the ruin of their hearers: “If he was begotten, he was not”; “Before he was begotten, he was not”; “From things that are not he received his subsistence.” …

So that no one may be permitted to say such things, the Holy Spirit spoke beforehand through the Gospel: “In the beginning,” he says, “was the Word.” If you hold fast to this saying, you will suffer no harm from the evil craftsmen. For if he says, “If he was begotten, he was not,” you say, “In the beginning he was.” “But,” he says, “how was he before he was begotten?” Do not let go of the “was.” Do not abandon the “in the beginning.” The summit of the beginning is not grasped; the outside of the beginning is not found.
comments.author: Basil of Caesarea
comments.work: Homily on “In the Beginning Was the Word”

comments.capsule: The “beginning” in which the Word was is not one beginning among many but the first of all, beyond which thought cannot reach, and its “was” leaves no “before.”
comments.comment:
Do not let anyone deceive you by the many meanings of the word. For in this life there are many beginnings of many things, but there is one beginning over all things, the one beyond. “The beginning of a good way,” Proverbs said. But the beginning of a way is the first movement, from which we start our journey, and what lies behind it can be found. … But these beginnings are beginnings of certain things, and each is relative to something. For the beginning of a line is the point, and the beginning of a surface is the line, and the beginning of a body is the surface, and the beginnings of a composed word are the letters. But that beginning is not like these. It is bound to nothing; it serves nothing; it is not considered together with anything. It is free, without a master, released from relation to another, not to be passed beyond by thought—a beginning that reasonings cannot pass beyond, whose beyond cannot be found. For if you strive with the imagination of your mind to run past the beginning, you will find it running ahead of you and meeting your reasonings first. … For the beginning is always found to be outside and greater than what is thought.

“In the beginning,” then, “was the Word.” O the wonder! How all the words have been joined together with equal honor! The “was” has equal power with “in the beginning.” … Hear the Gospel: “In the beginning he was.” But if he was in the beginning, when was he not? … “But before he was begotten,” they say, “he was not.” Do you know when he was begotten, so that you can attach the “before” to a time? For “before” is a temporal word, setting one thing before another in antiquity. But how is it reasonable that the generation of the Maker of time should be subject to temporal names? “In the beginning,” then, “he was.” If you do not let go of the “was,” you will give no entrance to wicked blasphemy. For just as sailors, when they ride on two anchors, despise the swell, so you too will laugh at this wicked disturbance that comes into life from the spirits of wickedness and shakes the faith of many, if you keep your soul anchored in the safety of these words.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what “beginning” means here and why the “was” rules out a time before the Son.
comments.author: Basil of Caesarea
comments.work: Homily on “In the Beginning Was the Word”

comments.capsule: John calls the Son “Word” rather than “Son” to show a birth without passion or time, in which the Son, like a word from the mind, fully expresses the Father.
comments.comment:
But the word “word” carries a double meaning. One kind is the word spoken aloud, which perishes in the air as soon as it is uttered. The other is the inward word, dwelling in our hearts—the conceptual word. … For how could the human word have been in the beginning, when the human being received the beginning of his generation somewhere far below? … So the human word was not in the beginning—and neither was the word of angels. … But hear the word in a manner worthy of God. For when he speaks to you about the only Son, he called him Word. Just as he will shortly say “light” and “life” and “resurrection,” and when you hear “light” you do not sink down to this light perceived by the senses and visible to the eyes, and when you hear “life” you do not think of this common life that even the irrational animals live—so too, when you hear “Word,” guard yourself lest through the weakness of your understanding you be dragged down to lowly and humble thoughts.

Search out the meaning of the saying. Why “Word”? So that it might be shown that he came forth from the mind. Why “Word”? Because without passion he was begotten. Why “Word”? Because he is the image of the one who begot him, showing the whole begetter in himself, dividing off nothing from there, and existing complete in himself—just as our own word images forth our whole thought. For what we have conceived in the heart, that we bring forth in speech, and what is spoken is a representation of the thought in the heart. … Our heart is like a spring, and the word brought forth is like a channel flowing from that spring. What flows away is as much as what first rises up; and what is hidden is as much as what appears.

He said “Word,” then, to present to you the generation of the Father without passion, to proclaim to you the complete existence of the Son, and through these things to indicate the timeless union of the Son with the Father. … Take from the sound of the word “word,” then, as much as is reverent for the theology of the only Son; whatever you find incongruous and appearing out of place, reject it and pass beyond it by every means. “In the beginning was the Word.” If he had said, “In the beginning was the Son,” the thought of passion would have entered with the title “Son.”
comments.selected_reason: Explains why John calls the Son “Word” and not “Son”.
comments.author: Basil of Caesarea
comments.work: Homily on “In the Beginning Was the Word”

comments.capsule: John says the Word was “with God,” not “in God,” to mark the Son as a distinct person, and then adds “the Word was God” so no one thinks him less.
comments.comment:
“And the Word was with God.” Again the “was,” against those who blaspheme that he was not. Where was the Word? Not in a place; for the uncircumscribed things are not contained by place. But where was he? With God. … “And the Word was with God.” Marvel at the precision of each phrase. He did not say, “The Word was in God,” but “with God,” so that he might present the distinctive character of the person. He did not say, “In God,” so that he might not give an occasion for the confusion of the persons. For that blasphemy is also wicked—the blasphemy of those who attempt to mix everything together and say that Father and Son and Holy Spirit are one subject, and that differing names are attached to the one reality. …

“And the Word was with God.” Then, having used the term “Word” to present the passionlessness of the generation, he quickly also consoled us for the harm that comes to us from the word “Word.” And as if snatching him away from the slander of the blasphemers, he says, “What is the Word? The Word was God.” Do not devise for me distinctions among words, and do not attach any blasphemy from your own cunning to the teaching of the Spirit. You have the declaration; submit to the Lord.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why John says “with God” rather than “in God”, and why he adds “the Word was God”.
comments.author: Basil of Caesarea
comments.work: Homily on “In the Beginning Was the Word”

comments.capsule: The Son is called “Word” because every work of making depends on a word, and he himself is the maker of all things.
comments.comment:
Setting him forth as craftsman of all things, the name ‘Word’ is predicated of him.

For since, as a rule, every work of crafting depends on a word, there was no other way to declare him maker of all … But the Son of God, being none other than the craftsman of wisdom and art, is fittingly named ‘Word.’ For it is not some other substance, distinct from the Word, that makes existing things through him; he himself is the maker, being God the Word.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: John says the Word “was” in the beginning but “became” flesh, using “was” for his Godhead and “became” for the incarnation in time.
comments.comment:
Then, since this Word — being God in substance and being in himself the Son of God — became man for the sake of human salvation, the Word was named ‘Flesh.’ [John 1:14] And since some, having fallen from right faith, suppose that he exists only from the time when he came forth having become man from the virgin, the theologian most rightly writes against such people: In the beginning was the Word.

And using the verbs fittingly, by ‘became’ he signifies his flesh, and by ‘was’ his Godhead. It would have been more proper to say ‘is’ of the Word of God; but since he was declaring the Word’s existence by way of distinguishing the incarnation, which happened at a certain time, the evangelist used ‘was’ instead of ‘is.’ But one must not take the proper significations of verbs when they are applied to eternal things; for it is when the things signified by them have an existence measured by time that ‘was’ means what is no longer but once was — just as ‘is’ signifies what now exists, as ‘will be’ what is going to exist. …
comments.selected_reason: Explains why John says the Word “was” (and later “became” flesh): “was” for his Godhead, “became” for the incarnation.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The “beginning” is the Son as God's Wisdom turned toward creation, and as maker of creatures the same Son is rightly called “Word.”
comments.comment:
The Son of God is also called ‘Wisdom,’ created as ‘beginning of God’s ways’ [Proverbs 8:22] according to the writing of Proverbs — because God’s Wisdom, existing in relation to him whose Wisdom she is, had no relation to anything else, but by God’s good pleasure willed that the creatures should come into being.

This Wisdom, then, willed to take up a creative relation to the things that were to be; and this is what is signified by her being created ‘beginning of God’s ways’ — along which ways he traverses, ordering beings, exercising providence, doing good, bestowing grace, in this Wisdom who was created.

They say, then, that the Word is ‘beginning’ — not being other than her in substance, but in our conception and in relation — so that it is the same existence which the scriptures now name in respect of substance: Wisdom insofar as she has been made God’s own, and the creative Word insofar as he has inclined, so to speak, toward the things made.

But it is not only here that the Son of God is called ‘Word’; sayings can be set alongside not only from the New Testament but also from the Old: ‘By the word of the Lord the heavens were established’ [Psalm 33:6]; and ‘He sent his word and healed them’ [Psalm 107:20] …
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Genesis says God “made” the world and then it “was,” but John says the Word simply “was” in the beginning, so his “was” is not that of creatures.
comments.comment:
But are their things then strong against the 'In the beginning was the Word' (John 1:1)? It was written also concerning creation, he [the heretic] says, the 'was'. For it has 'In the beginning God made the heaven and the earth, and the earth was formless and void' (Gen 1:1-2), and 'there was a man of Ramathaim-Ziphah' (1 Samuel 1:1). There is nothing common to the 'In the beginning was' and the 'In the beginning God made', nor to the creator in relation to the creation. For the 'was' concerning the creation is said and believed only regarding the flowing and passing time.

For the creation was after the non-existent came to be. For he said in advance that He made it, and then he added the 'was', so that it might not be thought automatic. But concerning the God the Word, it signifies the super-beginning. For 'In the beginning', he says, 'was' and 'was God' (John 1:1), and the 'In the beginning was' pushes out from non-existence.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The three clauses of verse 1 are three witnesses: the Word is in the Father, acts with God, and shares one undivided Godhead.
comments.comment:
The holy apostle John, both disciple and student of the Lord, clearly and explicitly teaches at the beginning of the Gospel, as something previously unknown among men, naming it the Word of the Pantokrator [the Almighty], thus saying, 'In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God' (John 1:1). He employs more than one witness to signify the eternity of the Word.

In saying 'In the beginning was the Word', he shows by power that the Word is in the Father (for God is the beginning of all things 'from whom all things are') cf. Rom 11:36; and in 'and the Word was with God', he shows the Word to be with God in activity ('for all things were made through him, and without him not one thing was made' ); and in 'the Word was God', he says not to divide the divinity, since the Word is in Him and He is in the Word; for he says, 'the Father is in me, and I in the Father' (John 14:10).
comments.author: Marcellus of Ancyra

comments.capsule: John's “beginning,” “with God” and repeated “was” show one eternal Godhead in distinct persons, and “Word” shows the Son was begotten without passion.
comments.comment:
The Word knows one beginning, not two, … For the Father is called beginning, and the Son beginning, and the Spirit beginning, because of the co-eternity of the Trinity, not because there are three beginnings; since we also call the Father God and the Son God and the Spirit God, not as worshipping three gods, but because of the consubstantiality of the one Godhead of the three hypostases [persons].

Through this [“with God”] he overthrows Sabellius’s heresy by signifying the hypostases of Father and Son … He was not uttered-forth, but hypostatic, and not only hypostatic but also God. … Since some heretics, hearing that the Father begot the Son, take offense and think a flowing or passion happens to the Father—such as naturally sometimes happens with thick bodies—the evangelist, anticipating their folly, from the preface called the Son Word once and twice and thrice, to present the passionlessness of the begetting; for as our word is begotten from the mind without flowing, without diminishment, and without passion (likewise also our spirit), so also is the begetting of the Son. …

[John 1:2] That is: he was co-eternal with the Father, existing in the Father’s nature, having as most ancient place the nature of the one who begot him; for the beginning surpasses the ages. For the Father is called beginning of the Son only according to the “from whom”; for in cause the Father will be conceived before the Son, but not in existence contemplated before him. And everywhere he inserts the “was,” sending the Son on toward the beginningless; for he did not say he had a beginning, but “in the beginning he was” (John 1:1–2).
comments.author: Ammonius of Alexandria

comments.capsule: “Was God,” “all things were made by him” and “in him was life” show that the Word was not created but eternally begotten.
comments.comment:
The phrase 'was God the Word' (John 1:1) establishes that the Word is of the essence, and that he is such a God as that Word is; and again, the uncaused. The phrase 'all things came through him, and without him nothing came into being' (John 1:3) demonstrates him, as has already been said, not merely as creator, but that he was not even created. For if not even one created thing received being apart from him, it is evident everywhere that he himself did not come into being, but was divinely begotten. …

The Father made through him as light through an inherent radiance, and as mind through a word. The phrase 'in him was life' (John 1:4) discloses that he is without beginning, being the life of the one and highest nature …
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Verse 2 sums up the whole teaching of verse 1, and its fourth “was” answers anyone who says the Son once was not.
comments.comment:
“The Word was God. He [literally “This one”] was in the beginning with God.” Again he recapitulates in a few words all his theology, which the evangelist handed down to us concerning the only Son. Who is “this one”? This one, the Word who is God. … Which “this one”? Do not look outside, searching around with the demonstrative word for the one being pointed out to you; but enter into the hidden places of your own soul, and recognize the one you were taught is God, the one who was in the beginning, the one who came forth as Word, the one who was with God. … Know that this one was in the beginning—that is, always with God his own Father.

Preserve for me these few phrases, as if sealing them as a signet upon your memories. They will be an unbreakable little wall against the assaults of those who plot against you … If someone comes to you and says, “He was begotten when he was not; for if he was, how was he begotten?”—turn away the blasphemy against the glory of the only Son as you would the voice of demons. But you yourself return and come to the phrases of the Gospels: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God. He was in the beginning with God” (John 1:1–2). Say the fourth “was,” and you will abolish their “he was not.”
comments.selected_reason: Explains why verse 2 repeats verse 1.
comments.author: Basil of Caesarea
comments.work: Homily on “In the Beginning Was the Word”

comments.capsule: All things were made through the Son, not through angels, and the Father and Spirit act with him in creating.
comments.comment:
He casts out another heresy by teaching that through the Son all things that came to be were created, not through good or evil angels, as some wrongly supposed …

The wording has emphasis that not the Son alone created all things, but also the Father and the Spirit; for whatever the Father does, he works through the Son in the Holy Spirit, and where one of the three hypostases [persons] is said to act, the remaining hypostases of the one essence are conceived with it.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what “all things were made by him” rules out, and how Father, Son and Spirit act together.
comments.author: Ammonius of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The Word gives life, even through his own flesh, leads people by light to know God, and the truth he brings is never overcome by falsehood.
comments.comment:
All things whatever the Father made through the Son were made alive from him.

The Word did not come to be in a man, but in a certain way he himself, strengthening the virgin through the Spirit and dwelling in her womb, became a foundation; and in him he built the rational ensouled flesh united to him from Mary, which is life. For as he himself is life, so also is the flesh united to him, of which those who partake are made alive, freed from death and corruption and sent into the enjoyment of the unceasing goods of the age to come, which is truly life.

The incarnation of the Only-begotten leads people by light toward true knowledge of God and toward every kind of virtue, through which life-giving happens, that is, the enjoyment of the goods.

[John 1:5] Darkness is the whole world by comparison with the inexpressible and unapproachable light. Yet the Son also enlightens the mind toward what must be done, and truth always prevails; falsehood does not overcome the truth. …
comments.selected_reason: Explains “life”, “the light of men” and why the darkness does not overcome the light.
comments.author: Ammonius of Alexandria

comments.capsule: John was sent out of the desert to proclaim Christ, and he surpasses the prophets because he witnessed to one he had seen.
comments.comment:
John is sent as one who has passed from the desert into the inhabited land, that he might proclaim Christ to the peoples. …

[John 1:7] For this reason John is greater than the other prophets: those proclaimed the one awaited, but this one, having seen him and been persuaded by signs that this is he, came bearing witness from what he heard and saw.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why John is “sent” and why his witness is greater than the prophets'.
comments.author: Ammonius of Alexandria

comments.capsule: John's witness did not give the light its standing; a witness proves his own knowledge and virtue, not the truth he testifies to.
comments.comment: Concerning God, if it is said that God testifies, we do not mean that the one testifying establishes Him. John came "that he might testify about the light" (John 1:7); for John, the one testifying about the light, did not provide faith and standing to the light. The one testifying shows himself to be knowing by his knowledge, and the one testifying is shown to be diligent by his virtue. So also those who have been well-pleasing and have struggled in persecutions are called witnesses as is fitting. They showed themselves to be lovers of truth, they showed themselves to be knowers of the truth. They did not confirm the truth, but they confirmed themselves.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what it means that John came “to bear witness of the Light”.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The Son is light by nature, while we are not light but are lit by him so that we shine with wisdom.
comments.comment: The natural Son, then, was born unique from the very substance of the Father, being what the Father is—God from God, light from light. But we are not light by nature; we are illuminated by that light so that we can shine with wisdom. For it says, “He was the true light, which illuminates every person coming into this world” (John 1:9).
comments.author: Augustine of Hippo

comments.capsule: The true light enlightens every person through the natural law written in us at creation, and again through the new covenant at Christ's coming.
comments.comment: Taking the words in their universal sense and giving their meaning, we say that in the beginning the God of all fashioned man and engraved on him a natural law, training him toward the knowledge of evil and good. And this, I think, is what was said through the voice of John about the only-begotten Son of God: “He was the true light, which enlightens every man coming into the world” (John 1:9). We understand that this also came about in the last times, I mean the times of his coming. For it is written: “In those days, says the Lord, putting my laws into their mind, I will also write them on their hearts” (Jeremiah 31:33; Hebrews 8:10).
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Christ alone is light by nature and enlightens all through creation, while the “world” that did not know him means people attached to earthly things.
comments.comment:
Even if John and the saints are light, they are not so as the Christ who is theologized, who is light by nature; for the saints received illumination by grace. Therefore concerning Christ he says: “He was the true light” (John 1:9).

The Lord enlightens his rational creatures from natural notions unto believing that he is God, as they infer from the beauty and good order of his creatures the excellence of his power.

[John 1:10] As God he was in the world not according to essence, but according to providence. … Here he calls “world” only human beings, naming the world from a part—that is, those who mind the things of the world and are nailed to it, who through attachment to earthly things did not know him at all: idolaters and slaves of the passions.

[John 1:11] He is said to have come to his own inasmuch as, having been incarnate, he was made known to those who saw him with their eyes, or that he came to his own, who seemed to be his according to “from whom is the Christ according to the flesh” (Romans 9:5).
comments.selected_reason: Explains “the true Light”, what “the world” means, and in what sense he came “to his own”.
comments.author: Ammonius of Alexandria

comments.capsule: In “the world knew him not,” the “world” means the mass of unbelievers, not the unreasoning elements.
comments.comment: For he [John] had also said in his Gospel: “The world was made through him, and the world did not know him” (John 1:10). He certainly did not mean that the elements, which lack reason, could appear capable of knowing or denying Christ. He meant the multitude of unbelievers to be designated by the name “world.”
comments.author: Julian of Eclanum

comments.capsule: Only God could give the right to become children of God, so the one who gives it, and in whom we believe, is God.
comments.comment: And we believe into his name, not believing that he is a common human and one of us, but that he is God become human. And giving authority to become children of God is not a human thing (John 1:12), but rather God-befitting and beyond creation. When therefore the faith is into him, and he himself gives the grace of adoption, how is Christ not God?
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On the True Faith, to the Princesses Arcadia and Marina

comments.capsule: Believers are reborn of God through his word, not of human seed, and so rank above everyone merely born of a woman.
comments.comment: Together with the others who came before him, he [John the Baptist] is born of a woman (Matthew 11:11). But those who have accepted the faith are no longer called born of women. As the most wise evangelist says, “As many as received him, he gave them authority to become children of God, who were born not of bloods, nor of the will of the flesh, nor of the will of a man, but of God.” (John 1:12–13) For we were reborn into God’s adoption not from corruptible seed, but through a living and abiding word. So those born not from corruptible seed but rather from God are better than everyone born of a woman.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what it means to be born “not of blood … but of God”.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The Word became flesh without change, and John chose “flesh,” not “body” or “man,” to shut out false accounts of the incarnation.
comments.comment:
When the Word became flesh, he was not changed in essence, but having become visible through the flesh he remained having his own glory as only-begotten Son of God and Father; for the one pitching tent is other in essence from the tent. He did not say “body,” lest some say he wore a heavenly body; nor “he became man,” lest others say he took not the outer but the inner man; nor “from the Word flesh came to be,” lest others say he was changed from this into that. Flesh is also called body, but body is not in every way flesh. Therefore the Lord also said: “he who eats my flesh” (John 6:54), and elsewhere: “Handle me and see, that a spirit does not have flesh and bones as you see me having” (Luke 24:39).

How did we behold? Through the star of the magi, the angels, the shepherds, Anna, Simeon, Gabriel, the ineffable birth from the virgin, the Father’s voice bearing witness to him, the Spirit’s descent upon him, and countless divine signs and healings.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why John wrote “flesh”, not “body” or “man”, and how “we beheld his glory”.
comments.author: Ammonius of Alexandria

comments.capsule: “Became flesh” means no change; “tabernacled” means dwelt with people.
comments.comment:
For no one will dare to hear a change in the Word becoming flesh (John 1:14).

But the tabernacling of him among us is to dwell with men.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: “Became flesh” means the Word himself became human, with a human soul and mind, not that he dwelt in a holy man as in the prophets.
comments.comment:
… that the Word of the Lord did not come to dwell in a holy man at the end of the ages as he came to the prophets, but the Word himself became flesh (John 1:14). And being in the form of God, he took the form of a servant (Philippians 2:6-7), and from Mary he became human according to the flesh for us. In this way the human race is completely and wholly freed from sin in him, made alive from the dead, and brought into the kingdom of heaven.

For they also confessed this: that the Savior did not have a body without a soul, without sensation, or without understanding. For it was not possible, when the Lord became human for us, that his body should be without understanding, nor was salvation only of the body, but also of the soul, in the Word himself. Being truly Son of God, he also became son of man; and being the only Son of God, the same one also became firstborn among many brothers. Therefore there was not one Son of God before Abraham and another after Abraham; nor was there one who raised Lazarus and another who asked about him. The same one spoke in human fashion when he said, “Where does Lazarus lie?” (John 11:34), and raised him in divine fashion.
comments.author: Athanasius of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Even as man his glory was seen, for he did divine deeds through the body, hungering yet feeding the hungry, asking for Lazarus yet raising him.
comments.comment: And even though he became man, we behold his glory, the glory of the only Son from the Father, full of grace and truth (John 1:14). For the things he endured through the body he ennobled as God: he hungered in flesh, yet with God’s power he fed the hungry. And if anyone stumbles at the bodily things, let him trust what God does. For as man he asked where Lazarus lay, yet as God he raised him.
comments.selected_reason: Explains how “we beheld his glory” in the incarnate Christ.
comments.author: Athanasius of Alexandria

comments.capsule: John says the Word “tabernacled,” pitched a tent, among us, because a tent is a dwelling on the move, unlike a settled house.
comments.comment: … the Word having become flesh, he did not dwell, but tabernacled among us (John 1:14), so that after this we might behold his glory, a glory as of the only-begotten from the Father, full of grace and truth. For to dwell differs from to tabernacle, just as a house differs from a tent; for the house always remains immovably established, but the tent is a portable dwelling. Certainly those making progress tabernacle, but those having reached perfection dwell; for I shall travel in a place of wondrous tabernacling until the house of God [Psalm 42:4].
comments.selected_reason: Explains the wording “dwelt” (literally “pitched his tent”) among us.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: John says “only-begotten from the Father,” not merely “only-begotten,” to mark Christ as the Father's only Son, not a unique creature like the sun.
comments.comment:
Aetius, the leader of the Eunomian heresy, says to some: 'How great a thing you grant by saying that the Christ is the only-begotten of God. And many other creatures are only-begotten. The sun, indeed, is only-begotten.' I say to him: it is not the same thing to be something 'only-begotten' and to be an only-begotten offspring or an only-begotten Son. Therefore, these things said to others as 'only-begotten' are not said with the addition of 'Son,' or 'from the Father,' or 'offspring.' But the Savior, if He is ever so named, is called with such an addition: 'and we beheld His glory, a glory as of the only-begotten from the Father' (John 1:14). And the one who is the only-begotten Son from the Father is the Father's only. …

And nothing of the creatures is only-begotten; for even if the sun were only-begotten, it is not an only-begotten creature, nor an only-begotten work, but an only-begotten sun. So also among humans we say 'only-begotten child,' not because he is the only one that exists, but because he is the only one to that parent.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: John's “he was before me” joins the Word's becoming to his eternal being, for in his divinity he always was.
comments.comment: … therefore he also added beautifully, 'because he was first of me,' so that the 'having-become' might be joined to the 'was' in such a way that it might not be thought to be something else … And he was, he says, first of me always, clearly having being according to the divinity, never beginning as if not ceasing.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: Christ gives from his fullness without being diminished, which shows he is God.
comments.comment: As root of all goods and spring, giving his own goods to many, he is not diminished; yet from what he supplies and creation receives, it is clear that Christ is God. …
comments.author: Ammonius of Alexandria

comments.capsule: “Grace for grace” means the grace of rebirth given in place of the grace we lost when the first law was broken.
comments.comment: … we received from the fullness because of his goodness. Which we by nature as slaves did not have, John saying: 'And from his fullness we all have received, and grace for grace' (John 1:16), that is, the grace of the rebirth instead of the grace which we were cast away from, striking at the first law given upon the single stock.
comments.selected_reason: Explains “grace for grace”.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Grace through Christ surpasses the law through Moses, as gifts from the true Son surpass those of a faithful servant.
comments.comment: Then, after him, he must learn the greatness of the Savior and the newness of the grace, because, as the apostle [John] says, "the law was given through Moses; grace and truth came through Jesus Christ" (John 1:17). And the things given through a faithful servant are not equal to the things bestowed by the true-born Son.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the contrast between law through Moses and grace through Christ.
comments.author: Clement of Alexandria
comments.work: Who Is the Rich Man That Shall Be Saved?

comments.capsule: No one has seen God's essence, not even in the incarnate Son, so only the Son and the Spirit can make the Father known.
comments.comment:
Not only the Father is invisible, but also the Son; for even if he was seen in flesh, it was not according to the essence, which not even angels behold as it is; for many know God, but the essence no one knows. It is not the hidden body that is called invisible, but the incorporeal that is not naturally seen even by mind.

Through the trustworthy person he establishes this high and more-than-human doctrine: “For who knows the things” of God and Father to speak, except the Son begotten from him and his Holy Spirit who also knows “the depths of God” (1 Corinthians 2:10–11).
comments.selected_reason: Explains in what sense no one has seen God, though the Son was seen in the flesh.
comments.author: Ammonius of Alexandria

comments.capsule: No one has seen God because God is incorporeal.
comments.comment: For our Scriptures plainly say that God is incorporeal. That is why “no one has ever seen God” (John 1:18), and “the firstborn of all creation” is said to be “the image of the invisible God” (Colossians 1:15), as if it said “of the incorporeal God.”
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: John's strange and holy life made the Jews ask whether he was the Christ or Elijah, and he denied being Elijah in person though he shared Elijah's spirit.
comments.comment:
The Jews, he says, sent from among the most tested of their own to those chosen to ask him who he might be, clearly having the expectation from their fathers of the coming Savior. … Since John's life was indeed strange and holy, it led them to investigation and seeking, asking who he might be and whether he is the expected one.

[John 1:20] He, he says, immediately spoke openly and did not hide the truth, that he is not the Christ.

[John 1:21] The second time they asked if he might be Elijah; for Malachi had clearly foretold that Elijah would come, saying, “Behold, I will send you Elijah the Tishbite” (Malachi 4:5). John said no; for he was not Elijah according to his own nature, even if he shared in the Spirit, and because of this he was called Elijah by the Lord (Matthew 11:14).
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the Jews questioned John and why he denied being Elijah.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: John refused honors not his own and called himself a voice, because a voice goes before a word as he went before Christ the Word.
comments.comment:
It is a work of virtue not to be lifted up by their praises and to adorn oneself in ornaments that are not one’s own. He said: “I am a voice of one crying in the wilderness: make straight the way of the Lord,” as Isaiah the prophet said (John 1:23; Isaiah 40:3).

As a voice runs before a word, so also John runs before Christ who is Word, as a voice.

If Isaiah had not previously commanded me to proclaim Christ, who is Lord, I would not have dared to speak.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why John calls himself a “voice”.
comments.author: Ammonius of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The Pharisees asked why John baptized because they held that only the Christ, Elijah or the prophet could, and John humbly called his baptism mere water.
comments.comment:
As more exact about knowledge of the Scriptures these came, whom John gently proved to be uneducated and senseless for not knowing the passage said about him from the prophet worn smooth among them.

[John 1:25] As it seems they had such traditions from their teachers that only those were allowed to baptize—either the Christ or Elijah or the prophet.

[John 1:26] John himself is a trustworthy witness of his own, since he spoke nothing great about himself, but even called his own baptism mere water, much humbled.

Until the time of the economy [his saving work] Christ was present in the midst of all and was unknown. … he says Christ stood in the midst and was unknown because of the wrapping of the flesh.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the Pharisees asked “Why baptizest thou then?” and John's humble answer.
comments.author: Ammonius of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The Baptist's answers separate the prophet from the Christ, treat his own baptism as bodily, and point to the unseen divine Christ who comes after him.
comments.comment:
The prophet is one thing, while they suppose something else regarding the Christ. These indeed sinned by dividing the prophet from Christ.

But the Baptist answered correctly that he was not the prophet, saying the same thing, which he first answered by declaring 'I am not the Christ', even though he clearly did not teach them that the Christ and the prophet are the same (John 1:25, 27). They speak obstructively to John, 'Why then do you baptize?', as if they did not know that not even the Christ himself, being the prophet, was baptizing, but his disciples. Even Elijah, during the time of Ahab, did not baptize the wood of the altar with washing, but commanded the priests to do this.

Regarding 'Why then do you baptize?', John presents his own baptism as bodily; but regarding 'If you are not the Christ', he speaks a glorification of the preceding essence of Christ, saying that he is invisible by divinity, present to the whole world. He also exposes their lowly opinion concerning Christ and joins the 'In the beginning' Word to his incarnation, connecting the unknown with 'he who comes after me' (John 1:27).

He shows the superiority of Christ toward himself through 'I am not worthy' …
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: The Baptist's “there stands one among you whom you do not know” shows that the Son of God is present everywhere, not confined to Jesus' visible body.
comments.comment: John the Baptist, prophesying that the Son of God would very soon appear, not as one confined to that body and soul but as one who reaches everywhere, says of him: “Among you stands one whom you do not know, who comes after me” (John 1:26–27). If, then, he had thought that the Son of God was only where the visible body of Jesus was, how could he have said, “Among you stands one whom you do not know”?
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Animal sacrifices could not remove sin, but Christ, the true Lamb, offered himself and, being worth more than all, freed the whole world from sin and death.
comments.comment: The worship under the Law was of no use to those on earth for taking away sin, since the sacrifices of oxen and the slaughter of sheep were not what God wanted. So the true Lamb, “who takes away the sin of the world” (John 1:29), offered himself for us “as a fragrant aroma” (Ephesians 5:2). Then, having endured death in the flesh, he set the whole world under heaven free from both death and sin. For One who outweighs all in worth suffered for all, so that he might rule and reign over all.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why Christ is “the Lamb” who takes away sin, against the sacrifices of the Law.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Christ is the Lamb who always takes away sin, he ranks before John, and he is called “man” for several reasons, chiefly as the Church's bridegroom.
comments.comment:
He is a lamb as given for forgiveness of sins of those being regenerated “through washing of rebirth” (Titus 3:5); and by saying “taking away” he shows that he always takes away.

[John 1:30] Christ came to be before John as loosing “the sin of the world” and baptizing in the Holy Spirit, John’s baptism being mere water. He is called “man” as born of a woman “according to the flesh,” or because he was thirty years old (for they call a man him who has entered that time), or because he was perfect in every practical and contemplative virtue, or because he is bridegroom of every rational nature, that is of the church. As the church has the face of a woman, Christ is called man as betrothing the souls of the faithful.

[John 1:31] For the sake of proclaiming Christ and making him evident to the people John baptized.
comments.selected_reason: Explains “taketh away” (always), why Christ ranks before John, and why he is called “a man”.
comments.author: Ammonius of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The Spirit's visible descent was for our sake, and John's “I knew him not” makes his witness trustworthy.
comments.comment:
This is said by way of economy; for it [the Spirit] is inseparable from the Son as also from the Father; for to see something of the Trinity sensibly is impossible.

[John 1:33] As living in the deserts from first age he establishes the unsuspiciousness of the witness, as having learned him through revelation.
comments.author: Ammonius of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The Word did not need the Spirit; he received the Spirit as man for our sake, so that it might rest on us, yet he gives the Spirit as God.
comments.comment:
“And John testified saying: I have watched the Spirit descending as a dove from heaven, and it remained on him… this is the one who baptizes in the Holy Spirit… this is the Son of God.” (John 1:32–34) … what then shall we say, the Holy Spirit having flown down on him from heaven? Shall we suspect that the Word from God the Father has needed to share in the Holy Spirit? … For the Spirit is his own, just as it is also the Father’s… So it is impious even only to suspect that the Word from God the Father himself has needed participation in the Spirit.

How then did the Spirit fly down on him? For he receives in a human way… For he receives not rather for himself, but for us… having descended on him as on a firstfruit of the second race, so that it may settle and rest again in us… Yet even if he receives in a human way for us, see him giving in a divine way: “for on whomever you see the Spirit descending… this is the one who baptizes in the Holy Spirit.” And this is a divine operation; for our Lord Jesus Christ puts the Father’s Spirit into those baptized as his own Spirit (Galatians 4:6) (Romans 8:9).
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the Spirit descended on the Word who did not need it.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On the True Faith, to the Empresses Pulcheria and Eudocia

comments.capsule: John repeats “Behold the Lamb of God” because a good teacher repeats words to fix them in slow hearers.
comments.comment:
This is found the third day from when the Pharisees made their meeting with John, in which they asked him who he is.

[John 1:36] Because of the hearers’ slackness he uses the same words; for it is a teacher’s virtue to use the same so that the words may be fixed in the hearers’ souls.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why John repeats “Behold the Lamb of God”.
comments.author: Ammonius of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Jesus turns to his followers out of kindness and asks what they seek to draw them into talk, and staying in a house does not mean he owned one.
comments.comment:
Since those following Christ cannot overtake him, he turns toward them condescendingly, showing them his face, that they may know that he is the one who fills “the law” and teaches the things in it.

He asks not as not knowing, but calling them into conversation.

[John 1:39] This is not contrary to what was said: “the Son of Man has nowhere to lay his head” (Matthew 8:20); for even if he remained in a house, he did not acquire his own lodging.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why Jesus turned, why he asked “What seek ye?”, and where he stayed.
comments.author: Ammonius of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Jesus praised Nathanael as a true Israelite because, knowing the prophecy that the Christ would be born in Bethlehem, he was not carried away by Philip's news.
comments.comment:
All the prophets foretold that Christ would come not from Nazareth, but from Bethlehem, and would be born there. For it is written: “And you, Bethlehem, land of Judah, are by no means least among the rulers of Judah; for out of you shall come a ruler who will shepherd my people Israel” (Micah 5:2). …

For this reason, when Nathanael said to Philip—because Philip had said, “We have found Jesus of Nazareth”—“Can anything good come from Nazareth?” Christ says of him: “Behold, truly an Israelite in whom there is no deceit” (John 1:45-47). And why did he praise him? Because he was not carried away by Philip’s announcement, but knew clearly and precisely that Christ was not to be born in Nazareth or in Galilee, but in Judea and in Bethlehem—which is indeed what happened. Since Philip was ignorant of this, but Nathanael, being learned in the law, answered according to what had been said in the ancient prophecy, knowing that Christ would not come from Nazareth, for this reason Christ says: “Behold, truly an Israelite in whom there is no deceit.”
comments.selected_reason: Explains why Nathanael doubted and why Jesus praised him as an Israelite without guile.
comments.author: John Chrysostom

comments.capsule: Nathanael doubted because Scripture placed the Christ's birth in Bethlehem, though Jesus was raised in Nazareth.
comments.comment: “The one you announced to me as good news,” he says, “how is it possible that the Christ be from Nazareth, whom Scripture said would come from Bethlehem?” But there in Bethlehem he was born, and Nazareth was recorded as fatherland as reared there and living until full age.
comments.author: Ammonius of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Christ's praise of Nathanael's guileless heart moved him to confess Jesus as Son of God, though still only as king of Israel.
comments.comment:
Great glory and boast it is to have from the truth itself—that is Christ—witness of a pure heart, which sees God with the mind and is led toward saving faith to run to Christ without guile …

[John 1:49] Nathanael was wholly ready. Therefore persuaded from this bare saying alone he confessed him to be the Christ, who is Son of God by nature and truth and king of the truly faithful; for still incomplete he did not call him king of creation, but only of Israel according to what was said: “And the Lord’s portion became his people Jacob, the measured inheritance of his inheritance Israel” (Deuteronomy 32:9).
comments.selected_reason: Explains Christ's praise of Nathanael and why Nathanael says “King of Israel”.
comments.author: Ammonius of Alexandria

comments.capsule: “Amen” stresses certainty, the angels serving Jesus show he is more than a man, and “Son of man” shows his humanity was real.
comments.comment:
Sometimes simply, sometimes doubled, the Savior uses “Amen,” presenting the firmness of what is said. The word is Hebrew, declaring “so be it” that you be found faithful so as to see heaven opened and what follows. Not sensibly, he says, is it possible to see heaven opened, but only by mind that watches the angels approaching to serve Jesus. “Amen” is also said for “truly and really,” which is better here.

Since Nathanael named Christ king of Israel alone, he teaches him through this that Christ was not a bare man, since somehow angels serve him.

He shows through this [the title “Son of man”] that not by appearance but in truth he became man. Incarnate from Mary as alone sinless he preserved for himself the “according to the image” which the first man had who came to be “according to the image and according to likeness” of God (Genesis 1:26).
comments.selected_reason: Explains “Verily, verily”, the angels serving Jesus, and the title “Son of man”.
comments.author: Ammonius of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Heaven, shut since the fall, was opened in Christ, and the angels now go up and down in his service for our salvation.
comments.comment: Long ago, when we were ruined, heaven was shut, and the angels took no account of any of us, as if sharing the Master of all’s indignation at the insult. But when God was pleased “to sum up all things in Christ,” [Ephesians 1:10] he came to earth, brought the holy angels down, and appointed them guardians of our life (Matthew 18:10). That is why he also said, “You will see heaven opened, and the angels of God ascending and descending on the Son of Man” (John 1:51) — “of Man,” that is, for the sake of the human. Heaven, shut in the times already past, he opened for us, so that running up and down for our sake they might be servants of the economy [God's plan of salvation] accomplished for us through Christ.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why heaven is “opened” and what the angels' ascending and descending means.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: By attending the wedding Jesus sanctified marriage and its children, showing he ordained it at creation.
comments.comment: The Lord came to the wedding that he might sanctify not only those living but also those about to be born, showing that he from the beginning ordained marriage, having given Eve to Adam, and that he might put to shame certain heretics who slander marriage.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why Jesus came to a wedding at all.
comments.author: Ammonius of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Jesus speaks to his mother as God, who has no mother, and his "hour" is the cross, where as a man he acknowledged her.
comments.comment:
…Nor does what he said force us to deny Christ's mother: "Woman, what have you to do with me? My hour has not yet come" (John 2:4). Rather, it warns us to understand that according to his divinity he had no mother, for he was preparing to reveal the person of his majesty when he turned water into wine.

But he was crucified according to his humanity, and that was the hour which had not yet come when he said, "What have you to do with me? My hour has not yet come"—that is, the hour in which I will acknowledge you. For then, as a man crucified, he recognized his mother and most humanely entrusted her to his beloved disciple.…
comments.selected_reason: Explains the hard saying 'What have you to do with me?' and what 'my hour' means.
comments.author: Augustine of Hippo

comments.capsule: Jesus checks his mother's untimely prompting: he is also God, and his hour of revelation has not come.
comments.comment: He rebukes the mother for untimely reminding a God who needs no reminder—as if to say, do not think me to be only man, but also God. The time of my manifestation has not yet come; it is not yet known who I am. …
comments.selected_reason: Explains 'mine hour is not yet come' as the hour of his self-revelation.
comments.author: Ammonius of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Jesus would not rush into public signs before people sought him as teacher and savior, yet his mother, trusting he would yield to her, told the servants to obey him.
comments.comment:
The Lord does not move too hastily into the work of manifest signs (John 2:4), since he had not yet taken the rank of a public teacher or a preacher of manifest things. For it was necessary that he be approached as a teacher and pursued as a savior to obtain healings, because it is also fitting that the one praying should approach the fulfillment of the need. Therefore, he says that his hour for signs—that is, according to reason and according to what is fitting—must not pass.

The mother knew the Lord as becoming a son to her through persuasion (John 2:4). And indeed her response demonstrated this: 'What to me and to you, woman?' (John 2:4). For, being able to be offended, he answered in such a way as God's speech toward Moses was: 'Leave me,' [Exodus 32:10] meaning he was able to be offended and to persuade. Knowing indeed that he was staying toward her in faith, and seeing from the response that he was drawing near to the worthiness of the ministers, she commands them to do what he orders [John 2:5].
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: The Maker of vines turned this water into wine.
comments.comment: He who by water waters the vine and makes it bear wine is himself the one who also now changes the water into wine.
comments.selected_reason: Shows the miracle as the Creator's own work, in terms anyone can follow.
comments.author: Ammonius of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The disciples already admired Jesus as holy, but the sign showed them power beyond a human, so they believed in him as God.
comments.comment:
“This beginning of the signs Jesus did in Cana of Galilee, and he manifested his glory, and his disciples believed into him.” (John 2:11) When the sign had therefore happened, and Christ had manifested his glory, into whom have the blessed disciples believed? Into a holy human simply? And yet even before the sign they followed him, marveling at him as holy. But through the sign they have seen him having power and authority beyond a human. Therefore they have believed as into God.

And one must know that many of the saints have done many wonders and were marveled at, yet no one believed into them.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what changed in the disciples' faith when they 'believed' after the first sign.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On the True Faith, to the Princesses Arcadia and Marina

comments.capsule: Whether or not his first miracle ever, the Cana sign revealed his glory and opened the disciples' faith.
comments.comment:
Some say this the first sign in Cana, but not first of all. Some indeed say the wedding in Cana the first sign, but first of all.

He opened them a door of faith through the divine signs, revealing himself—that is, his glory and power.
comments.author: Ammonius of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Jesus replaced the law's sacrifices with spiritual worship, calls God his own Father by nature, and wants a trade in spiritual goods.
comments.comment:
He cast out the things sacrificed according to law, that he might bring in spiritual worship in their place.

[John 2:16] Christ calls God his own Father as himself alone existing from him according to nature.

The house of God is a house of merchandise, but not of these fleshly things that go “into the belly,” [Matthew 15:17] but of spiritual goods.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why Jesus cleared the temple and why he says 'my Father's house'.
comments.author: Ammonius of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Allegorically, Jesus drives from the Church those who traffic in the Spirit's gifts, and his whip of cords shows that sinners are punished by their own sins.
comments.comment: Allegorically, regarding those who have come through shamelessness to provoke the silver which belongs to the Word of God (John 2:13-16), and moreover selling the gifts of the Spirit—pigeons named as such because they have a natural affinity for the Holy Spirit who, in the form of a pigeon, descended upon the Savior, casting out from the church of God—it is also good to say that the scourge of Jesus being made of ropes, by which he drove everyone out, occurred; for since through which things one weaves a rope, he is punished in sinning. Appropriately this has been written: for sins are called ropes [Proverbs 5:22].
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: The whip warns those who cling to the law's worship that a spirit of slavery earns a slave's punishment.
comments.comment: Another evangelist says Jesus also “made a whip of cords,” (Matthew 21:12–13) (John 2:15) threatened blows, and raised it against them. Those who honor legal worship needed to know, after the truth was shown, that having a “spirit of slavery” (Romans 8:15) and refusing to be freed, they will be under scourges and subject to slavish punishment.…
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Though Scripture says the Father raised Christ, the Son promises to raise his own body, for he is the Father's life-giving power.
comments.comment:
…even if God the Father is said to accomplish something, he does not shut the Son out of his activity over all things. For if all things came into being through him (John 1:3), how could anyone doubt that he worked through the Son the resurrection of that holy body as well?

Indeed the Son, showing himself active in this, said to the Jews, “Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up” (John 2:19). See, then, how he promises to raise his own temple himself, although God the Father is said to have raised it. For since he is himself the life-giving power of God the Father, he gave life to his own temple.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why Jesus says 'I will raise it up' when elsewhere the Father raises him.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Jesus' body is the truest temple, and those who plotted against it could not overcome the Godhead that built it.
comments.comment: …the temple better and more excellent than all those so named was the holy and pure body of our Saviour Jesus. He knew that the temple of the God within him could be plotted against by the impious, yet not in such a way that the purpose of the plotters would be stronger than the Godhead that built the temple. So he says to them: “Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up” (John 2:19). And this “he was saying about the temple of his body” (John 2:21).
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Jesus meant his body, but his accusers, not listening for the speaker's meaning, took him to mean the stone temple.
comments.comment: …the great proof against Jesus was the one his accusers stated: “This man said, ‘I am able to destroy the temple of God and to raise it up in three days’” (Matthew 26:61). For he himself “was speaking of the temple of his body” (John 2:21), while they, not knowing how to hear according to the speaker’s intention, thought that he meant the temple of stone, which the Jews honoured rather than honouring, as was right, the true temple of God the Word, of Wisdom and of Truth.
comments.selected_reason: Explains which temple Jesus meant and why his hearers misunderstood him.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Jesus withheld deep teaching from those whose faith rested on signs and was easily shaken.
comments.comment: To such people [who believed because of signs, John 2:23–24] one must not entrust deep doctrines as if they were already made faithful; for those who believe because of signs are easily shifted, if some men persuade them with sophistry that the signs did not happen rightly.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why Jesus 'did not commit himself' to those who believed because of his signs.
comments.author: Ammonius of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Only God knows what is in the human heart, so Jesus' knowledge of all people shows that he is God.
comments.comment: From John’s Gospel: “But Jesus himself did not entrust himself to them, because he knew all people, and because he had no need that anyone should testify about the human; for he himself knew what was in the human.” (John 2:24–25) Of God it is written that “he who alone forms their hearts” (Psalm 33:15); and he himself says something similar. So if he knows all things and knows what is in the human, how would he not be God as the one who searches hearts and kidneys (Jeremiah 17:10)?
comments.selected_reason: Explains what it means that Jesus 'knew what was in man'.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On the True Faith, to the Princesses Arcadia and Marina

comments.capsule: Nicodemus is at fault for wanting to believe in secret, and Jesus answers his merely human view with heavenly teaching.
comments.comment:
Nicodemus is blameworthy for wanting to be faithful in secret.

Since Nicodemus came to him as to a bare man, wanting to draw him to himself he [Jesus] speaks things beyond man to him as one who is above in the heavens and knows what is done there and brought from there to human beings.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why Jesus answers Nicodemus' polite greeting with teaching about birth from above.
comments.author: Ammonius of Alexandria

comments.capsule: To be born from above is to be reborn through baptism and the Spirit into a heavenly life, and the kingdom of God is the kingdom of heaven.
comments.comment:
Kingdom of God and kingdom of the heavens are the same, because the faithful has dwelling in heaven and “citizenship” (Philippians 3:20), or because such a one is mastered by God who reigns over the heavens.

The one living the upper life of the angels and learning high doctrines through Christ is born from above. The one undergoing the second birth through the washing is born from above, and the one partaking of Holy Spirit. “From above” signifies rebirth through the Spirit and shows that the Spirit is from the Father’s essence; for thus, naming himself also from above, he signifies that he is from the Father’s essence.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what 'born from above' and 'the kingdom of God' mean.
comments.author: Ammonius of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Water and Spirit work together in rebirth: water cleanses the body and pictures burial and resurrection, while the Spirit sanctifies the soul.
comments.comment:
Water cleanses the body and the Spirit sanctifies the invisible soul. Water is taken in the place of a mother, and the Spirit in the place of God who forms. Sensible water is re-elemented toward divine power and sanctifies those in whom rebirth happens.

Water differs from Spirit only in conception, since it is the same in activity; water is a symbol of burial and resurrection, and therefore is necessarily taken. Three immersions and three emergings happen so that we may know that by power of Father and Son and Holy Spirit all is fulfilled.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why rebirth is 'of water and of the Spirit'.
comments.author: Ammonius of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Rebirth is a work of grace, ministered through bodily water.
comments.comment: The Lord lifts him [Nicodemus] up to the true understanding by ascribing the rebirth to grace (John 3:5), which is accomplished through the ministry of water for the body.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: Like begets like: the Father who is spirit begets the Son, Mary's flesh bore true flesh, and believers are remade in spirit through Christ.
comments.comment:
The Father is spirit as God, and the Son is spirit as God; therefore the Spirit, which is God and Father, begets spirit, which is the Son and God. So Christ is consubstantial [of one nature] with the Father according to Godhead and consubstantial with the mother according to flesh, even if Christ is one from both, without change and without confusion.

And according to the word now set out canonically by the Lord, we are reshaped through Christ as our mind is formed into spiritual quality.

If Mary is rational ensouled flesh, her fruit also is consubstantial with her: rational ensouled flesh, and not a phantom or anything other than the flesh that bore—the Word’s flesh having a rational soul, in which “all the fullness of the Godhead dwelt bodily” (Colossians 2:9).
comments.author: Ammonius of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The Spirit speaks through prophets; "our" includes Father and Spirit.
comments.comment:
One hears the voice of the Holy Spirit through the prophets.

[John 3:11] He said “our” as having in himself by nature the Father and the Spirit.
comments.author: Ammonius of Alexandria

comments.capsule: "Earthly things" means baptism, done on earth, compared with the Son's heavenly generation.
comments.comment: He calls baptism earthly though it is divine and spiritual, because it is completed on earth toward sanctification of humans who are on earth. The birth of the washing is called earthly by comparison with the Son’s generation from the Father’s essence.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what Jesus means by 'earthly things' as against 'heavenly things'.
comments.author: Ammonius of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The Son of Man came down from heaven because the Word from God became man and made the properties of his flesh his own.
comments.comment: “If I told you earthly things and you do not believe, how will you believe if I tell you heavenly things? And no one has gone up into heaven except the one who came down from heaven, the Son of Man.” (John 3:12–13) How has the Son of Man come down from heaven? Because the Word from God became human, and what belongs to the flesh is the Word’s own, apart from sin alone.
comments.selected_reason: Explains plainly how the Son of Man 'came down from heaven'.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On the True Faith, to the Princesses Arcadia and Marina

comments.capsule: Christ is one person, so the Son of Man is said to descend from heaven though his body did not.
comments.comment:
…After the hypostatic union [the union of God and man in one person] he makes common the things of flesh and of Godhead according to activities, not by change of the things from which Christ is. Descent and ascent are also activities.

The Lord’s body is not heavenly; for it is subject to passions. And as being one, even with flesh, he is called Son of Man.
comments.author: Ammonius of Alexandria

comments.capsule: "Heaven" here means the state proper to God, which the devil craved and only the Son, who came from it, has entered.
comments.comment:
…Regarding a certain superiority fitting for God by the name of heaven, according to 'the heaven of the heaven belongs to the Lord' (Ps 103:19), becoming later a devil while being in heaven, when he was once a holy one, he said, 'I will ascend into heaven,' as if happening below toward that heaven. Into this so-called heaven no one has ascended [John 3:13] except only the Son of God, since also alone from there He has descended, being called the Son of Man because of the economy [God's plan of salvation].

And even if the angels ascending into heaven and descending by a ladder were seen by Jacob, it is not about the heaven previously mentioned that the vision is said in the Scripture.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Like the bronze serpent, Christ's flesh was real yet sinless, and his lifting up made him known.
comments.comment:
Just as the bronze serpent was not the venomous beast but a likeness, so also the Lord’s flesh. It was flesh in truth, yet not flesh of sin, but likeness of flesh of sin.

Being lifted up declares Christ becoming manifest and notable.
comments.author: Ammonius of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Jesus himself made the serpent hung on wood, not the Passover lamb, the type of his passion.
comments.comment: For the Savior himself says: "As Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, so must the Son of man be lifted up," (John 3:14) according to the type of the serpent hung on the wood by Moses, signifying nothing other than the passion of the Savior insofar as he was hung on wood. It is clear, then, that the passion will be taken according to the type of the serpent and not according to the type of the Passover (Numbers 21:8–9) (Deuteronomy 21:23).
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The bronze serpent pictures the Word made in the likeness of sinful humans yet life-giving as God, so whoever looks to him in faith conquers death.
comments.comment:
“And just as Moses lifted up the serpent in the desert, so must the Son of Man be lifted up, so that everyone who believes in him may have eternal life.” (John 3:14–15) The serpents were biting those of Israel in the desert; then the God of all commanded Moses to set up a bronze serpent: “And it shall be,” he says, “if a serpent bites a human, and he looks toward the serpent, he shall also live.” (Numbers 21:8–9) What then is the riddle? And why is the one who looks at the serpent saved?

Therefore the Only-begotten Word of God, existing as life by nature, became in the likeness that is as we are—that is, human (Romans 8:3); and the human is evil and as it were the serpent; yet even if he became as we are, if someone looks to him, he conquers death. And what is it to look to him, except precisely to understand carefully the mystery upon him? For then one will see him in the likeness of the evil ones—that is, of humans—yet life-giving as God, and making the bites of the evil serpents vanish. So there is one Lord and Son, the same one, both life-giving as God and in the form of the evil ones through economy.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the bronze serpent is a fitting picture of the crucified Christ.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On the True Faith, to the Princesses Arcadia and Marina

comments.capsule: God "gave" his Son in that the Son's own flesh died while he stayed beyond suffering as God, and "only-begotten" means a true Son, not merely something unique.
comments.comment:
Here again he makes the whole common, knowing no separation after the union; for when the flesh was sacrificed for the world’s life and given to death, the Son is said to have been given to death though remaining impassible [unable to suffer] as God, only his own flesh suffering what is proper when he permitted and willed.

The Arians say the Son is called only-begotten because he alone came to be from God. To them one must say that some also call the sun only-begotten inasmuch as it alone is sun, yet it is no longer also a son.
comments.author: Ammonius of Alexandria

comments.capsule: God's love is proved by the gift of his Son, who took flesh in order to die, defeat death and Satan, and lift the ancient curse.
comments.comment:
…Our Lord Jesus Christ, making plain the truly admirable love of God the Father which he showed toward us, brought forward as proof the goal of his work in the flesh and his suffering on the cross, saying somewhere: “For God so loved the world that he gave his only-begotten Son, so that everyone who believes in him should not perish but have eternal life” (John 3:16). For he truly gave his own Son for us; and we have been redeemed, set free from death and sin.

For the Word “became flesh and dwelt among us” (John 1:14) for no other reason than this: that by enduring the death of the flesh he might triumph over the rulers and authorities (Colossians 2:15) and destroy “the one who has the power of death, that is,” Satan (Hebrews 2:14); that he might do away with corruption and, with it, remove the sin that had tyrannized over us; and that he might thus make powerless from then on that ancient curse which human nature underwent in Adam, as in the firstfruits of the race and as in its first root.…
comments.selected_reason: Explains what God's 'giving' of the Son was for.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Scripture calls Christ not just "only-begotten" but the only-begotten Son, which no unique creature, such as the sun, can be called.
comments.comment:
…it is not the same thing to be something 'only-begotten' and to be an only-begotten offspring or an only-begotten Son. Therefore, these things said to others as 'only-begotten' are not said with the addition of 'Son,' or 'from the Father,' or 'offspring.' But the Savior, if He is ever so named, is called with such an addition: 'and we beheld His glory, a glory as of the only-begotten from the Father' (John 1:14). And the one who is the only-begotten Son from the Father is the Father's only. And again: 'so God loved the world that He gave His only-begotten Son' (John 3:16).

I say: since there is an only-begotten Son, it is impossible for there to be another son belonging to that only-begotten Son. And nothing of the creatures is only-begotten; for even if the sun were only-begotten, it is not an only-begotten creature, nor an only-begotten work, but an only-begotten sun. So also among humans we say 'only-begotten child,' not because he is the only one that exists, but because he is the only one to that parent.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Christ came first to save, not to condemn; unbelievers are already condemned and need no further trial, like the devil.
comments.comment:
If Christ had come to judge the world, he would have condemned all. But first he came to save the world. He judges incidentally those who rebelled—not as Moses’ law came to condemn the world, but to save.

Note that universally everyone not believing in Christ is condemned, to be handed over to punishment. Therefore these are not even led to judgment as already condemned. So also of the devil: “the ruler of this world has been judged” (John 16:11)—not only because he did not believe, but also because he tempted the Lord and “entered into Judas” (Luke 22:3) to hand him over to death.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why Christ did not come to condemn and what 'condemned already' means.
comments.author: Ammonius of Alexandria

comments.capsule: "Already judged" is Scripture's way of speaking of a sentence still to come, since every believer was once an unbeliever.
comments.comment: …Scripture’s practice of calling condemned someone still to be condemned. Thus the Lord says in the Gospel: ‘Everyone who has not believed in me is already judged, because he has not believed in the name of God’s only-begotten (John 3:18) Son’ (John 3:18). This does not mean that unbelief denying Christ was already joined to eternal punishment before the time of judgment, since everyone who comes to faith was formerly an unbeliever. Rather, to display the lawgiver’s judgment, sins are spoken of as already punishments.
comments.author: Julian of Eclanum

comments.capsule: People reject the light not from ignorance or by necessity of nature but because they love their evil deeds and fear exposure.
comments.comment:
…Those who loved the darkness rather than the light are without defense (John 3:19); for it is not through ignorance that they do not believe in Christ, but because they want to do base things, which the teaching of Christ does not accept.

Therefore, when we hear that 'they were not able to believe' (John 3:19), let us not understand a power of nature or some other dominance, but the self-tyrannical thought that enslaves itself to shameful passions and does not want to depart from the worst habit; for these indeed recognize the light, but they do not come to it, so that their hypocrisy might not be exposed—those who say they know God but deny him by their works.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why people 'loved darkness rather than light'.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: Jesus "baptized" through his disciples' hands, and their baptism, like John's, led the crowds to Christ before the Spirit was given.
comments.comment:
He himself did not baptize, but his disciples, since he baptized in Spirit and it was not yet time for the Spirit’s gift before the passion. He was already handing over the evangelical baptism, which differed much from John’s; for Christ baptized through the apostles’ hand, as he clearly says in what follows [John 4:2].

Neither John’s baptism nor the disciples’ supplied the Holy Spirit, but so that they might not go around person by person proclaiming Christ, they established baptism to lead the crowds running to them toward Christ.
comments.selected_reason: Explains in what sense Jesus 'baptized' (John 3:22) though John 4:2 says he did not baptize in person.
comments.author: Ammonius of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The dispute arose by God's design so that John could show how his baptism differed from Christ's.
comments.comment:
…John’s baptism gave forgiveness of voluntary sins to those truly repenting, and Christ’s of all sins, and also supplied Holy Spirit and the dignity of adoption.

A dispute arose economically [by God's plan] while John still lived, so that through his voice the difference of the baptisms might appear.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the dispute about purifying arose and how the two baptisms differed.
comments.author: Ammonius of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Christ is the bridegroom and the church his bride, joined to him in baptism, and the bridal door stays open until the end.
comments.comment:
Christ is bridegroom and the church bride and the bridal chamber the place of baptism, where spiritual joining happens, since all is bright and full of joy and gladness. For what is more blessed than to be cleansed of sins and cleave to God and “become partaker of divine nature” (2 Peter 1:4) through sharing the Holy Spirit? These are the earnest [pledge]; the more perfect things are in the future, when the bridegroom enters again and brings with him the virgin souls and the bridal door is shut and only those inside enjoy the gladness and no one enters there anymore. So as long as today’s age, or each one’s particular death, the bridal door is open to souls willing to be betrothed to Christ.

Through baptism Christ betroths the church reborn. This spiritual yoke joins to God through the teaching word.
