The bride is a pure virgin through rightness of doctrines; she is also Christ’s wife as bearing good deeds not from herself but through Christ who sows in her—of whom none of the generated can be bridegroom, since none of them is primarily giver of goods. So every rational nature of angels and humans is bride.
comments.selected_reason: Explains who the bridegroom and the bride are in the Baptist's saying.
comments.author: Ammonius of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Christ grows by being revealed; John fades like a star at sunrise.
comments.comment:
Neither does Christ increase nor John decrease, but like a morning star John is covered by the intelligible sun.

Christ as God increases the more he is manifested; but I must remain in what I am.
comments.selected_reason: Explains in what sense Christ 'increases' and John 'decreases'.
comments.author: Ammonius of Alexandria

comments.capsule: John shrank only by comparison with Jesus' greater teaching and life.
comments.comment: Regarding the saying, 'That He must increase and I must decrease,' John was not diminishing in terms of actual magnitude, but was comparing himself to the superiority of Jesus's teaching and way of life (John 3:30).…
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Christ "comes from above" not by moving from place to place but by stooping to us while remaining in the Father, and so he is above all.
comments.comment:
Saying “coming” does not signify transfer from above to below, but that always remaining in the Father above he comes by a relation of condescension to those over whom he is. So when he says coming, he speaks as about God; when he says having come, he speaks as about man, since he himself is God and man.

The one who is from the Father’s root has by nature the Father’s superiority, being above all things made as their God and maker.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what 'he that cometh from above' means without implying movement in space.
comments.author: Ammonius of Alexandria

comments.capsule: He speaks humanly of hearing, and "no man receives" expresses amazement at unbelief.
comments.comment:
He speaks more humanly because of the flesh; for being all-perfect by nature he knows all from himself.

He did not say this as of some not persuaded, but as marveling at the madness of unbelievers.
comments.author: Ammonius of Alexandria

comments.capsule: No one receives Christ's testimony in its full greatness, yet beginners can still receive it in part, so the two verses do not conflict.
comments.comment:
‘And no one receives his testimony’ [John 3:32] — and yet many have received his testimony, as John himself goes on to add, saying: ‘He who has received his testimony has set his seal that God is true.’ [John 3:33] But how can it be true, when some do receive his testimony, that ‘no one receives his testimony’? The difficulty must be resolved as follows.

Jesus, having come from above and speaking what he heard and saw, speaks a most lofty and very great testimony concerning the Father and himself; and no one receives this testimony as he himself speaks it, because the hearers, who are only beginning to receive, fall far short of the greatness of the testimony.

Yet even though no one is able to receive his testimony in this way, it is still possible to receive it as those just now coming to faith are able to receive it. Hence ‘he who received his testimony’ is not at odds with no one’s having received it…
comments.selected_reason: Resolves the apparent clash between 'no man receiveth his testimony' and the next verse.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: To set one's seal is to be fully assured; the Son is "sent" by taking flesh, and unlike the saints he has the whole Spirit and gives it.
comments.comment:
[“Set his seal,” John 3:33] means he was fully assured and has proof and seal.

[John 3:34] The Son is said to be sent from the Father either because of the enfleshed presence or because the Father, having the Son in himself, did not hide him but shone him forth from his own nature as “radiance” from light (Hebrews 1:3); for the Son has come out into his own existence even while he is in him by nature.

As spring of the Spirit he gives it. He means the Spirit’s activity, which humans receive by measure; for he himself has the whole complete. The Son has the whole Spirit essentially, not partly as a creature. Therefore he himself also gives it, while the saints by entreaty make Christ supply the Spirit through them.
comments.selected_reason: Explains 'God giveth not the Spirit by measure unto him'.
comments.author: Ammonius of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The Father loves the Son by nature and puts all things in his hand, meaning his own power, while God's wrath means unending torment.
comments.comment:
Even if the Father loves “the world,” it is not as he loves the Son, whom he loves exceedingly because of natural generation as his own Word and wisdom and sanctification.

This [all things given into his hand] is fulfilled when at the time of the second presence “every knee” bends to him (Philippians 2:10), having cast off the evil they have. Here he calls hand the power which the Son has by nature and not by participation, as every good is essentially in the Father and conceived in power as the Son. He also receives as man the authority he had before the incarnation.

[John 3:36] Wrath of God is being in continual torments, which is harder than every death.
comments.selected_reason: Explains 'hath given all things into his hand' and 'the wrath of God abideth on him'.
comments.author: Ammonius of Alexandria

comments.capsule: All things come into the Son's hand once cleansed of evil, and refusing to believe in a life one can see is the graver fault.
comments.comment:
…since in all these things there are also things becoming worse, one understands how these things can exist in the hand of the Son [John 3:35], having clearly cast off the malice which they had and having taken up virtue…

But it is not the same to not have life as to not see it; this is made clear from 'you shall see life in front of your eyes' and 'you shall by no means believe' (Jn 3:36). If someone were to seek this, what is worse? Whether not seeing life and not believing in it, or not having life but seeing it? And one might say that the one lacking either is more inferior than the one having the one. Another might say it is a lesser evil not to see life and to disbelieve in it; for there will be forgiveness to such a one having this. But rather it is to be blamed when one is not believing in life, even if he is sufficient to see it, the beauty of it drawing him toward agreement.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Jesus, who knows all, acts at the fitting time, and the disciples' baptizing is credited to him because it was done with his consent.
comments.comment:
Even if he knows all as God, it is also of God-fitting economy to do something at the right time and then seem to learn when there is need.

[John 4:2] Whatever subordinates do by consent of leaders who see and do not contradict or hinder, the leaders are said to do; for first saying that Jesus “baptized,” here he says that Jesus himself did not baptize, assigning the disciples’ act to him in power even if he did not do the baptism in activity.…
comments.selected_reason: Explains how Jesus can be said to baptize (John 3:22, 4:1) though 'Jesus himself baptized not'.
comments.author: Ammonius of Alexandria

comments.capsule: He went to bless the nations.
comments.comment: He came there that before the passion he might benefit the nations through the evangelical proclamation.
comments.author: Ammonius of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Jesus was truly tired because the Word took a real body like ours, though as God he could not suffer.
comments.comment:
The Samaritans were neighbors of the Jews; that is why they also drank from Jacob's spring. Though they were by race of the Medes and Persians, they claimed Jacob as their own.

Since "the Word became flesh" (John 1:14), it follows that he grew weary from the hard road taken at midday. Midday is the bright season of his appearing; for he had a body like ours, composed of the same things as ours, apart only from a man's intercourse. Therefore he was subject not only to toil but also to thirst and wounds, because he let the body remain within the natural limits of humanity, lest it seem a phantom. As one Christ with his own flesh he makes the sufferings of humanity his own, though as God he remained impassible [unable to suffer].
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the Son of God was 'wearied' at the well.
comments.author: Ammonius of Alexandria

comments.capsule: John calls it a spring and the woman calls it a deep well, because knowledge is a spring to the pure and a deep well to beginners.
comments.comment: …Knowledge is both a well and a spring; for to those approaching, virtue seems to be a deep well, but to the dispassionate and the pure, it is a spring; even so the Savior sat by the spring, when it was about the sixth hour (John 4:6); and the Samaritan woman calls it a well; for she says, 'Lord, you have nothing to draw with, and the well is deep' (John 4:11).…
comments.author: Evagrius Ponticus

comments.capsule: Jesus asks for water in order to give living water, setting aside the scruples that kept Jews from touching foreigners.
comments.comment:
He asks the Samaritan woman—the shadow of the law—that he may give her "living water" (John 4:10), just as he asks faith of everyone, that he may grant what is beyond speech. By this he teaches contempt for Jewish scruples, showing that "what enters the mouth does not defile a person" (Matthew 15:11).

How did she perceive that he was a Jew? Either from his appearance or from his speech. Because the law had said, "Do not touch what is unclean," they did not dare even to touch the flesh of foreigners, thinking they would be polluted by it.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why Jesus asked her for a drink and why she was surprised.
comments.author: Ammonius of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Living water is Christ's word and Spirit; the "gift of God" is the Word's coming.
comments.comment: The Lord's sayings are a drink of immortality—the life-giving gift of the Spirit, by which human beings live again. The gift of God is the Word's sojourn among people, which came by the Father's grace and which waters the soul.
comments.selected_reason: Explains 'the gift of God' and 'living water'.
comments.author: Ammonius of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The old Scripture needed the gospel after it, but the gospel needs no successor, so whoever drinks it never thirsts again.
comments.comment: The old Scripture needs the evangelical teaching that succeeds it; for the new has no successor, since the gospel's instruction keeps flowing and lifts the one who drinks into life. This is a pledge of the coming resurrection, not allowing the one who has drunk it to fall into sin that leads to death.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the one who drinks Christ's water 'shall never thirst'.
comments.author: Ammonius of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Earthly water quenches thirst briefly, but the Spirit's water gives lasting life, unlike the law learned by letters, though the woman still thought of material water.
comments.comment:
This, he says, the perceptible water will heal the thirst for a little while (John 4:13-16), but the invisible, just as it delivers from thirst, no longer leaves men in need of life; for it springs forth incorruption for them. This, that the Holy Spirit is promised as a gift through the following, is evident.

Therefore, there is an examination of the so-called spiritual water against material water, and also of the gift of the Spirit against the teaching of the law. For one was learning through letters, which man always needs because of forgetfulness, but the Spirit of wisdom provides a continuous supply. Having heard these things, the Samaritan woman remained upon the material concept and, passing over the small things as great, remained unfeeling toward the great things.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: We eat Christ by good deeds and drink him by true knowledge, and those he satisfies still long for more without ever lacking.
comments.comment:
…since it is necessary not only to come to him through deed, but also to believe scientifically the things true according to theory, someone drinks from him 'living water' (John 4:14) from the spring and from the vine (John 15:1) wine gladdening the 'heart of man.' Therefore, receiving according to practical virtue we eat, but according to the intellectual we drink, as having been filled and never having thirsted from him.

And if 'blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness' (Matt 5:6) seems contrary, it is by no means a disagreement; for if someone, having eaten of this bread and having drunk of the immortal drink, does not hunger nor thirst, but nonetheless, because of the lovely and worthy food and the drink, having been satisfied, still hungers and drinks, so as to be always filled and to hunger.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Christ's water leaps up to the drinker by itself, so it gives rest, nourishing and cleansing the soul.
comments.comment:
The 'water of rest' can be said because the one drinking it does not grow weary; for 'the one drinking' (John 4:14) 'from the water which I will give' (John 4:14) will have 'a spring leaping into eternal life' (John 4:14). The water is not moving downward, but it comes toward the drinker by leaping itself. Hence it is 'water of rest.'

This water serves for nourishing and for cleansing. And since the soul being cleansed casts out sin—for this was compared to a 'talent of lead'—the water provides rest. It casts out both thirst and filth.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Jesus asked for her husband in order to draw the Samaritan nation to faith through him as well.
comments.comment: But the Lord, at least until these things, spoke toward the woman, desiring to lead the Samaritan nation to faith by joining to the call toward her the call toward the man. In this it is shown toward the knowledge of the word that the nature of a better man is more suitable than that of the woman, who was not reaching the spiritual teachings of the Lord.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: Jesus exposed her life to reveal his deity, and she then asked him, as a prophet, where one must worship.
comments.comment: For this reason he said to her, "Call your husband" (John 4:16): that by convicting her of lying he might show her his own deity. They say that on that mountain Abraham offered Isaac, which the Samaritan woman pointed out to the Lord; so she asks him as a prophet where one must worship.
comments.author: Ammonius of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Jerusalem was only the meeting place for the feasts; "the hour" is Christ's coming, after which God is worshipped everywhere.
comments.comment: Not that God is only in Jerusalem, but that gathered there together they may keep the appointed feasts and sacrifices in harmony. He calls his own sojourn "the hour," since God, being spirit, is not bounded by place. Each person fittingly worships from his own place; for worship confined to a place is rather an insult.
comments.selected_reason: Explains 'the hour cometh' and why worship is no longer tied to Jerusalem.
comments.author: Ammonius of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Jesus taught that God, who is spirit, is to be worshipped with the mind, not with bodily rites and sacrifices.
comments.comment: So it is, then, with “God is spirit” (John 4:24). Since both Samaritans and Jews were carrying out the commands of the law in a bodily way and in figures, the Saviour said to the Samaritan woman: “The hour is coming when neither in Jerusalem nor on this mountain will they worship the Father” (John 4:21); “God is spirit, and those who worship him must worship in spirit and truth” (John 4:24). By these words he taught that God must be worshipped not in the flesh and with fleshly sacrifices, but “in spirit.” Indeed, he himself may be thought of as “spirit” in keeping with the way one serves him “in spirit” and with the mind.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Salvation is from the Jews because Christ took flesh from them and they first knew the one God, and he says "we worship" as man.
comments.comment:
He said "salvation is from the Jews" (John 4:22) because he took flesh from them, or because from them the world began to know the one God through the law and the prophets. By comparison, the word of truth was then practiced among Jews.

He said "we worship" toward the woman's suspicion; for of those who are worshipped he is God, even if, as man by economy [God's plan of salvation], he said "we worship."
comments.selected_reason: Explains 'salvation is of the Jews' and why Jesus includes himself in 'we worship'.
comments.author: Ammonius of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Jesus, whose name means salvation, is himself the salvation that came from the Jews according to the flesh.
comments.comment: “You worship what you do not know; we worship what we know, for salvation is from the Jews.” (John 4:22) Do you hear that he says salvation is from the Jews? Yet we have enrolled God as Savior. For he has saved us “not an elder, not an angel, but the Lord himself,” (Isaiah 63:9) according to the Scriptures. He is named Christ Jesus, having come to be from the Jews according to the flesh; and Jesus is interpreted “salvation.” So he himself is the salvation from the Jews. Therefore even if the Word has become flesh and has taken hold of Abraham’s seed, he is God also with the flesh (Hebrews 2:16).
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On the True Faith, to the Princesses Arcadia and Marina

comments.capsule: True worship offers virtue from the mind in any place, and God is "spirit" as bodiless, life-giving being, not as wind.
comments.comment:
True worshippers in every place offer God spiritual sacrifices—that is, virtue and godliness. So the law came into being for the sake of the gospel, and the condescension of the shadow was allowed for the sake of the coming truth. "In spirit and truth" (John 4:23–24): by spirit he means the intelligible part of the human being, which by relation and disposition before God worships God as the angels do; worship in a place is not worship in spirit and truth.

God is called spirit not as wind, but as bodiless and life-giving substance; for as we live by breathing air, so we live when God gives what supplies life. God is spirit with respect to bodiless nature.…
comments.selected_reason: Explains 'in spirit and in truth' and 'God is a Spirit'.
comments.author: Ammonius of Alexandria

comments.capsule: God is called spirit as bodiless, life-giving being, and worship "in spirit and truth" replaces the letter and the types of the law.
comments.comment:
Since God is invisible, and the incorporeal immediately follows the invisible, God being incorporeal is therefore invisible.…

Therefore, being called light because it enlightens not sight, but intellect, not the body, but is a spiritual light; and being called love, it is not a disposition, but a loving essence that creates and provides for things; so being called spirit, it presents not wind, but an incorporeal and life-giving essence [John 4:24].

Everyone who has learned that God is spirit worships him spiritually with spirit and truth, no longer in a ritualistic way, the God of all things. In contrast to the letter, it says 'in spirit', while regarding the type, it says 'and in truth'; for these things were necessary until a certain time, but when the truth has come, that is the presence of Christ, all things have ceased.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Jesus openly told the simple woman what he hid from scheming Jews, and the disciples marveled at his humility but trusted his judgment.
comments.comment:
What he did not say to Jews who asked with guile—"I am he" (John 4:26)—he said to the woman, who was simpler; and he did not set before her anything from Moses to establish what concerned him, since she was unused to Scripture, but from her own conscience alone he persuaded her.

[John 4:27] Yet no one said anything; for they knew that he does everything with measured understanding and reverence. They wondered that he spoke with a foreign and poor Samaritan woman, and they also wondered at his lack of pride.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why Jesus revealed himself to her and why the disciples marveled yet kept silent.
comments.author: Ammonius of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Good news must be shared.
comments.comment: It is among the most absurd things not to publish what benefits the common good.
comments.author: Ammonius of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Christ craves human salvation as one craves food.
comments.comment: As teachers of the inhabited world he teaches the disciples to prefer God's will to any food whatever. As one desires food, so I desire the salvation of human beings.
comments.selected_reason: Explains 'my meat is to do the will of him that sent me'.
comments.author: Ammonius of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Jesus accepted food from others, though he needed none, because feeding Christ is a blessing.
comments.comment: They show that he accepted the services of those offering food, even though he was able to feed and not to be fed; for to feed on Christ is a greatest blessing, of which he is not envious toward those willing. Therefore he also ordered the same for the disciples.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: Godly work is a harvest stored in heaven, repaid hereafter.
comments.comment: The spiritual harvest—that is, godly work—has its storing and treasure in heaven, and in the age to come unending enjoyment; for that is the time of repayment.
comments.author: Ammonius of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Christ, speaking through the prophets, sowed, and the apostles reap, gathering Greeks and Jews into the church.
comments.comment:
The sower is Christ, sowing saving doctrines even when speaking through prophets; the reapers are the apostles. The prophets are the sowers, even if they had much toil as the first to cast piety's seeds into human souls; for the disciples did not have so much labor when persuading people from the Scriptures.

As the seed being mine even if spoken through prophets, I send you to reap. The disciples cut Greeks away from earthly things and Jews from the fleshly worships of the law and set them on the threshing floor—that is, the church—where the ear, threshed, becomes wheat that gives life to the faithful.
comments.selected_reason: Explains who sows and who reaps in 'one soweth, and another reapeth'.
comments.author: Ammonius of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Foreign Samaritans welcomed Christ while his own people persecuted him, and they confessed him Savior of the whole world.
comments.comment:
Samaritans ask Christ to stay with them—they who are foreigners—while his kin according to the flesh, the Jews, persecuted him, because "a person's enemies are those of his own household" (Matthew 10:36).

"This is the Savior" (John 4:42) stands for the Christ, as one who is going to save the whole inhabited world; he said this continually.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the Samaritans' welcome and their confession 'the Saviour of the world'.
comments.author: Ammonius of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Jesus left not to seek honor but to spare his angry townsmen, calling himself the prophet Moses foretold.
comments.comment:
He did not leave as one seeking honor, but sparing the citizens; for when they saw him they were angry. He who was in divine honor took flesh and underwent the most dishonorable death for our salvation.

Here he calls himself the prophet proclaimed beforehand by Moses, who was also called prophet by economy though he himself, as God, is the Spirit's supplier, through whom prophets prophesied.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why John links Jesus' departure with 'a prophet hath no honour in his own country'.
comments.author: Ammonius of Alexandria

comments.capsule: A wonder goes beyond nature, while a sign, like healing the sick, does not.
comments.comment: A sign differs from a wonder: a wonder is what happens contrary to nature—opening blind eyes and raising the dead—while a sign is what is not outside nature, such as healing a sick person and the like.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the difference between 'signs' and 'wonders'.
comments.author: Ammonius of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Like Moses, Jesus worked signs because people who had learned to ask for signs and wonders needed them in order to believe.
comments.comment: …just as Moses needed the signs he is recorded to have done, so that he might be believed not only by the elders but also by the people (Exodus 4:29–31), why should not Jesus too, so that he might be believed by those of the people who had learned to ask for “signs and wonders” (John 4:48; compare 1 Corinthians 1:22), need such works of power as, being greater and more divine in comparison with those done through Moses, were able to draw them away from Jewish myths and from the human traditions among them (compare Titus 1:14; Mark 7:8), and to make them accept the one who taught and did these things as greater than the prophets? For how was he not greater than the prophets, who was proclaimed by the prophets as the Christ and the Saviour of the human race?
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: He believed first, then saw it fulfilled, for God perfects faith.
comments.comment: The day before he believed, and on the next he also heard in deed that what he believed would happen had happened; for faith is strong when it has God as fellow-worker and perfecter.
comments.author: Ammonius of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The Sheep Gate was where sacrificial sheep gathered, and the pool's angel-stirred healing prefigured baptism.
comments.comment:
It was called "Sheep Gate" because there the sheep to be slaughtered for the feast were gathered and their entrails were washed there.

[John 5:4] Here the mystery of baptism was prefigured, in which every kind of sin was healed. An angel coming down into the water and stirring it put healing power into them. It is unclear on what day and hour the angel came down.…
comments.author: Ammonius of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The pool healed only when the angel stirred it, showing that baptismal water helps only when Christ comes to it.
comments.comment: …so that they would not attribute everything to the waters, the waters did not heal before an angel stood over them and stirred them, so that they might learn that the waters of baptism do not benefit the soul by themselves before the angel of great counsel [Christ], putting on a human body, comes to baptism.…
comments.author: Amphilochius of Iconium

comments.capsule: The angel's rare healings picture the law's limited grace, and Jesus asks only to stir the man's desire.
comments.comment:
…This was a type of the legal worship given through angels to one nation only and at one time only—at the feast's end—that is, healing advancing at the last times and not continuing into what follows.

[John 5:6] He asks not as one ignorant, but rousing him to desire to be healed.
comments.author: Ammonius of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Healing in the thirty-eighth year, short of the forty years of punishment, shows the Lord sparing the full penalty by grace.
comments.comment: The thirty-eighth year of the lying paralytic signifies a time of punishment already being fulfilled, that just as the people for forty years tested the judgments in the wilderness, and forty days the destruction fell, and the law punished the sinners for forty years, so the Lord, sparing the fullness of the punishment, heals the sick man in the thirty-eighth year, just as he also spared the legal punishments through grace, the cosmic time having been fulfilled.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: Jesus humbly asked whether the man wanted healing in order to expose the cruelty of those who never helped him, then healed him without the water.
comments.comment:
See his lack of arrogance. He did not say, “Do you want me to heal you?” For he did not wish to speak boastfully or to proclaim himself before the miracles. The man says, “I do want it, but I have no man.” For where there is no friend, there is no man anywhere.

“This is also why I ask,” Jesus says, “not so that I may learn—for what sick person does not want to be made well?—but so that you may expose the cruelty of your good citizens, because they did not even give you a hand to throw you toward the spring, something even an enemy would have done if asked. Since until now you have had no man to put you into the pool, look: I, who for your sake became man, heal your suffering even without waters. Rise, take up your mat and go” (John 5:8).
comments.selected_reason: Explains why Jesus asked 'Wilt thou be made whole?' and the man's 'I have no man'.
comments.author: Amphilochius of Iconium

comments.capsule: Jesus had the man carry his mat, as he had the leftover bread gathered, to make the miracle plain and beyond suspicion.
comments.comment: He does not simply command him to carry the mat. What he did with the loaves, he does here as well. Just as there he commands the leftover pieces of bread to be carried, so here too, to make the miracle clear and to free the healing from Jewish suspicion, and to show that he is not some deceiver but a savior and the common physician of nature, he commands him to carry the mat. So the Jews said, “It is the Sabbath; it is not lawful for you to carry your mat” (John 5:10).…
comments.selected_reason: Explains why Jesus told the man to take up his bed.
comments.author: Amphilochius of Iconium

comments.capsule: Since God rested from creating, the Father's "working until now" means his providence, not new creation.
comments.comment: …Moses says God rested from all his works which he had begun to make (Genesis 2:2). Keep creating souls today and that rest is emptied.… When it is said 'My Father is working still' (John 5:17), the sense is providence, not minting new soul-essences.
comments.author: Nemesius of Emesa

comments.capsule: Jesus calls God his own Father and works as he does, as an equal Son.
comments.comment:
"My Father," he says, "is mine alone and no one else's"; so by what with which he holds creation together—the sun and heavens, and causes bodies to grow, he works.

[John 5:18] The one equal to the Father is especially called Son as consubstantial [of one nature].…
comments.author: Ammonius of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Like his Father, who is bound by no law, Jesus works by his own authority, which the Jews took as a claim to equality with God.
comments.comment: What then does Christ do? He brings forward the Father, saying, “My Father is working until now, and I am working” (John 5:17). For just as, he says, my Father is not subject to boundaries, does not serve laws, and does not wait for commands, but by his own judgment does whatever he wills, so I also work all things with authoritative authority, equally with the Father. But for this reason they sought all the more to kill him, because he not only broke the Sabbath but also called God his own Father, making himself equal to God (John 5:18).
comments.selected_reason: Explains how 'My Father worketh hitherto, and I work' answers the Sabbath charge.
comments.author: Amphilochius of Iconium

comments.capsule: "Cannot do anything of himself" means not weakness but unity: the Son has one nature and will with the Father and never acts apart from him.
comments.comment:
Jesus answers: “To weaken the madness of the Jews who think I am legislating against the Father. Since they accuse me about the breaking of the Sabbath, I said, ‘My Father is working until now, and I am working’ (John 5:17), wanting to show equal honor from both sides. But those utterly foolish people thought I was building works against works and introducing one opinion against another, and they were stirred to envy. So to correct their opinion I said, ‘The Son cannot do anything of himself unless he sees the Father doing it’ (John 5:19).

What I meant was this: ‘Why are you so angry with me, you ill-timed examiners of the Sabbath, because I break the Sabbath? I am not opposing the Father. It is not that he wants to establish the Sabbath and I to dissolve it. I am not fighting against him; I am not rebelling against his will. He does not will one thing while I wish something different. What he wills, I will; what he wishes, I wish; what he does, I do.’ For in this way I do nothing and will nothing outside of him.…

I do not have an opinion separated and cut off from the Father. Since the nature is one and the will is one, the result must also be one. So the Son cannot do anything of himself, because he cannot do anything without the Father, having the Father whole within himself: ‘I am in the Father and the Father is in me’ (John 14:10). If the works of soul and body are indistinguishable because of their union—even though their nature is divided, the body being one thing, mortal, and the soul another, immortal—how can my works and the Father’s be distinguished? Where counsel and word and knowledge and wisdom and nature and divinity are one, the Son cannot do anything of himself because he is not separated from the Father, unless he sees the Father doing it—that is, unless he sees the Father willing it.…
comments.selected_reason: Explains 'The Son can do nothing of himself' as unity of will, not weakness.
comments.author: Amphilochius of Iconium

comments.capsule: "Likewise" does not mean the Son copies the Father's works, or there would be two worlds; they do the very same works.
comments.comment: …“Amen, I say to you, the Son cannot do anything of himself unless he sees the Father doing it. For whatever that one does, these things the Son also does in the same way” (John 5:19). Not because he creates some things and I, by imitation, produce other things. For if that were so, there would have to be two heavens, two suns, two seas, two races of human beings, and a double world—one belonging to the Father, the other to me. For it would be necessary that, just as with painters the lines are prescribed and with teachers the letters of the alphabet, so the Father’s creation was prescribed, and I produced mine by imitation.
comments.author: Amphilochius of Iconium

comments.capsule: Father and Son share one activity, so whatever the Father does the Son does at the same moment, not as a copy.
comments.comment:
Regarding what is said by Jesus: whatever he does (and it is clear that it is the Father) , the Son likewise does, which refers to what has paradoxically happened through him in the Gospels, overseeing how the Father did these things. To what must be said: since the Son, being consubstantial [of one nature] with the Father, has an inseparable energy of the Father's energy, being an unquenchable mirror, whatever the Father does, the Son also acts inseparably at once, and whatever the Son works, the Father immediately leads to existence, so as not to make the Son without the Father or the Father without the Son do anything.

This view must also be applied to the created things; for it is not that the Son is of a different essence when the Father creates other things. For this would follow that there are two suns and each of the existing things is double, but the creatures do not appear to be so. Therefore, the first thing is seen as the same in the energy of the Father and the Son in the things being created.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: For the dead, being raised and being made alive are one thing.
comments.comment: If it is said of a dead person that they are raised and made alive, the words differ alone; for making a dead person alive and raising them is the same…
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The Father delights when the Son is honored as God and accepts no honor that dishonors the Son.
comments.comment: And he does all things for this reason: so that all may honor the Son just as they honor the Father (John 5:23). For the Father most of all delights in honor when he sees the Son who comes from him honored in a way worthy of God. The one who does not honor the Son does not honor the Father who sent him, for the Father does not accept honor at the cost of the Son’s dishonor.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why honoring the Son is honoring the Father.
comments.author: Amphilochius of Iconium

comments.capsule: We honor the Son, and so the Father, by living by his word.
comments.comment: Just as the one transgressing the law dishonors God through transgressing, but the one keeping it honors the giver, so the one honoring the Son by doing according to the law and the right word will honor the Father likewise (John 5:23).
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Justification in Christ washes away every stain, so the believer escapes judgment because no charge is left against him.
comments.comment: …justification in Christ is by no means partial; it is rather a complete washing away of whatever tends to stain us. Therefore he also said: ‘Truly, truly, I say to you, he who believes in me has eternal life, and does not come into judgment, but has passed from death to life’ (John 5:24). If, then, the one who through Christ has justification by faith conferred on him has escaped being judged, we are bound to say that he has escaped the charges; and no kind of accusation, I say, could prevail against such a person. For ‘it is God who justifies; who is he that condemns?’ (Romans 8:33–34).
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 15

comments.capsule: The "dead" who hear are unbelievers raised by faith, and some escape judgment altogether, going straight either to life or to punishment.
comments.comment:
The dead are those once unbelieving and through faith in Christ called into life. Even if other rational animals received life, they cannot also give life.

[John 5:24] Those who do not come into judgment are either sent into Gehenna's fire as godless and impious, or into enjoyment of unspeakable goods—that is, true life; for this is to pass from death to life, freed from Gehenna and counted worthy of divine honors. Those who lived in the middle stand "on the right" and "on the left" (Matthew 25:33).

Before the passion and resurrection, and apart from being baptized, those who received Christ's word and believed that he was the Father's Son were saved.
comments.selected_reason: Explains who 'the dead' are and what 'shall not come into condemnation' means.
comments.author: Ammonius of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The Son "receives" life and judgment as man: his body, united to the living Word, became life-giving.
comments.comment: And together with judging he also receives the life, although he is judge as God. And what the manner of the receiving would be, he himself will teach, saying: “Because he is Son of Man.” (John 5:26–27) For it is not proper to a human to be able to have the life from himself; but since the body united to him has become own to the living Word, for this reason also, very reasonably, as having its life-giving energy, he is said to receive the life; and he himself again appropriates the matter, whose own the receiving body has also become.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On the True Faith, to the Empresses Pulcheria and Eudocia

comments.capsule: Jesus judges because he is Son of God, yet also as the man who shares our weakness, and all the dead, wherever their bodies lie, will rise.
comments.comment:
Punctuate it thus, and not as some think who, after adding "and he gave him authority to execute judgment," then add "because he is Son of Man" (John 5:27). That is not right; for he is not judge because he is Son of Man, but because he is Son of God—and for that reason he is also judge.

He says "Do not marvel" (John 5:28) because to those who saw him he seemed a mere man, yet what was said was greater than a man and for God alone to do. He did not say that he is Son of God, but that he is Son of Man—this he had said above—so that they might understand him as both man and God. What he means is this: not only as God does he judge, but also as one who became man and was tried in all our diseases apart from sin, and as one who sympathizes with our weaknesses and forgives the rest.

Or he says this: if I raise Lazarus, do not marvel at my power from that; for I am going to raise all the dead; "all who are in the tombs" (John 5:28) means all who have died. Since bodies consumed by beasts or fire or otherwise are not laid in tombs, yet they rise; for there will be a resurrection of all humans, and these too will be numbered among those in the memorials; for those who do good and evil are not the bodies in the tombs. So nothing prevents receiving also bodies consumed by fire or otherwise.…

[John 5:29] Through both fear and honor, then, he urges the human being toward salvation. So faith alone is not enough to save unless one also has good works.
comments.selected_reason: Explains how to read 'because he is the Son of man' and who 'all that are in the graves' are.
comments.author: Ammonius of Alexandria

comments.capsule: "All in the graves" means all the dead, even the unburied, and only believers who sinned face the "resurrection of judgment".
comments.comment:
'All those in the tombs' (John 5:28) signifies 'all those having died'; for if he did not say this—those whose bodies have been consumed by beasts or fire and are not placed in tombs, they do not rise. But since there will be a resurrection of all men, these also shall be numbered among those in the tombs. If the disputants were to contend, they must be stopped by noting that those doing good and bad things are being judged, not the bodies placed in the tombs. Therefore the word will not prevent them from receiving the truth even if the bodies were consumed by fire or otherwise.

Of men divided according to the opinion into the ungodly, that is, the unbelieving, or the godly, that is, the believing (John 5:28–29), of all the same rising men, the unbelieving and ungodly indeed rise, but not unto judgment, since he who does not believe has already been judged. But those who have believed in the Savior and have also done good works, those who rise for a resurrection of life, shall not be judged among those being raised unto judgment who sinned after believing. As for the state of infants, since they also rise, God alone knows, perhaps even those to whom the revelation of this truth has come.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Father and Son share one will; Jesus speaks this way only as man.
comments.comment:
…in the Trinity there is not another will and another, but one; the Word puts on weakness. Yet it is not so in truth, since he is equal to the Father, even if as man "under the law" (Galatians 4:4) he speaks.

"I do not seek my own will" (John 5:30), as you Jews, teaching and doing everything lawlessly by your own will.
comments.selected_reason: Explains 'I seek not mine own will' without setting the Son's will against the Father's.
comments.author: Ammonius of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Jesus avoided speaking about himself and preferred to show by deeds that he was the Christ.
comments.comment: …One may see this also in the character of Jesus, who everywhere avoided speaking about himself and for that reason said, “Even if I speak about myself, my testimony is not true” (John 5:31). And since he avoided speaking about himself, and wished to show that he was the Christ by his deeds rather than by his words, for this reason the Jews say to him, “If you are the Christ, tell us plainly” (John 10:24).
comments.selected_reason: Explains the startling 'If I bear witness of myself, my witness is not true'.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Jesus cites John's witness yet refuses human witness, because John spoke what he learned from God.
comments.comment:
Having said that another is the one who bears witness about me, and I know that his witness is true, to show that he means John he added: "You have sent to John, and he has borne witness to the truth" (John 5:32–33). Then, silencing them from the surplus and still speaking to their suspicion—they were about to say, If you do not receive witness from a human, why bring John's witness forward?—he showed that John's witness was not a human's witness but God's; for learning from him he said what he said. Therefore he added: "I do not receive the witness from a human" (John 5:34).

John's witness is above suspicion; for he did not run to the witness self-called. He bore witness to the truth—that is, to me the Christ, who is truth.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why Jesus appeals to John's witness while saying he receives no witness from man.
comments.author: Ammonius of Alexandria

comments.capsule: John was the lamp foretold for Christ, and the Jews rejoiced in him only briefly before letting him be killed.
comments.comment:
Or do you not know that for those under the law in Judea the inspired Baptist was a kind of lamp going before Christ, and that God the Father spoke of him beforehand: ‘I have prepared a lamp for my Christ’ (Psalm 132:17)? The Savior himself also bore witness to this, saying of him to the teachers of the Jews: ‘He was the lamp that burns and shines, and you were willing to rejoice for a while in his light’ (John 5:35).…

Yet the Jews took delight in John for a very short time, in that they ran to the baptism he gave and marveled greatly at him; then they put the ever-shining lamp to sleep in death, all but quenching it. For even if the crime may perhaps be called Herod’s (Matthew 14:10), still he was of Israel’s blood.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 10

comments.capsule: John is a lamp, shining with borrowed light and no longer needed once the sun, Christ, has risen.
comments.comment:
John is a lamp beside Christ's way of life, who is a sun: John shines, yet is covered by the excess of the solar light's glory; so also sun and moon in the regeneration shine, yet are so mastered by the glory of the saints' light as to seem not to shine at all. He called John a lamp as not having light from himself but from the Spirit's grace, and because when the sun has risen the lamp's need is superfluous.

[John 5:36] By "gift" he means the Father's good pleasure and understanding, or he says this because of the form of humanity.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why John is called 'a burning and a shining light' (a lamp).
comments.author: Ammonius of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Those who reject Christ, the Father's Word and true form, have neither heard the Father's voice nor seen his form.
comments.comment: You believed neither the prophets nor the voice brought from above nor the wonder-working of the deeds; for it belongs to simpler knowledge to say that some have seen God. These are those who have neither seen the Father's form nor heard his voice—those who did not believe in Christ, who is the Father's Word and his true form.
comments.author: Ammonius of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The sights at Sinai were only shadows; the true sight of the Father is Christ, so those who reject him have never seen God.
comments.comment: …those visions [at Sinai] were shadows of the true sight of God, and that the true revelation is Christ, in whom we have seen the Father himself (John 14:9). Indeed, when the Jews supposed that on Mount Sinai they had truly seen the God of all things, he showed them how utterly foolish their thinking was, saying: ‘You have not heard his voice, nor seen his form, and you do not have his word abiding in you, because you do not believe the one whom he sent’ (John 5:37–38).
comments.selected_reason: Explains 'Ye have neither heard his voice at any time, nor seen his shape'.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 9

comments.capsule: Christ does not force belief, needs no human glory, and shows that their zeal against him did not come from love of God.
comments.comment:
Even if Christ wants the Jews persuaded by his teaching, he does not force free will.

As one who needs nothing, I have from myself the fullest glory and do not want human glory, but I have known you, that you do not have the love of God in yourselves (John 5:41–42). He said "I have known you…" showing that they did not persecute him from love of God, even if they pretended so.
comments.selected_reason: Explains 'I receive not honour from men' and 'ye have not the love of God in you'.
comments.author: Ammonius of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Christ came for the Father's glory, but the coming son of lawlessness will claim divinity for himself.
comments.comment: …‘I have come in the name of my Father, and you do not receive me. If another should come in his own name, that one you will receive.’ (John 5:43) For Christ has visited unto glory of God the Father. And the son of lawlessness will come according to times, not unto glory of God the Father—for this I think is the, In the name of the Father—but setting around his own head, the wretched one, the name of the divinity. ‘For he will sit into the house of God showing himself, that he is God.’ (2 Thessalonians 2:4)
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 8

comments.capsule: The one who will come in his own name is the antichrist, and Moses accuses them through his own writings.
comments.comment:
Even though he knows they are not persuaded and do not receive him, as God he does his own part, convicting and admonishing them. The antichrist promises the glory of this life, and for that reason you believe him.

[John 5:45] A written accusation against you lies in the Mosaic books; Moses, disbelieved by you, will accuse you.
comments.selected_reason: Explains who will 'come in his own name' and how Moses 'accuses' them.
comments.author: Ammonius of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Love of human praise destroys faith, so we must despise it and seek only the glory that comes from God.
comments.comment: In many places, then, our Savior is seen pressing against ambition as a passion that destroys… But we must remember the 'How can you believe, who receive glory from men, and seek not the glory that comes from the only God?' (John 5:44) — and despise all glory from men, even if it is thought to come of the good — and seek the sovereign and true glory, the glory from the only God, who becomingly glorifies, beyond the worth of the glorified, the one worthy of glory.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Rulers and people trade honor with each other, and that mutual flattery keeps them from faith.
comments.comment: He says this, reproving the minds and stating the cause of unbelief: for the rulers pursue the approval from the people, but the people love the honor from the rulers, and so you stand away from the faith toward me; the rulers do this so that the glory in you might not be diminished, and you do this so that you might not lose the honor from them.
comments.selected_reason: Explains 'which receive honour one of another' as the cause of unbelief.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: The "sea" is a lake, the mountain suits mystery, and God tests to draw out faith.
comments.comment:
He means across the lake; for Scripture's custom is to call "seas" the gatherings of waters.

[John 6:3] And because he wanted to hand something mystical to the disciples he went up onto the mountain.

[John 6:6] God also tests, calling the hearer out toward faith…
comments.author: Ammonius of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Jesus counts the men by the law's custom and gives thanks to teach us, and the barley loaves and fish picture the law and the apostles' teaching.
comments.comment:
So that they may not suppose Andrew hides something for his own need, he said that a child still has five barley loaves and two fish.…

[John 6:10] He counts only the men, according to the law's custom: those who have nothing childish or womanish, but a youthful mind, whom he also feeds with the bread that strengthens the heart and fills with delight.

[John 6:11] For this reason he gives thanks: lest he seem opposed to God, and that he may teach us to give thanks when we eat; yet also as man he gives thanks, that until the passion he may escape the notice of the ruler of this age.

Christ feeds the faithful through the five barley loaves, which signify the coarser teaching of the Pentateuch, and through the two fish, which are the apostolic teaching of the evangelical and apostolic proclamation.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why only the men are counted, why Jesus gave thanks, and what the barley loaves and fish signify.
comments.author: Ammonius of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The twelve baskets are the servants' wage, and the barley loaves and fish picture the law of Moses and the apostles' writings.
comments.comment: And now he also filled baskets, and that rather each of the disciples was given one as the wage of service — which signifies that those who serve will have a great wage. Since another evangelist also calls the loaves “of barley,” (John 6:9) the aim of contemplation looks to this: barley is beastlike food, which is the contemplation through Moses brought to the more irrational. That is also why we say five loaves, because of the fivefold writing of Moses, and two fish, through which is shown the double writing of the fishermen — both apostolic and evangelical (John 6:9).
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Unlike God's promise to Moses, Jesus shows the sign by deed, giving thanks over the loaves as if the food were already there while he was creating it.
comments.comment: …To the disciples, the sign that has happened he does not promise by word, but by deed he demonstrates (John 6:10-11); for this was fitting for the economy, not as it was said then to Moses, 'Will not the hand of the Lord suffice? You shall already see if my word descends upon you,' [Numbers 11:23] but here he commands only that the people rise up quickly and quietly, and having taken the loaves and the fishes, he gives thanks as if they were food lying before him, and as if feeding with these and giving with these, yet in this he was producing those which were not.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: The miracle teaches trust in Christ in hardship and boldness in hospitality.
comments.comment: Through the sign he teaches them to take heart in him and not to lose heart in distress, or not to shrink from hospitality, but to be bold toward the good.
comments.author: Ammonius of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Those truly fed by Jesus seek him the more, and believing in the Word he sent is the work of God and the food that lasts.
comments.comment:
…He says in John, to those who came to Capernaum seeking him: 'Amen, amen, I say to you: you seek me not because you saw signs, but because you ate of the loaves and were filled.' (John 6:26–58) For he who ate 'of' the loaves blessed by Jesus and was filled with them rather seeks to grasp the Son of God more exactly, and hastens to him. That is why he well commands, saying: 'Labor not for the food that perishes, but for the food that abides unto eternal life, which the Son of Man shall give you.' (John 6:27)

And when his hearers asked and said, 'What shall we do, that we may work the works of God?' (John 6:28) Jesus answered and said to them: 'This is the work of God: that you believe in him whom he sent.' (John 6:29) And God sent 'his Word and healed them,' as written in the Psalms — plainly, those who were sick. With this Word, those who believe work 'the works of God' — which are food abiding unto eternal life.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: "Labour not" forbids anxiety, not work, and the lasting food is spiritual teaching and the sacrament the Son gives.
comments.comment:
He does not forbid working, but worrying and fretting about tomorrow…

He means the intelligible, rational, and spiritual food that remains; for this helps us enjoy the goods to come, which faith in Christ procures.

He means the mystical participation which the Son has given, that sanctifies soul and body, weaving the human together with what befits God.
comments.selected_reason: Explains that 'Labour not for the meat which perisheth' forbids anxiety, not work, and what the lasting food is.
comments.author: Ammonius of Alexandria

comments.capsule: "Sealed" means anointed with the Spirit in his flesh, or confirmed by the Father's witness, since the Son bears the Father's exact imprint.
comments.comment: He "sealed" him—that is, anointed with the Holy Spirit the Lord's human flesh, not the Godhead; for almost all the names of the economy are taken concerning the flesh. He said this either because he is naturally formed toward the Father, that is, anointed (for those anointed are sealed), or "sealed" means the Father confirmed or undeniably disclosed the Son by his own witness; for the Son is impress and seal of the Father's essence, seen without difference as the Father.
comments.author: Ammonius of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The lasting food is life-giving faith, which makes us like the Lord's flesh that the Father sealed.
comments.comment: He changes the focus not to fly toward food that is perishing, but toward that which remains for the age, which feeds the soul (John 6:27). This was the life-giving faith, through which one is made like to the flesh of the Lord, which has been sealed by divine power by the Father.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: "Sealed" means the Son bears the Father's whole likeness, as wax takes the full imprint of a seal.
comments.comment:
…The Son of Man has given us the food that remains into eternal life — clearly his flesh; for it is life-giving. Then how is the one who can give life even through his own flesh not God, and like in all things to God the Father?

For this I take to be what it means to say he has been sealed by God — “to have been sealed” (John 6:27) signifying the exact likeness. For just as if someone presses a gold seal — or one made of another material — into wax, he marks the whole impress of it from the whole, so also God the Father has the characters of his own nature essentially shining in the Son. And this is what it means to say he has been sealed by the Father.
comments.selected_reason: Explains 'him hath God the Father sealed' with the image of a seal in wax.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On the True Faith, to the Princesses Arcadia and Marina

comments.capsule: God's work is not keeping the law's shadows but believing in Christ.
comments.comment:
Even if he knew those people would gain nothing, still for the common benefit of the teaching he answered.

It is not the one serving the shadows of the law who does God's will, but the one who believes in Christ.
comments.selected_reason: Explains 'This is the work of God, that ye believe'.
comments.author: Ammonius of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Faith is called God's work because it is the soul's highest activity, so it justifies even without other works.
comments.comment:
Here, the work of God is called that which is suitable to God. And he says that for the Lord to be the faith toward him is to declare faith as a work, making it both priestly and perfect.

Therefore, even without human works, it appropriately justifies and sanctifies, since it possesses the most excellent activity of the soul, not some idleness or inaction.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: The manna was a true type, but Christ is the real bread from heaven, his flesh being called heavenly because it is united to the Word.
comments.comment:
He did not say this as if the manna food were a lie, but because that was a type, not itself the truth. Christ is the manna who is life by nature and gives life to all things—that is, bread as feeding soul and body.

[John 6:33] Here again he calls the bread—that is, the flesh—from heaven, not because it was from heaven, but because it was united to the Word who came down from heaven; and after the union the saints speak without distinction as of one person and one hypostasis [person], even though they know the difference even after the union of flesh, soul, and Godhead.

For he frees from sins and makes friends of God and partakers of the "divine nature" (2 Peter 1:4) and frees from Gehenna and counts the worthy of the kingdom—those who share as they ought in the flesh of the Word of God; for all these are life and food of the immortal soul.
comments.author: Ammonius of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The true bread is the Word, which nourishes the true man made in God's image toward his likeness.
comments.comment: And 'my Father,' he says, 'gives you the true bread from heaven. For the bread of God is he who comes down from heaven and gives life to the world.' (John 6:33) And true bread nourishes the 'true' 'man' — made 'after the image of God' — who, nourished, becomes 'after the likeness' 'of him who created.' And what is more nourishing to the soul than the Word? What more precious to the mind that holds her than God's wisdom? What more fitting to the rational nature than truth?
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The manna was a shadow pointing to the Word, the true bread of heaven, so Jesus rebuked those who admired Moses instead of him.
comments.comment:
…God sent the manna down like rain on the people of Israel in the wilderness; for this was their food and bread from above, from heaven (Exodus 16:4). But what was done did not stop at things of sense. As through a type and a shadow, it leads us up to understand that in due time the Word would come to us from above and from the Father, as bread from heaven, just as the divine David hints to us when he says: ‘He gave them the bread of heaven; man ate the bread of angels’ (Psalm 78:24–25).

We certainly do not say that the physical manna was the bread from heaven and of angels. For a spirit is fed spiritually, and a body according to its own nature, that is, bodily. The food of angels, the bread fit for the heavens and for the spirits above, is the Word who is from God the Father. So the manna signified Christ. Yet the type is of no use unless the truth has been received. For it is a shadow of the truth, not made chiefly for its own sake, but so that it might paint in itself a picture of something better.

That is why Christ gave the crowds of the Jews a wise rebuke, because they admired, not him as the truth, but Moses, the servant of the types. For he said: ‘Truly, truly, I say to you, Moses has given you the manna; but the bread of God is he who came down from heaven and gives life to the world. I am the living bread’ (John 6:32–33, 51).
comments.selected_reason: Explains why Jesus says Moses did not give the true bread from heaven.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 10

comments.capsule: Christ is bread of life by remaking the whole person through his words, and the drink is the Spirit.
comments.comment:
He is bread of life not as soothing bodily hunger, but remaking the whole living being from end to end into life, through the spiritual words of which we are filled, which is life.

Water and drink here mean either sanctification through the Spirit or the Holy Spirit himself.
comments.selected_reason: Explains 'I am the bread of life' and the promise 'shall never thirst'.
comments.author: Ammonius of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Faith needs a push from above as well as our effort, and Christ promises not to cast out but to save all who come.
comments.comment:
…And "I will not cast out" (John 6:37) means this: I will not destroy, but will save and arrange for much care to be enjoyed.

Faith in me, he says, is no chance thing, but needs a tilt from above so one may know what is beyond mind, even if our own zeal is also sought. As a physician the Father brings weak humans to Christ, and by economy as man he assigns what befits God to the Father, since as God Christ is able to bring them to himself.
comments.selected_reason: Explains 'All that the Father giveth me shall come to me' and 'I will in no wise cast out'.
comments.author: Ammonius of Alexandria

comments.capsule: "Came down from heaven" is not a move in space but the Word, in the form of God, taking a servant's form and becoming flesh.
comments.comment:
The Lord, sent from heaven to save, says: 'I have come down from heaven, not to do my own will' (John 6:38). For God sent this word of His and healed those wounded by their corruptions, as David himself says elsewhere.

If anyone seeks to ask whether the one sent from heaven signifies a local emission from the physical heaven, it would seem absurd to attribute a local descent to God. For does the voice of heaven not signify the incorporeal and intellectual essence, according to 'Store up in the heavens' (Matt 6:20) and 'God is in the heaven above' (Psalm 115:3)? Therefore, the one being in the form of God and being healed as God, having taken the form of a servant, came to men (Phil 2:6-7). And this is the sending from heaven, so that the Word of God might become flesh and, having appeared upon the earth, might walk among men (John 1:14).…
comments.selected_reason: Explains what 'I came down from heaven' means without implying movement in space.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Coming down from heaven shows Jesus is God incarnate, his will is the Father's, and he raises the faithful into immortality.
comments.comment:
Therefore Jesus is not a bare man, but God incarnate, not deified after the resurrection; for the descent precedes the ascent.

I did not come having a will of my own apart from the Father; for all that is mine is the Father's and the Father's is mine, and I came to do nothing except what the Father also wills.

[John 6:39–40] All humans rise, but only the faithful are counted worthy of the goods. The Son gives life to the faithful by putting the Spirit's life-giving power into humans corruptible by nature and remaking them wholly into immortality.
comments.selected_reason: Explains 'not to do mine own will' and 'I will raise him up at the last day'.
comments.author: Ammonius of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Christ raises those given him through his own resurrection, which opened for human nature the way to life.
comments.comment:
…He says that those who have believed in him have been given to him by the Father, so that he may not lose them but raise them on the last day (John 6:39). How then did he raise them, if not clearly through his own resurrection from the dead? For having made alive his own temple even before the others, and having shaken death’s power through the death of his own flesh, he became a way for human nature toward resurrection and toward being able at last to overpower corruption.

So what is proper to the God-Word who came down from heaven is that through which he became firstborn from the dead (Colossians 1:18) — so that what was given him may also follow the raised one toward life, no longer being lost through the first-formed man’s transgression, but rather being saved through Christ’s obedience.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On the True Faith, to the Empresses Pulcheria and Eudocia

comments.capsule: Knowing his earthly parents, they could not see his heavenly origin.
comments.comment: Because of his mother according to the flesh they thought it impossible that he had come down from heaven, or looking at what appeared and not considering his invisible nature they took offense.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the crowd murmured at 'I came down from heaven'.
comments.author: Ammonius of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The Father draws people through the sense of good and truth he sowed in them as his image, and through revelation, as with Peter.
comments.comment:
Someone is drawn from the Father in this way (John 6:44–45), of a rational man becoming 'according to the image and according to the likeness' of God. The concepts concerning virtuous actions and the word concerning truth and knowledge are sown within him. Therefore, the one having heard according to common concepts and judging the good and having learned from the Father, comes to Christ through faith, or even through revelation.…

…the Father, teaching through revelation the things concerning the Son, leads those hearing and learning to him; for so also he led Peter through revelation into believing in the Son, having revealed to him.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The Father's drawing helps but does not force our free will, all who are willing are taught by God, and only the Son has seen the Father.
comments.comment:
If the Father draws and God raises, great is the dignity of the faithful. He does this as God by nature.

The Father draws those good by choice and leaves the wicked. The saying does not abolish what is in our power of free will, but shows that we need help; for one is drawn not unwillingly, but enjoying much alliance. The mystery concerning Christ is a good taught by God.

[John 6:45] Even if the Father drew through the prophets' teaching, the difference is great: the first were taught through the prophets, but the faithful through the Son or the Holy Spirit. "All shall be taught by God" (John 6:45) stands for the greater number, or that God teaches all who are willing.

Hearing is common; learning belongs only to those who give themselves to grace.

[John 6:46] The only Invisible appears in nature only to the Invisible. Only the Son sees the Father as existing outside all things and alone being from the Father's essence.
comments.selected_reason: Explains how the Father 'draws' without forcing, and what 'taught of God' means.
comments.author: Ammonius of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Believers may taste death, but resurrection means they do not remain dead.
comments.comment: As giving eternal life to the faithful, or as sustaining our life both now and to come. For even if one tastes death, one does not remain so because of the hope of the resurrection.
comments.author: Ammonius of Alexandria

comments.capsule: "Heaven" means God's own state, and the bread that comes down is God's word, eaten by practicing virtue.
comments.comment: Regarding 'Heaven,' he says it signifies the like appearance and state of God, which is not other than his intelligible essence. And 'life' and 'bread' and 'the one coming down' is the nourishing word of God, which the one coming to him eats by exercising virtue.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Christ gives his flesh as bread because only through his body, joined to the divine power, can we have communion with God.
comments.comment: …'the bread which I will give' to you is 'my flesh for the life of the world' (John 6:51), and the blood is living in the body;… Thus, eating and drinking showed the participation which would not have occurred without a body; for if the divine power had not been joined to a body and unified by blood, we would not have had communion through it to God.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: Christ calls his flesh bread because it is received in the sacrament, which his hearers, thinking only naturally, could not grasp.
comments.comment:
He calls his own flesh bread because it is eaten in the mysteries [the sacraments].

[John 6:52] As if the matter were contrary to nature they disbelieve; as soulish they do not understand the Lord's spiritual body. He does not speak of eating flesh, but of sharing in the mysteries.

[John 6:53] You will be without share in eternal life who have not received through participation in the mysteries Jesus who is life by nature.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why Christ calls his flesh bread and why the hearers stumbled.
comments.author: Ammonius of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Eating his flesh cannot mean chewing it with the senses, so the saying must be understood spiritually.
comments.comment: And that the Passover is intelligible and not this sensible one, he himself says: "Unless you eat my flesh and drink my blood, you have no life in yourselves." (John 6:53) Must we then chew his flesh according to sense and drink his blood? But if he says this intelligibly, then the Passover too is intelligible and not sensible.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: We share in the Word's eternal life only through his flesh, which, united to him, gives life to all who partake.
comments.comment: There is no partaking of the word of God unto eternal life, except through his flesh; for previously it was not mixed with flesh, as all flesh was held by death. But now life-giving flesh is given, nourishing all the only-begotten into life through the strength being reinforced in it, and by remaining sharing in the flesh, it makes them shine through likeness.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: His flesh gives life because it is God's own, and the sacrament joins the believer to Christ as food joins the body.
comments.comment:
He says these things showing that the flesh was not of a bare man, but of the Son filled with all the Godhead as one of the Trinity.

[John 6:56] Just as sensible foods mixed into us constitute the body, so also mystical participation makes a kind of natural joining of the believer with Christ by mixing.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why his flesh gives life and what 'dwelleth in me, and I in him' means.
comments.author: Ammonius of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Christ's flesh is true food and drink because it prepares eternal life and quenches thirst for good, as he told the Samaritan woman.
comments.comment: True is the food which is not an attacker of the temporary and perishing life, but a preparer of the eternal.… This also is a true drink, which if not sufficient for a little time to the thirst, but providing always the one who has filled it and making it unrequited, just as the Lord was saying to the Samaritan woman.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: The Son is life itself, not a creature that receives life.
comments.comment: The Son is life by nature, not having received living from another; for that is called a living being. So neither is the name living being assigned to God, nor the name life to the creation.
comments.author: Ammonius of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The Son lives by the Father as begotten from the living Father, and his body gives life because it is the body of Life itself.
comments.comment:
When therefore we all live because of the Father (Acts 17:28), how is only one human’s body life-giving for that reason, and why do the bodies of others not have the same energy, if indeed all, as I said, both are and live because of the Father? What then do we say to this?

The Word of God, having appeared in human form, has been named apostle; for he was sent to proclaim release to captives and recovery of sight to the blind (Luke 4:18) (Isaiah 61:1). And he lives because of the Father (John 6:57), for he has been begotten from the living Father. For the Son sprung from God and Father who is living and life had to be life by nature in every way. And since he made his own the body taken from the holy virgin, he showed it life-giving, and very reasonably; for it is the body of the life that generates life in all things.…
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On the True Faith, to the Empresses Pulcheria and Eudocia

comments.capsule: The manna was not the true heavenly bread, Jesus taught openly in the synagogue, and his saying seemed hard only to those who heard it too humanly.
comments.comment:
The one who believes that the bread is given from heaven also believes that he gives eternal life. Therefore those who ate the manna did not eat the bread from heaven, from which they died.

[John 6:59] Why did he say these things in a synagogue? To teach the crowd the doctrines and that he was not opposed to God.

The evangelist said "the word is hard" (John 6:60) because they heard the Lord's words too humanly. Not understanding what was said, they could not bear even to ask and learn.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the disciples called it 'an hard saying'.
comments.author: Ammonius of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Son of Man means God incarnate.
comments.comment: The incarnate God himself is the Son of Man. The body itself is not called Son of Man…
comments.author: Ammonius of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The Son of Man "ascending where he was before" does not mean his body came from heaven; it is said of the whole Christ, as some things are said of the whole person.
comments.comment:
If then you see the Son of Man ascending where he was before (John 6:62), we do not even take it to mean the body, so that we may not bow down to those who say that he was brought down from heaven as a body.…

In composite things, we often speak of the parts in regard to the whole; just as if we say, 'A man who is intelligent, sensible, mindful, healthy in body, well-formed, and large-statured', we speak of some things from the body and some from the soul; for some of the things belonging to a composite being cannot belong to each of the individual parts in the composition. But to be awake or to sleep is said neither of the soul alone nor of the body alone; for neither does the soul do this apart from this body, nor the body without the soul. Therefore, it is said concerning the composite.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: "Spirit" here is Christ's flesh filled with the Spirit's life-giving power, though it remains flesh.
comments.comment:
That is: they are spiritual. They have no natural sequence, but are outside such necessity. Here he calls spirit the flesh filled with the Spirit's life-giving energy; for the flesh remains flesh.

[John 6:64] Even if as God he knew they were going to disbelieve, still he speaks what benefits the common good.
comments.selected_reason: Explains 'It is the spirit that quickeneth; the flesh profiteth nothing'.
comments.author: Ammonius of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Christ's choice did not take away Judas' free will, so Judas, made like the devil by his own choice, lost the gifts he had.
comments.comment:
"Many of his disciples" (John 6:66) does not mean the Twelve.

[John 6:70] Knowing what would be, Jesus as God does the good and grants things worthy of wonder, yet he does not overturn our free will; for he does his own part, and it is in us to keep it. Hence one must not blame God for the benefits he gives, but those who willingly lost the gifts, as Adam, Eve, Judas, and all such. Even if I chose you, virtue and vice in humans are free. He calls devil the one clinging to the devil, made like him, and doing what pleases him.

As amazed the evangelist said "one of the Twelve" (John 6:71), that the devil wars so far as to be able to snatch one of the Twelve who raised dead and drove out demons and enjoyed the Lord's life-giving and spiritual teaching.
comments.author: Ammonius of Alexandria
