comments.capsule: Judas was called a devil not by nature but by choice: he was chosen for the virtue he then had and became a devil by betraying.
comments.comment:
Immediately also, regarding Judas, a man, the Lord named him 'devil,' not because of his essence, but because of his choice, saying to all the disciples at once, counting Judas among them: 'Did I not choose you, the twelve, and one of you is a devil?' (John 6:70). As the writer brings it forth: He said this concerning Judas, the one about to betray him.

For if he was called a devil because of the coming betrayal, he was not a devil then, when he also shared the election with all. For he had become elect among all, because of the virtue present in him then; but he was called a devil when he performed the things of the betrayal.
comments.selected_reason: Explains how one of the chosen Twelve could be called 'a devil'.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Fleeing shows his humanity; his brothers called him cowardly and vain; 'world' means worldly people.
comments.comment:
He shows the things of humanity by fleeing the Jews …

[John 7:3–4] His brothers seemed to blame him as cowardly and as doing signs in secret, wanting him as glory-loving to be in the open.

Here "world" means humans who mind the things of the world.
comments.author: Ammonius of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Jesus waits to show his power through his passion and resurrection.
comments.comment: [John 7:6. Christ to his brothers:] You do what you want without looking around; I do not, because I arrange each thing toward what is useful. I wait for the passion, that rising I may make my power plain to all.
comments.author: Ammonius of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Jesus' time to feast had not come, for the saints cannot feast with the wicked amid present troubles; his feast comes when good prevails.
comments.comment:
He who blesses those who mourn over the present age also speaks now, something common also passing through all the saints, saying to himself that there is no time of feast for us in the midst of the present tribulations, in as much as malice is being mustered and truth is being set aside by the majority and the will of God is not prevailing on earth. Because of these things the Lord was saying that his own time is not here; for it was not possible to feast together with the evil, nor with those who hate the one who remains hating.

You, he says, ascend having feasted together, you who neither hate nor are hated by them. But I do not ascend; for the time of my feast is different, when clearly the good will prevail, the hand being cast down, and the evil will be seen nowhere.
comments.selected_reason: Explains 'my time is not yet come' and 'I go not up yet unto this feast'.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: Jesus kept his word by going up late and secretly, not to keep the feast but to counsel, as God once relented toward Moses.
comments.comment: It was not the same to stay at the feast's start while the Jews boiled with anger; so later, when the feast was about to end, he goes up, having done nothing contrary to what he said; for he did not go up to keep festival, but to counsel. Therefore he also went up secretly, not with the cheer festival-goers use. And in the old covenant, having said to Moses "I will not go up with you," [Exodus 33:3] later when Moses pleaded he promised to go with them.
comments.selected_reason: Explains how 'I go not up yet' fits his going up later.
comments.author: Ammonius of Alexandria

comments.capsule: His unschooled learning should have shown he is God, and he calls his teaching the Father's because he is the Father's likeness and Wisdom.
comments.comment:
From the difficulty they ought to have known that he is God.

[John 7:16] Because of extreme likeness he calls his teaching the Father's, or because he himself is the Father's "wisdom" [1 Corinthians 1:24] through which the Father speaks all things, or also as man by economy [accommodation to his hearers] he assigns the teaching to the Father because of the Jews' unbelief. He says he was sent because of the flesh, or as Word from mind—that is, from the Father—or as "radiance" from the sun (Hebrews 1:3).
comments.selected_reason: Explains why Jesus calls his teaching 'not mine, but his that sent me'.
comments.author: Ammonius of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Jesus speaks only by the Father's will and proclaims the Father's glory, not his own, to avoid giving offense.
comments.comment:
That is: privately and separately; for I would not speak otherwise than according to the Father's will.

[John 7:18] What concerns himself he is silent about by economy [accommodation to his hearers] because of the Jews' readiness to take offense and for blamelessness, and he proclaims the Father's glory. He weaves this argument so they may know he does not seek glory.
comments.author: Ammonius of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Jesus calls the law Moses' because the Jews could not yet bear hearing he is God.
comments.comment: Being Lord of Moses and of the law, because of the Jews' weakness he somehow alienates himself from the law by calling it Moses'; for they could not hear that he was God by nature, nor the deep mystery of the economy [God's plan of salvation].
comments.selected_reason: Explains why Jesus calls the law Moses' rather than his own.
comments.author: Ammonius of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Leaving the paralytic unhealed would have broken the Sabbath, and blaming Jesus while excusing circumcision is mere partiality.
comments.comment:
Why are you troubled? For healing the paralytic did not loose the Sabbath; not healing did. When, he says, a person receives a sign that causes pain [circumcision], no one is angry that the law is loosed; yet here, when a whole person has been healed, you are vexed as if lawlessness occurred.

[John 7:24] If you do not blame those who circumcise or sacrifice or fight on the Sabbath, do not blame me either; for this is nothing other than respect of persons.
comments.author: Ammonius of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Jesus traces circumcision to the patriarchs rather than to Moses to show that the custom is older than the Law and was never binding on everyone.
comments.comment:
Wishing to introduce the circumcision performed on the Sabbath as being the beginning of the precision regarding the Sabbath, he presents the argument made concerning circumcision.

He says that this does not even profane the people, showing especially first, not even from Moses is the custom of circumcision, but from above and from the fathers, since it begins from Abraham.

Saying this, he refers them back to things more ancient than Moses, in which this thing is not yet law—that which they most admire as their own, the legal order—demonstrating it to be older and not yet legal. He always introduces the greater things of the law, referring to the more ancient and primordial, since it was neither in Enoch nor in Noah.

Therefore he did not say 'from Abraham' but 'from the fathers' regarding the circumcision, so that, having viewed the matter over all things, you might not consider its use to be absolutely necessary, since it was not even upon all.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why Jesus says circumcision is 'not of Moses, but of the fathers'.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: If the Sabbath gives way to circumcision, it cannot forbid the far greater work of healing a whole body.
comments.comment: Coming to Moses, having used circumcision on the Sabbath, he left the Sabbath-rest having been dissolved by him because of the more divine work of Moses. If, he says, because of the circumcision as a divine work the Sabbath does not cease, he leads it as idle, but there is a time when it is also active; how do you accuse the much greater thing of the circumcision, the healing of the whole human body, as not having been required to be done in a time of rest?
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: The crowd exposes the leaders' murderous lie.
comments.comment: The crowd convicts the Jews who want to kill him and deny it—lying—while Christ speaks truth about himself.
comments.author: Ammonius of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The crowd knows Jesus' earthly origin from Mary but not his origin from God, whom they do not know, while he knows the Father because he is nearest to him.
comments.comment:
The Lord introduces two opinions concerning him (John 7:28), and they know indeed whence he is, because his mother is Mary, but they also have the unknown, that he has both come and is from God.

Therefore, one should not be an arbitrary and self-appointed teacher, but should come to teaching having been sent by God the Father; yet the one who sent him was not known to them, because they were most far removed from the true knowledge of God, both in their judgment and in their actions.

It is natural, then, for one to know the Father, since he is near him; for the most known is that which is most intimate.
comments.selected_reason: Explains how the crowd both knows and does not know where Jesus is from.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: No wonder they do not know Jesus is the Christ, since they do not know the Father, whom only the Son, God by nature, truly knows.
comments.comment:
… has been unknown to you, he says, and it is no wonder if you do not know me, that I am the Christ, since you do not know the one from whom I am. …

[John 7:29] He is visible to me alone, since I am God by nature and not of created nature, who know the Father only by thoughts as they can. But his Son contemplates the whole Begetter in himself and paints the Begetter's essence in his own nature, and so knows him as cannot be said; for the things concerning God are inexpressible.
comments.author: Ammonius of Alexandria

comments.capsule: His 'hour' shows that he suffered willingly.
comments.comment: From this we learn that he suffered willingly and was not seized by Jewish greed. By hour he means the timely outcome of the affairs.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what 'his hour was not yet come' means.
comments.author: Ammonius of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The leaders acted because the people were starting to believe in him.
comments.comment: By what they murmured they appear accepting Christ and wanting to split from the leaders. Sensing this, the leaders sent to seize him for this alone—that he was believed to be the Christ—so that they might destroy him.
comments.author: Ammonius of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Since the Word fills all things, his being sent and his going to the Father are said of his human life and bodily ascension, in human words for what is beyond us.
comments.comment:
“A little while I am with you, and I go to the one who sent me.” (John 7:33) Where is the Word of God not present, if he fills all things by the nature of the deity? How then is he sent by the Father? And how does he go to him? So he is sent in a human way, according to the manner and account of the sending, that he may proclaim release to captives and recovery of sight to the blind (Luke 4:18) (Isaiah 61:1); yet he goes to the Father and God no longer in the same way, but as embodied, having gone up into heaven, that he may appear for us before the face of the Father (Hebrews 9:24), as it is written.

And if “being sent” is also taken of the Word himself, let no one be harsh: for inspired Scripture is sometimes accustomed to use such voices too; and it does not drag the divine and supermundane nature under places and limits — for it knows that nature is bodiless and beyond boundaries and far from being thought of as in a place — but rather tries to make clear, by human voices, the things beyond our mind.
comments.selected_reason: Explains how the Word, present everywhere, can be 'sent' and 'go' to the Father.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On the True Faith, to the Empresses Pulcheria and Eudocia

comments.capsule: Jesus calls out as the crowds leave, inviting those who thirst for faith, and the day is 'great' because the Law named it a holy convocation.
comments.comment:
When all were running together and about to go home, then he teaches, that they may have his words as provision for the way.

I drag no one by force, but the one who has much eagerness. He spoke thus to teach that those who run to faith ought to have the thirsting ones' desire, who when they drink find rest.

Since the law calls the seventh a "holy convocation," following old custom the evangelist also called it great.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the timing of Jesus' cry, the 'thirst' he asks for, and why the day is called great.
comments.author: Ammonius of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Believers receive so rich a gift of the Spirit that they pass his grace on to others.
comments.comment:
The faithful will receive as faith's repayment abundant goods, and will have such a gift from the Holy Spirit that they not only rejoice themselves but also share the Spirit's grace with others, so that those too no longer thirst for knowledge of the truth.

He does not refer the saying to the hypostasis [the Spirit's own being], but to the Spirit's energy, which came after Christ's resurrection.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the 'rivers of living water' as the Spirit's grace flowing on to others.
comments.author: Ammonius of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The Spirit 'was not yet' not because he did not exist, but because his sanctifying grace could be given only after the Word made flesh had carried humanity into glory.
comments.comment:
Having taken upon himself, for our sake, communion in the flesh, he was going to grant from the Spirit a sanctification to men — one not truly given before the Word was made flesh and had run the whole human course of life and carried our dishonor into divine glory; for it is here that God, having made humanity receptive in Christ, bestows the Spirit as upon his own and upon those received, and now the Spirit is present.

And it is in us from that Spirit; for the Scripture calls the sanctification in the Spirit 'the Spirit', as is shown in Acts where Paul is inquiring: 'Having received the Holy Spirit?' [Acts 19:2] they were saying when asked, 'We have not even heard that there is a Holy Spirit'; saying this, they meant that if a sanctification of the Spirit is given to men, they have not heard of it, …

… for one is a prophetic energy of the Spirit, and another is sanctification and renewal, making manifest sons of God born of women. And prophecy often follows the sanctification of adoption, when it is necessary, but regeneration did not coincide with prophecy, because the Holy Spirit was not yet.

It does not refer to the substance, but to the energy; for it was not yet working in the disciples, otherwise he would not have spoken concerning the substance of the Spirit, saying that it was not yet (but making it clear that it was), but concerning the grace which was about to come upon the apostles and through them upon the rest.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: 'Glorified' refers to Christ's flesh ascending into heaven, after which the Spirit of adoption could come to human beings.
comments.comment: And when he says, "The Holy Spirit was not yet, because Jesus was not yet glorified" (John 7:39), he means that his flesh was not yet glorified. For the Lord of glory is not glorified, but the flesh of the Lord of glory is; this flesh receives glory as it ascends with him into heaven. Therefore the Spirit of adoption was not yet among human beings, because the firstfruits taken from us had not yet gone up into heaven.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what 'Jesus was not yet glorified' means and why the Spirit waited for it.
comments.author: Marcellus of Ancyra
comments.work: On the Incarnation and against the Arians

comments.capsule: They rightly expected Bethlehem but wrongly assumed Jesus came from Nazareth.
comments.comment: They said well that the Christ must be from David's seed and from Bethlehem. They err because of Nazareth, where he was raised, though he was born in Bethlehem from the virgin of David.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the crowd's mistake about where Jesus was born.
comments.author: Ammonius of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Divine grace kept anyone from seizing him.
comments.comment: Having left the opinion of the multitude, they decided to seize him through the servants. But no one began against all, being prevented by the divine grace.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: Nicodemus calmly rebukes the council for judging before hearing.
comments.comment: Being one himself among those who believed, and having been led along with the accusers, he [Nicodemus] thunders at them, calmly rebuking, showing how they had judged before knowing, if they believed irrationally (John 7:50).
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: Each accuser knew he too was guilty of something, so no one dared to throw a stone.
comments.comment: We bring therefore in some gospels: a woman, he says, was judged by the Jews on account of sin and was being sent to be stoned in the place where it was customary to happen. The Savior, he says, having seen her and having perceived that they were ready to stone her, said to those about to cast stones at her: 'He who has not sinned, let him take a stone and cast it at herself' (John 8:7). If anyone understood to himself that he had not sinned, having taken a stone, let him strike her. And no one dared; having realized for themselves and knowing that they also are responsible in some way, they did not dare to strike her.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why none of the accusers threw a stone.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: By saying 'I am the light' rather than 'the light is in me', Jesus claims Isaiah's prophecy for himself and shows that he is one Christ, not two sons.
comments.comment:
He shows that he is the one of whom it was proclaimed beforehand, "I have set you as a light for the nations" (Isaiah 49:6), and not one of the prophets but Lord.

He called himself the light, not that the light is in me, lest someone cut the one Christ into a duality of sons; for there is one Christ Son both before flesh and after flesh, and one and only true Son from God and Father, and when he became man human nature is not set in a part; for the body is his own, and to cut Christ after the incarnation into two sons or two natures (for it is the same) is blasphemous.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why Jesus says 'I am the light' and not 'the light is in me'.
comments.author: Ammonius of Alexandria

comments.capsule: They judge by his visible body and so miss his divine origin, and he does not judge now because he came to save, though he will judge together with the Father.
comments.comment:
If they had known that he was God's Son and came down from heaven, they would not have taken offense because of the visible body. "I am God," he says, "and I witness to myself worthily; but you do not know me for this reason, because you want to understand nothing except what appears." He did not say "I am God," but "where I come from," mixing lowly with high. "You do not know where I come from and where I go"; for they were willfully wicked and pretended not to know.

[John 8:15] Looking at my appearing body you judge my affairs wrongly.

For I did not come for these things, since it is not a time of judgment; if I wanted to judge, you are among the condemned. "I did not come" now "to judge the world" but to save (John 12:47).

[John 8:16] He says this toward the hearers' suspicion—that is, my judgment is the Father's, and I do not judge otherwise than the Father, nor the Father otherwise than the Son. He did not say this as weak about judging, but that with the Son the Father is going to judge those who disbelieve the one sent from him.
comments.selected_reason: Explains 'ye judge after the flesh' and how Jesus both does and does not judge.
comments.author: Ammonius of Alexandria

comments.capsule: By appealing to the Law's two witnesses, Jesus shows that he and the Father are distinct yet of one essence, and the Father backs his words by working wonders with him.
comments.comment:
He wants to show not only that he and the Father are two, but also that they are of the same essence. If Father and Son were one person according to Sabellius, he would have seemed to bring the law's witness against himself.

We should not take this simply as said of humans; for it is not because there are two that the witness is true; nor are there two when the one witnesses to himself. He says this for no other reason than to show himself consubstantial with the Father and through himself to show again that he needs no other witness, and lest someone think it was taken for the sake of number, he shows the authority: having said "the witness of two men is true," he added, "I am the one who bears witness about myself," and what I am I will not refuse to say; for I witness that "I am the light of the world" (John 8:12). And if I do not seem trustworthy, since I am alone and have witnessed to myself, I will take the Father as voting with my words by the deeds; for he works wonders with me, as you see, and works together.
comments.selected_reason: Explains how Jesus and the Father are the 'two witnesses' the Law requires.
comments.author: Ammonius of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Their question 'Where is your father?' sneers at his birth, and his answer shows that the Father is known only in the Son, his image.
comments.comment:
Not understanding this, the wretched supposed these things were said about the father reckoned according to flesh. Therefore talking nonsense they said, "Where is your father?"—that is, insulting him as not knowing his father, as if from adultery, they said "Where is your father?"

Thinking Joseph was his father they said this, or they reproach him as born of a virgin and not knowing his own father.

If you suspect my Father to be a human, then you do not know me either. But since the lovers of learning through knowledge of Jesus understand the Father, the Father is characterized in the Son as in his own image. Therefore the Son is equal to the Father. Saying that you do not know my Father and me, he teaches that he was neither of Joseph, whom they knew, nor did they ask for the account concerning his incarnation.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the insult behind 'Where is thy Father?' and Jesus' reply.
comments.author: Ammonius of Alexandria

comments.capsule: They ask 'Where is your father?' as if God were in a place, because they think the Son is mere flesh, yet no one can lay hands on him.
comments.comment:
Because they were asking as if he were contained in a human place: 'Where is your father?' (John 8:19), he marvelously said that their not knowing the Father is something they suffer because they also think the Son is nothing other than flesh, the one being seen in a place. And if you know, he says, that even though the Son has borne flesh, he is nothing inferior to the flesh, you would also recognize the Father as not being held by any local containment, but carrying all things in himself.

[John 8:20] The evangelist, marveling, appears upon such boldness of speech and such reproofs, with no one being able to lay hold of the Lord, even though they were prepared and ready for this. But nevertheless, teaching in their midst in the temple near the treasury, he was speaking with boldness, providing proofs of divinity, rebuking their ignorance regarding these things, and no one laid hold of him.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: No one could seize him before the time he chose to suffer.
comments.comment: So then they laid hands on him when he himself allowed. He was teaching in the temple as a teacher, which stung them greatly. And no one seized him, because it was not yet the time in which he willed to suffer.
comments.author: Ammonius of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Those who reject the physician die of their sickness, and Jesus' going away is no human death but the Word's return to heaven.
comments.comment:
To those who will enjoy nothing of his presence, he threatens a painful destruction (John 8:21), and most appropriately; for those from the physician being present only heal, if not receiving the medicine, those who are dying from their sufferings. And even if it seemed he was refuting himself according to their impious suspicion (John 8:22-23), they were able at any time, being mortals themselves, to go to him; for there is one exit for all, even if the path may seem different and the place receiving all is one before the resurrection of the Lord, even if after these things the order of the saints is transferred into paradise.

What then is the Lord? He shows it even at their feet, having stated the reason and refuting their suspicion: 'You are of the world' (John 8:22-23). The Word has such a power, that he will be transferred toward himself and toward the heavenly things; therefore this is not death as it is toward a truth, as it would be for a man being of the earth and according to the transfer from the body being drawn under the earth.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: Rejecting the one from above, unbelievers stay shut out of heaven and die still carrying their old sinful self.
comments.comment:
You will remain outside the goods of the kingdom, unable to ascend into the heavens, since you did not receive the one who came from above.

[John 8:23] By "world" here he means fleshly thoughts, saying that he himself is not of the world.

[John 8:24] The unbeliever of necessity departs having "the old man," whom if he does not put to death through faith, he will die in him and depart to give account for former sins.
comments.author: Ammonius of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Jesus speaks only what is from the Father, and their question about his father shows they missed that he meant God.
comments.comment:
Much is, he says, what even God has spoken through the prophets, rebuking your hard-heartedness and disobedience (John 8:26). And I, whatever I speak concerning you, is not from another, but I speak from the Father. And he spoke in a more human and clearer way, reasoning with those listening.

For if they had understood that the Lord was speaking concerning God, they would not have asked, “Where is your father?” (John 8:27); therefore he rightly spoke to them not saying, “You do not know my father.”
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: After they kill him, the signs of the passion and the resurrection will show who he is, and his words about the Father show one essence, not opposition.
comments.comment:
From the signs that were going to happen at the time of the passion you will know that I am the Christ. … When you destroy me and seem to be rid of me, then you will know that I am Son of God—from the signs, from the resurrection, from your capture.

He speaks thus because of the hearers' weakness—that is, I am not opposed to the Father because of the indistinguishability of essence. Since I am consubstantial with the Father, I do nothing that the Father does not do; for he also works on the Sabbath as I do, and what he speaks I speak, and in vain you accuse me as opposed to God. Lest by saying "the one who sent me" they conceive diminution, he says "he is with me," saying both because of the Godhead and because of the economy [God's plan of salvation] of the incarnation.
comments.selected_reason: Explains how the cross would reveal who Jesus is, and what 'he that sent me is with me' means.
comments.author: Ammonius of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Jesus tells believers to seek freedom not in descent from Abraham but in virtue and in serving no sin.
comments.comment: It is now time to discuss the Gospel's statement. The evangelist John says: “Jesus said to the Jews who had believed in him, ‘If you remain in my word, you will truly be my disciples; you will know the truth, and the truth will set you free’” (John 8:31–32). That is, our Lord Jesus was telling those who believed in him not to rejoice in worldly nobility or claim glory from Abraham's descent, but to strive and labor for virtue and, after recognizing Christ, to serve no sins. They would thereby retain true freedom with a joyful conscience and, through hope in things that are certain, that is, eternal, be freed from desire for everything else, which because of its fragility is frequently called empty and false.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what kind of freedom Jesus promises.
comments.author: Julian of Eclanum

comments.capsule: Believing and knowing differ, which is why Jesus promises those who already believe that they will come to know the truth.
comments.comment: But to believe and to know are not the same; as neither is it the same to believe the truth and to know the truth, and to believe God and to know God. Therefore to the apostles already having believed the Savior says: “If you remain in my word, you are truly my disciples, and you will know the truth, and the truth will free you” (John 8:31-32). For as Isaiah says: “If you do not believe, you will not understand” (Isaiah 7:9).
comments.selected_reason: Explains why people who already believe are promised that they 'shall know the truth'.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Moses brought a bodily freedom, but Christ gives the far better freedom of the Spirit, even to Israelites already free in body.
comments.comment: It is settled, then, that the hierophant [sacred teacher] Moses was mediator of a bodily freedom, of letter and shadow; but our Lord Jesus Christ is the one who brings in the things above the Law, and who gives the incomparably better freedom, that is, the one according to the Spirit. That is why he also said, even to those from Israel who had been freed in a bodily way, 'If you remain in my word, you are truly my disciples, and you will know the truth, and the truth will free you.' (John 8:31–32) And again, 'Everyone who does sin is a slave of sin. The slave does not remain in the house forever; the son remains forever. If then the Son frees you, you are free indeed.' (John 8:36)
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 2

comments.capsule: True freedom comes through faith in Christ, not through sacrifices, while every sin enslaves the soul.
comments.comment:
Sacrifices and sprinklings never freed from sins, but those who perform the worship in spirit through faith in Christ are freed, no longer ranked among slaves but among sons.

[John 8:34] Each sin, taking the soul captive as it were, makes it a slave of the passion.
comments.selected_reason: Explains in a few words what freedom and slavery to sin mean here.
comments.author: Ammonius of Alexandria

comments.capsule: 'Freedom' has several senses, and here it means holiness, the release from guilt that Jesus offers.
comments.comment: Then the Jews, not understanding what freedom Jesus meant, answered him: “We are Abraham's offspring and have never been anyone's slaves. How can you say, ‘You will be free’?” (John 8:33). “Freedom” is commonly used in many senses. Here it means holiness. In the apostle it means resurrection, when he says that creation is to be freed from slavery to corruption into the glorious freedom of God's children (Romans 8:21). In its better-known sense it is spoken of in contrast to slavery. The same name is also used for freedom of choice. Let us therefore distinguish the cases, so that things far apart are not confused because they share a name. Here the Lord does not say that freedom of choice needs to be set free. Rather, while it remains intact, he calls on the Jews to receive forgiveness and be freed from guilt, obtaining the freedom that is greatest in God's sight: to begin to owe no debt for crimes.
comments.author: Julian of Eclanum

comments.capsule: Only one who has himself committed sin is its slave, and Jesus sets the saints apart from slaves as sons who stay in the house.
comments.comment:
He made plain the slavery of which he was speaking: “Everyone who commits sin is a slave of sin” (John 8:34). … He says that no one is a slave of sin except someone who has himself committed sin, and that sin cannot cling to anyone unless the person in question has personally committed it, either in action or even by will alone. …

Here Christ separated not only himself but each of the saints from the condition of slaves. Such people existed both before and during the Old Testament; he declares that they remain in his Father's house and rejoice at his table (Luke 13:28–29).
comments.author: Julian of Eclanum

comments.capsule: Those under the law were slaves who could not stay in the house, but those Christ sets free are kept with God.
comments.comment:
Death was snatching away those still led according to the law, not having perfection in the law, nor being able to remain in the house forever as slaves, as it has been said, not yet having obtained adoption (John 8:35).

But death no longer snatches those who are set free in Christ; for grace already keeps such ones always with God, and the power of God rescues them from death.
comments.selected_reason: Explains 'the slave does not remain in the house for ever': only those Christ frees are kept with God.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: Only the Son, eternal and God by nature, can set others free, by the cleansing from sin that God alone gives.
comments.comment:
[The one who does not remain into the] age and always stays the same is a slave by nature and can free neither himself nor another; for all things are slaves of the Creator; but the Son remains into the age always the same as God by nature.

[John 8:36] Here he hints at the cleansing of sin, which God alone gives, which is true freedom and no other; those others have freedom only as far as the name.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the contrast of slave and son, and what 'free indeed' means.
comments.author: Ammonius of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Jesus grants their descent from Abraham but rebukes their lives, which show whose slaves they are.
comments.comment: To make you understand that he reproaches their lives rather than their nature, he continues: “I know that you are Abraham's children” (John 8:37). There is the dignity of descent on account of which they had declared themselves free. Now he shows the slavery to which they are subject: “You seek to kill me, because my word finds no room in you. I speak what I have heard with my Father; and you do what you have seen with your father” (John 8:37–38).
comments.author: Julian of Eclanum

comments.capsule: Being Abraham's seed is not the same as being his children, which only those who do his works are.
comments.comment: And the seed is often called a child: 'the seed of Abraham'—his children—not necessarily being both seed and child already. Regarding the Jews who cry out that they are the seed of Abraham, the Savior did not say: 'You lie,' but led forward: 'If you are children of Abraham, do the works of Abraham (John 8:39); for not all these are from Israel, the descendants of Israel. Nor is it that they are the seed of Abraham always a child.' He therefore says to them as not being children of Abraham: 'Do the desires of your father.' But those doing the desires of the devil, accepting him as father, are not children of Abraham. …
comments.selected_reason: Explains why Jesus grants they are Abraham's 'seed' yet denies they are his 'children'.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: What the Son has 'seen' with the Father is natural knowledge, not eyesight.
comments.comment: He has seen, and while speaking with the Father, he revealed not a sight of the eyes, but a natural knowledge (John 8:38); since he says that even those whom he calls having seen with their Father will not see from anywhere, but rather they are made to belong to the schemes of the evil one by the evilness dwelling in them.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: When Jesus calls himself 'a man', he speaks as God the Word made man, who gave himself, not some other man, for us.
comments.comment: How can anyone say that Christ is a perfect man separately and God the Word separately, when the Lord himself says, “Why do you seek to kill me, a man who has spoken the truth that I heard from the Father?” (John 7:19; John 8:40) For God the Word, made man for our sake, did not give a man for us, but handed himself over for us. That is why he says, “Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up” (John 2:19). But he was speaking of the temple of his body (John 2:21).
comments.selected_reason: Explains why Jesus calls himself 'a man' without making him two persons.
comments.author: Gregory Thaumaturgus

comments.capsule: Love for Jesus marks God's children, and 'I came forth' means his eternal birth from the Father while 'I have come' means his coming in the flesh.
comments.comment:
If you loved me, that was a sign that you were from God; for if love leads into adoption, how can you be numbered among God's sons when you do not love me who remake into my own form the one who believes in him, or because he is God by nature and Son of God. Yet those who live piously call God Father without blame.

"I came forth" signifies the unspoken and beginningless begetting from the Father; "I have come" the passage into this world with flesh.

By the Father's good pleasure, he says, I was incarnate and came into the world to speak to you the things from the Father.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the difference between 'I proceeded forth' and 'came I'.
comments.author: Ammonius of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Unwillingness, not inability, keeps them from hearing, because they copy the devil, the first murderer and the first liar.
comments.comment:
"You cannot" stands for "you will not" imagine anything great.

[John 8:44] He said this not because the devil caused them to be, but to become wicked, which happens from ways; as in brief the mind of the saying means this. Even if it is unclear, more fittingly the devil would be named your father, the man-killer who has a liar as father.

He calls Cain father of the Jews, who first among humans became leader of envy and murder and lie and deceit after Satan, whose son he would justly also be called; like him are the Jews and everyone who imitates them. Therefore it is no wonder that I too am Son of the true God who speaks true things, and you must believe me who speak true things. This one [the devil] through disobedience killed Adam and through him the rest of humans.

He first begot the lie, saying other things instead of other things to Eve.
comments.author: Ammonius of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Saying the devil 'does not stand' in the truth shows that he once stood in it.
comments.comment: But you are from your own father, the devil, and you desire to do the desires of your own father. For he has been a manslayer from the beginning, and he does not stand in the truth (John 8:44). And it is well to say, 'He does not stand,' showing him previously standing in the truth.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what 'abode not in the truth' implies about the devil.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The devil lies 'from his own' because no one else made him evil, while all other evildoers learn evil from him.
comments.comment: This also the Lord teaches in the Gospels, saying concerning him: 'When he speaks a lie, he speaks from his own, for he is a liar and his father is the father of lies' (John 8:44); that is, the father of lies; for the devil does not have a father according to those who act mythically. But all those using evil, except him, do not do so from their own, but come to this from his wickedness, … For no one else cast pride upon him, but he himself upon himself; …
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Jesus dares them to convict him of sin because, as unchangeable God, he cannot sin.
comments.comment: He said this that he might shame them even from the purity of his life: you have nothing to charge against what was done or said by me. He did not say this expecting to be convicted, but declaring that God, being unchangeable, cannot fall into sin; for every sin passes by turning from the better to the base.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the point of 'Which of you convinceth me of sin?'
comments.author: Ammonius of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Being 'of God' means kinship with him through a godly life, and 'hearing' means the soul's assent.
comments.comment:
He calls the faithful from God not according to essence, but according to receiving from him the pattern of piety and being made akin to him from virtue and lawful life. And "hears" is not with sense ears but with the soul's assents.

He shows that they did not believe him for this reason: not because they attended to him as opposed to God, but because they were alien to God.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what 'of God' and 'heareth' mean in this verse.
comments.author: Ammonius of Alexandria

comments.capsule: They call him a Samaritan for loosening the Law, and he bears insults to himself gently while leaving his glory to the Father.
comments.comment:
They call demon-possessed the one who commands demons, from boundless madness. …

They called the Lord a Samaritan as indifferent about the legal commands and loosing the Sabbath; for the Samaritans do not Judaize exactly.

[John 8:49] Here he is insulted and bears it gently, teaching us to overlook insults against ourselves. But where they said God was their "Father," he strikes them hard, training us to avenge what concerns God.

[John 8:50] Even if I through humility overlook my own honor, yet the Father seeks my glory and honor.

If I sought glory, I would not, "being in the form of God," have taken "a slave's form" (Philippians 2:6–7) and humbled myself for your salvation, nor would I have overlooked insults against me, but would have exacted penalties at once. Now you sin against God and Father, the sin ascending to him; for nothing at all stands between Father and Son, as far as identity of essence, even while each exists as contemplated on his own.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the 'Samaritan' insult and why Jesus answers so mildly.
comments.author: Ammonius of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The death that keeping Christ's word escapes is not bodily death but endless punishment in the age to come.
comments.comment:
Here he hints not only at faith but also seeks the pure life which the one who keeps this word makes.

He does not mean fleshly death, which we all undergo, but that as God he did not reckon the death which as God he could easily overturn; for here he names death the being punished through the age; and life is also the unceasing enjoyment.

By age he means the coming one, which is properly called age as having no end, where no one dies any longer after the resurrection given through Christ …
comments.author: Ammonius of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The Jews confused 'seeing death' with 'tasting' bodily death, but Jesus promises escape from the death that follows sin.
comments.comment: The Jews present, having misunderstood the Savior's saying that the one keeping the word will not see death (John 8:51), supposed that to taste it meant the same as seeing death; for it seemed to them that based on His words, He would not taste death without having experienced the cosmic death; but this seems to overturn the Lord's promise, since those who kept His word have died, and their desire has become a deceitful trickery through a false similarity. For the one keeping the word of Jesus will not see the death that follows sin (John 8:51), even if he shall taste the common and bodily death. …
comments.selected_reason: Explains the misunderstanding in 'thou sayest, If a man keep my saying, he shall never taste of death'.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The death that Christ's word saves from is not bodily death but eternal punishment, which is why the Jews ask if he is greater than Abraham.
comments.comment:
Having foretold that “he who is from God hears the words of God” (John 8:47), he now shows himself to be God by nature; this one keeps the divine commandment, sinning in no way and transgressing the divine acts; this one also hears the divine words. He says that death here is not the fleshly death, which all undergo, but he names as death that which is to come, the punishment for eternity, which is Gehenna and “the worm” [Mark 9:48]; for indeed life is an unending enjoyment for the age, for he says, “the age to come” (John 8:52).

Then they say to him, “Do you make yourself greater than Abraham and the prophets, promising to make others greater than them? What are you making of yourself, promising to give less of the zeal from God?”
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: Jesus alone truly knows the Father, so saying so is truth, not boasting.
comments.comment:
That is: those who heard God's word died, and those who hear your word will not die?

[John 8:55] For only the Son knows the Father naturally and knowingly—or rather the Trinity knows itself. To say "I know him" is not boast; to say one does not know is a lie; for you, saying you know him, lie.
comments.author: Ammonius of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Abraham's 'day' is the cross, foreshadowed when the ram was offered in Isaac's place, and Abraham rejoiced at it.
comments.comment:
He shows them alien to Abraham even in this, since in what that one rejoiced these grieve.

He seems to mean the day of the cross, which was prefigured in the ram's slaughter and Isaac's offering. Therefore he did not come unwilling to the passion, if indeed he praises the one who rejoiced at the cross's passion.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what Abraham's seeing 'my day' means.
comments.author: Ammonius of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Jesus says Abraham 'came to be' but he himself 'is', setting a creature that perishes against his own eternity.
comments.comment:
The Jews' saying is senseless; for he was speaking to them about his own eternity, while they talked as to one just beginning to be; and the Lord said Abraham saw my day, but they took the opposite, that he himself saw Abraham.

[John 8:58] He was before all, but he mentioned only Abraham because the talk was about him.

Of Abraham he set "came to be," because what has come to be also perishes; of himself "I am," as eternal and better than corruption.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the contrast between 'Abraham was' and 'I am'.
comments.author: Ammonius of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Unborn people cannot sin, nor bear others' sins.
comments.comment: This question is mistaken; neither does anyone sin before being born who does not exist at all, nor is another punished for another.
comments.author: Ammonius of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Jesus' answer overturns the false teaching that souls sin before birth and are sent into bodies as punishment.
comments.comment: In this, the Savior himself was overturning an unlawful doctrine. For some people supposed that sinning souls are sent from heaven into a body for the sake of punishment, and that sometimes the soul remains pre-existing by itself apart from the body, while at other times it is intertwined with bodies on account of its own sins—so that a woman can conceive only when some soul sins. Destroying this error, Christ, when he was asked, said: "Neither this man sinned nor his parents, but this happened so that the works of God might be revealed" (John 9:3).
comments.author: Theophilus of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Since the man could not have sinned before birth, the disciples blamed his parents, but Jesus says the blindness serves to reveal God's power.
comments.comment: Since the blind man was blind from birth, it appears to the disciples to seek the cause; and as it was impossible for him to commit the same sin before being born, they look to that of the parents. For he knew through the grief of parents that there are sufferings concerning children. But the Lord says that blindness does not come because of some sin, but for the sake of the glory of God about to be, for the purpose of the power of God being known through the paradoxically occurring sight (John 9:7).
comments.selected_reason: Explains the disciples' question and Jesus' answer about the cause of the blindness.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: The 'day' is this life, the time for good works, and the 'night' is the age to come, when nothing more can be done.
comments.comment: … But the Savior, having said, 'Until it is day, work the works of light; night comes when no one is able to work' (John 9:4), urged the conduct in this life as providing us the time for works, but referred to the night as the things to come and the eternal, as when it is no longer possible to do anything, but as being in darkness in inaction, having lost the time for works.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what 'day' and 'night' mean in this saying.
comments.author: Diodorus of Tarsus

comments.capsule: By forming eyes from clay Jesus shows he is the one who formed Adam from clay, and the healed man stands for the nations who once were blind.
comments.comment:
He called himself light of the world as enlightening the faithful's souls and because he was about to open the eyes of the one "blind from birth" (John 9:1).

He spat on the ground and made clay from the spittle and anointed the clay on the blind man's eyes, wanting to show through the clay that he himself is the one who also fashioned Adam from clay; for to say "I am the one who did this" seemed offensive to the hearers. But being shown through the work, this no longer stood in the way. Therefore not simply, but in that manner, he crafted the eyes; and he not only formed and opened but also granted seeing, which is proof that he also ensouled Adam with the soul; for if that is not active, an eye, even if finished, would never see.

[John 9:7] This looks toward an image of those from the nations once blind, now enlightened and teaching Israel Christ's power.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why Jesus uses clay, and why he calls himself the light just before the healing.
comments.author: Ammonius of Alexandria

comments.capsule: John notes that Siloam means 'Sent' because the healing shows the Creator's power sent to renew his creation and cleanse it from sin.
comments.comment: The participation of Siloam in the work, which is interpreted as having been sent, just as the evangelist did not mark in vain, shows the sending of the Creator's power toward the renewal of his own creation, being made purifying from sins, of which the water of the bath was a symbol, and through the cleansing of sins bringing back health and bringing the diseased and purified nature into perfection.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why John translates the name Siloam.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: The Pharisees question the man not to learn the truth but to frighten him by the way they ask.
comments.comment: But the Pharisees and the rulers of the Jews, seeing that the wonder has many attracting to Christ, being bitten by the zeal of impiety, and being struck by the sting of the truth, call the once-blind man in. And it was to see an evil theater, of piety being avenged, and of evil judges judging, and of a great advocate contending, and of God rewarding and overseeing. They call the once-blind and having seen again, the children of the Jews, and they set him in the midst of the council, and say to him: 'Tell how you received sight, and who opened your eyes to you, and what he did to you?' (John 9:15). These things they said, not that they might know, but that by the form of the question they might instill fear. For often the form of the question becomes to the one asked a teacher to answer, or to be silent; …
comments.author: Severianus of Gabala

comments.capsule: The Pharisees ignore the healing and fault only the making of clay on the Sabbath, though serving God's work is the true keeping of the Sabbath.
comments.comment: And that he made the blind man see on the Sabbath, they do not consider; but that 'he made clay' , they judge, being scoffers of the Lord, working his works many times on this day, so that from the 'slavery under the elements' Galatians 4:3, as the apostle says, he might free the men having made them fit from the Sabbath-slavery into the slavery of God; for to work the work of God according to the Sabbath-rule is to serve God instead of the Sabbath.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the Pharisees fasten on the clay and the Sabbath.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: Unafraid, the man tells what happened, knowing the benefit though not yet who his benefactor was.
comments.comment: … How did you see? Who opened your eyes? But he, caring less for the threat, possessed more of the truth, and says: A certain man, called Jesus, having made clay, anointed my eyes and said to me: 'Go, wash in the Siloam' (John 9:6). And having gone, I washed, and I saw. He did not know the truth, but he recognized the benefit; he did not yet know the merit of the benefactor. A certain man, having made clay, anointed my eyes, and I see.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the man speaks only of 'a man called Jesus'.
comments.author: Severianus of Gabala

comments.capsule: They charge Christ for clay made with one finger on the Sabbath while they water and rescue animals with their whole hand.
comments.comment: From extreme impiety they preferred the Sabbath to his divine power and blaspheming said that this man is not from God. For Christ, having anointed the clay with one finger on the Sabbath, is charged, while they with a whole hand loosing animals and leading them to drink and pulling up sheep fallen into a pit are not accused.
comments.author: Ammonius of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The Pharisees hope to make the healed man disown Jesus, but he boldly calls him a prophet, as far as he yet understood.
comments.comment:
Not as needing to learn something, these approach the question from the blind man (John 9:15), but as if shaming him with something more defamatory against the Lord because of the perceived brevity regarding the Sabbath (John 9:17); for they thought that being among many, they would drag one down, and these things were meager and cheap, but they thought it great to stop the praise for him and to be able to condemn the thing done not being testified by him who was healed. But he did not show fear, having known the Lord through trial (John 9:17), but as much as he was able to grasp, he says about him to be a prophet, and this appropriately, since he did not know the authority of the divinity, not knowing that he had made him by his own power.

So much does a pre-conceived dogma and a certain disposition toward the passing of right upon things prevail, and to darken the reasoning.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the Pharisees ask the man's opinion and why he answers 'He is a prophet'.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: Failing with the man, they try to frighten his parents, for faith cannot live in a quarrelsome soul.
comments.comment: Not finding the denial they wanted from the healed one, they seek this from the parents, hoping that they, having been disturbed, would be accomplices to them in denying, because this one born blind is the one now seeing . But the evangelist says that they do not even believe; for faith does not dwell in a contentious soul and in a soul arraying itself against the power of God, so that they are not without cause for their unbelief, but are even greatly to blame, having constructed hardness within themselves, through which they did not receive the good of faith. They disturb the parents, accusing them, saying that they say their son was born blind; how, they say, to see a son [John 9:28].
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: God let the man be of legal age, so he could speak for himself and his parents' testimony could settle that he had been blind.
comments.comment:
Again the same form of questioning: 'This is your son, whom you say was born blind? (John 9:19) How then does he see now?' They, having perceived the way of malice, that they are bringing threats, say to them: 'We know that this is our son; and that he was born blind we know; but how he sees now, or who opened his eyes, we do not know; he has age, ask him; he himself will speak about himself. And see the wisdom of God.'

So that they might not divert his voice, the one who had seen, as if he were a child, or as if he did not know how to speak, as in common courts, God caused him first to be shown in the age of law [of legal age]. 'He has age,' they say; 'ask him'; because immature advocates are needed, but those bringing maturity, they themselves become their own advocates.

… The parents testified so that there would be no doubt that he was not blind.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the point of 'he is of age; ask him'.
comments.author: Severianus of Gabala

comments.capsule: If the healing is God's work and God is owed the glory, then the one who did it, Christ, is God.
comments.comment: Since they were not able to deny it, they endeavored instead to cover it, and they say: 'Give glory to God; we know that this man is a sinful human.' The glory of the Son is the glory of the Father, and the glory is undivided. … They say to him, 'Give glory to God.' How? By our law? And is it right to benefit another and for another to be glorified? 'Give glory to God.' Another benefactor, and to another should I give glory? They confessed that Jesus made clay and anointed his eyes; does the one who opened them confess, and should I give the glory to another? Why should I give glory to God? Because this work is the work of God. Therefore, seeing, you confess that Christ is God. 'Give glory to God.' For if the work is of God, and to Him the glory is owed, the maker of the work is God Himself.
comments.selected_reason: Shows how 'Give God the praise' turns against the Pharisees.
comments.author: Severianus of Gabala

comments.capsule: They praise God's work but condemn its doer.
comments.comment: Foolish are the Jews who bid God be glorified because of the wonder, yet condemn the one who did God's work.
comments.author: Ammonius of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The man answers as Jesus himself had answered, and by asking 'Will you also become his disciples?' he admits that he is one.
comments.comment:
“You did not hear; why do you wish to hear me again? Do you not also wish to become his disciples?” (John 9:27). And he who has not yet heard Christ's teaching imitates it. For the Jews, having surrounded the Savior in Solomon's Colonnade during the festivals (John 10:23), said to him: “How long will you lift up our soul? If you are the Christ, tell us plainly.” He says to them: “I said to you, and you did not hear; why do you wish to hear again?” And see the piety of the advocate.

Because he paid attention to the malice of the Jews, for they do everything and shape threats and fear to be cast upon him so that he might not confess himself teacher, he says to them: “I said to you already, and you did not hear; why do you wish to hear again? Do you not also wish to become his disciples?” By saying, “Do you not also?”, he showed that the “I am” is being confessed.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the force of 'will ye also be his disciples?'
comments.author: Severianus of Gabala

comments.capsule: The Pharisees' 'we do not know where he is from' betrays ignorance of both his births, and the healed man turns their words against them.
comments.comment: You say this out of arrogance. What they say is such a thing. We know that God through Moses gave law, but this one we do not know, except as one loosening the law; for on the Sabbath he healed the blind; for it is for this purpose they say they do not know him . And that you are a disciple of him, they say as if you are disparaging him; and that he does not know, they say as if they are able to conceive nothing concerning the suspicion of his birth according to the flesh, nor anything concerning his unspeakable birth. What then is against this the healed one? From these same words he perceives them and makes them fall upon themselves. This, he says, the wonderful thing, that you do not know where he is from, surpasses human comprehension. Furthermore, since he himself has not spoken from above, but knowing, for he says, 'we know that God does not hear sinners' , that he has spoken.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: One man stands alone against the crowd of his accusers and argues that a healing never heard of before proves Jesus is from God.
comments.comment: Then what was against him from the Jews? They mocked him and said: “You are a disciple of that man, but we are disciples of Moses. We know that God spoke to Moses; but this one we do not know from where he is.” Consider the multitude of the objectors, and the power of one standing against them. And the advocate of the truth did not be silent again, but stood firm, saying, “For in this it is wonderful,” saying, that you do not know from where he is, and he opened my eyes (John 9:30). … He stands struggling, and God is the overseer and the judge; many are terrible against one strong man, an unbelieving cloud against a single drop of faith. From the age, he says, it was not heard that someone opened the eyes of one born blind (John 9:32). If this man were not from God, he would not have been able to do anything. Because you magnify yourselves, he says, in the teaching of Moses. He does not mention Moses at all, …
comments.author: Severianus of Gabala

comments.capsule: God works wonders through the righteous, not through sinners.
comments.comment: Not as a respecter of persons—God forbid—but as just and lover of the just, God works wonders through the saints, not through those who sin.
comments.author: Ammonius of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The man's point is that no prophet ever opened the eyes of one born blind.
comments.comment: … For he says, 'From the beginning of the age it has not been heard that anyone opened the eyes of one born blind' (John 9:32), that is, 'Who else opened them, a prophet?' Nor did they see the superiority, nor the comparison. But as much as this man held to the truth, so much did they not cease from shamelessness.
comments.author: Severianus of Gabala

comments.capsule: Cast out of the synagogue for his bold witness, the man is met outside by Jesus, as a wrestler by the judge of the contest.
comments.comment:
… He spoke with such boldness that they ordered him to be cast out. And they cast him out, says the evangelist, out (John 9:34). Blessed is the one set apart from the synagogue of evildoers. And see what happens. Because he contended the good struggle, and sympathized with the glory of God, and confessed the Savior gloriously with much boldness; and while his theater was being filled with wrestling matches, the wrestler was cast out without receiving the crown, and the referee meets him outside.

For Jesus heard, he says, that they had cast him out; and finding him, he says to him. Oh, the speech of the one finding him! That which error destroys, truth finds. Why then did he meet him? The Savior saw a soul full of gratitude; he saw a soul not yet having been made known to speak concerning God, but considering him to be some faithful prophet; …
comments.selected_reason: Explains why Jesus seeks out the man after he is cast out.
comments.author: Severianus of Gabala

comments.capsule: Jesus asks in order to teach that faith in him is faith in God made man.
comments.comment: He asks not as ignorant; for he knew that he believed, since he had contended against Jews, but showing that he greatly delights in his believing, he teaches that the one who believes in Jesus does not believe as in one human among us, but as in God become man; for thus the mystery concerning Christ is full.
comments.author: Ammonius of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The man had never seen Jesus' face, so he asks who the Son of God is, but he knows the voice, and Jesus leads him from 'prophet' to faith in the Son of God.
comments.comment:
Suspecting a human, he struggles thus: what will he do if he learns the glory of the deity? … Therefore, moreover, the Lord corrected him toward knowledge, having received the struggle, and having sealed the faith for him.

The Savior answers him; for this one did not recognize the character. For when He sent him to the pool of Siloam to wash, He sent him blind; but when he returned seeing, he did not see the Savior because of the crowd being mixed there, but immediately, before seeing the Master, having been called into the struggle, he struggled. … When therefore He sent him out, Christ finding him, said to him: 'Do you believe in the Son of God?' (John 9:35). For it is not necessary for you to believe in a struggling man as a prophet, but as the Son of God.

That one, not having recognized the face, recognized the voice. 'Do you believe,' He says, 'in the Son of God?' He knew the voice, and with delight he cried out, 'And who is He, Lord, so that I may believe in Him?' … And the prophet replied: 'And you have seen Him, and the one speaking with you, He is that one.'
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the man asks 'Who is he?': he had never seen Jesus.
comments.author: Severianus of Gabala

comments.capsule: Jesus never blinded anyone's bodily eyes, so the blinding he speaks of is of those who see wrongly.
comments.comment: … Jesus says he works [this blindness] in the Gospel, saying: 'I came that those who do not see might see, and those who see might become blind' (John 9:39). But Jesus, according to history, has made no one blind, but has granted sight to the blind. It is therefore evident that he makes those who see badly blind, and makes those who are useful to see again with the useful eyes, …
comments.selected_reason: Explains how Jesus, who only gave sight, can say he came 'that they which see might be made blind'.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: We have two kinds of eyes, and the Word opens the soul's eyes while closing the eyes of sense so the soul can see without distraction.
comments.comment: That is why our Saviour too, knowing that we have this twofold kind of eyes, says: “For judgement I came into this world, that those who do not see may see, and that those who see may become blind” (John 9:39). By “those who do not see” he hints at the eyes of the soul, which the Word makes see; by “those who see,” at the eyes of the senses; and these the Word blinded, so that the soul might see without distraction what it ought.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: His condemners are themselves condemned as sinners.
comments.comment: That is: unto greater punishment; for those who condemned him as a sinner are themselves condemned as sinners.
comments.author: Ammonius of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Those blind from ignorance seem to have no sin, yet ignorance of good and evil is itself a sin of neglect.
comments.comment: The "eyes of the heart" have been enlightened (Ephesians 1:18), shining by the light of the true one. The one opposite, being blinded by that which causes ignorance, seems not to have sin because he does not act willingly or sluggishly sinning. But this ignorance in another way is sin; for it was logical to have the knowledge of good and evil. Therefore, he is accused for the neglect of this, in favor of that ignorance. For this, the "slave who did not know the will of the master will be given little" (Luke 12:48).
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The thief is one who seizes honor not given him or teaches by a way the Scriptures do not authorize, like the scribes.
comments.comment: A thief is the one who by force snatches honor not given him, which he cannot receive unless one who believes in Christ—or a thief is the one who does not use the teaching authorized from the Scriptures but comes through another unauthorized way. Therefore he also said "from elsewhere," that he might signify the scribes who teach "human commandments" (Mark 7:7) and transgress the law.
comments.selected_reason: Explains who the 'thief' is who climbs in 'some other way'.
comments.author: Ammonius of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The parable fits this moment, just after the man born blind was cast out.
comments.comment: The time for such a parable is most opportune, the present one, teaching about those exiting from the Jewish synagogue; for they indeed brought out those who, having “looked up blind from birth” through the testimony concerning Christ, had been healed.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the parable follows the casting out of the man born blind.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: The porter is Israel's guardian angel, who gladly opens to the King and hands over his charge.
comments.comment: And the one opening the door to the shepherd and opening the entrance decorously is the overseer of Israel, an angel who gladly receives the king's presence and hands over to the greater oversight those entrusted to him according to the measure of the domestic commission; for, he says, we were “under stewards” and “deputies” (Galatians 4:2).
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: The sheep take right teaching as food, and the shepherd walks in front to lead them to the truth.
comments.comment:
When the faithful hear from right teachers the divine teachings of the Scriptures, they receive them as some food; but as many as call Christ a deceiver have been cast out of the order of the sheep.

[John 10:4] Though shepherds customarily walk behind the sheep, this one walks in front of the sheep, showing that he [guides all toward the truth].
comments.selected_reason: Explains why this shepherd goes before his sheep.
comments.author: Ammonius of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The sheep who follow are the Israelites who leave bodily pursuits behind, and calling them by name shows that he chooses those with spiritual aims.
comments.comment:
For the sheep, being well-led by the shepherd, knowing his voice and following him as he leads, are the people of Israel—those who leave behind bodily pursuits and follow the Lord as he exits the world. …

The shepherd calling his own sheep by name also shows the election of those with spiritual pursuits, according to what was said in the prophets: “but you shall gather the sons of Israel one by one”; “for not all have faith.”

Nor are all able, since they do not even want to depart from the accustomed habits and be freed from the worldly effort, but to live according to divine discipline and the supra-cosmic, toward which also the Lord guides his own disciples, going before them.
comments.selected_reason: Explains calling the sheep 'by name' and the shepherd going before them.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: The 'strangers' are false messiahs, and a proverb carries two meanings.
comments.comment:
By strangers he means those around Theudas [Acts 5:36], whose hearers were scattered, and the other false christs.

[John 10:6] He calls the saying a proverb because through one saying two matters' meanings are understood.
comments.author: Ammonius of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Christ is the door that keeps the sheep safe and shuts out thieves, the way to the Father, and the entrance to the pasture of divine teaching.
comments.comment:
As God, knowing they did not understand, he clarifies the saying to them from the start, that they may still be benefited.

He is door as shutting in the sheep and keeping thieves out and convicting them; or because only through faith in him we enter toward the Father and are made his own; or because through him we come to rule peoples; or because he receives the worthy into the holy court and shuts entrance to the unworthy.

[John 10:8] Saying "all" the Lord does not mean the holy prophets but those pretending to be good and slipping into ruling peoples, whom those under them did not endure—or he means the false christs or those around Theudas.

[John 10:9] The faithful are sent on through Christ as through a door into eternal life.

Pasture is the divine teachings which the faithful enjoy. The Word of God is a door leading into knowledge of God; and those who enter through him become outside the world.

By pasture he means security, which happened for the apostles, who as lords of the inhabited world went in and out and no one could cast them out.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the door, the 'thieves and robbers', and the pasture.
comments.author: Ammonius of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The thieves before him are teachers who led people away from the Law into pagan life, not the Law itself.
comments.comment:
Who then would be the thieves and robbers who came before the Lord and were not heard by the sheep?

And who else but those who taught the law departed through the transfer to the Gentile life, those leading to the alienation of God and bringing destruction through that alienation.

Therefore the Lord most necessarily shows a difference from himself from those who transferred from the law, which the apostle also observes by saying: 'For I died by the law according to the law so that I might live to God' (Galatians 2:19); that is, the law was not set aside through lawlessness so that I might be driven into death, but through the truly lawful and divine polity, which leads toward eternal life.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: The Word is the door through which the mind enters toward God and goes out again.
comments.comment:
The word of God becomes a door to those entering toward God according to "enter before Him in gladness" (Ps 100:2); with this, the mind is inside the man, but the body is outside.

Saying that one, attending to the inner man, enters through the Word which is a door, just as the dead, surrounding 'the members upon the earth' and 'the death of Jesus in the flesh' around himself, goes out 'through the door' striving to be pleasing even to one not residing within.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Christ feeds his flock by the Spirit so they no longer need the Law's commands, and gives eternal life and the kingdom, which is the abundance.
comments.comment:
And he led the followers onto pasture and life-giving nourishment, because by the power of the Spirit he feeds them so that they no longer need legal commands, but are led by rational doctrines; for he says, 'having abolished the law of commandments in doctrines' (Ephesians 2:15).

[John 10:10] Indeed, law was given unable to give life, but the Word gives the life of Christ regarding eternal things from the good temporary things, and not life only, but also granting the kingdom within life, which is the abundance.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: The 'more abundant' life is the kingdom of heaven and the Spirit's glory given to the saints, and he came willingly to suffer for it.
comments.comment:
By "more abundantly" he means the kingdom of the heavens, which he calls life because the name is familiar to them; hinting at the resurrection he said the abundance. Or the abundance means participation in the Spirit, which only the saints enjoy, though all rise commonly, wicked and good; for only the saints are changed into glory. Here he speaks about the saving passion into which he came willingly.

When all had been slaughtered and destroyed, Christ came to save and give life.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what 'life more abundantly' means.
comments.author: Ammonius of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Where hired shepherds fed themselves and fled, the Lord took charge of the sheep and died to sin for us, as God promised in Ezekiel.
comments.comment:
For since false and not good shepherds have stood, shepherds of hire who were for a portion of pleasure, to whom the sheep did not matter, but they were feeding their own pleasure, fleeing from this—the coming of the wolf to the sheep, that is, the destruction that accompanies wickedness—the Lord, so that we might not perish before sin, having taken up such oversight and died to sin for us.

But those shepherds gave the sheep over to sin, feeding 'themselves' as Ezekiel says (Ezekiel 34:2) and 'not the sheep.'

Therefore also God said: 'I will shepherd the sheep' (Ezekiel 34:15) and fulfilled this through the Lord shepherding.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: The hirelings are the rulers, who did not care for a people not their own.
comments.comment: He names hireling neglecting the sheep each of the people's rulers, since they did nothing for the peoples' benefit but used them as foreigners; for they were not their own, therefore they were not grieved at the peoples' destruction.
comments.selected_reason: Explains who the hireling is.
comments.author: Ammonius of Alexandria

comments.capsule: We know God only because he first knew us by becoming man, and the Son knows the Father by sharing his nature and proves himself the good shepherd by dying willingly for the sheep.
comments.comment:
We do not know God otherwise unless first we are known from him. Therefore he also set that first; for first he was made akin to us by becoming man, and so we too to him.

"I am the shepherd" he said because of those who disbelieved; for not all the sheep heard him, but those known from him and knowing him.

[John 10:15] Through identity of nature as consubstantial with the Father I know him and am known by him.

From laying down his own soul that they may be saved he establishes himself as good shepherd and not a deceiver such as those around Theudas; for he offered himself as ransom for all.

Saying "I lay down" he showed that he suffered willingly.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why 'I know my sheep' comes before 'am known of mine', and what shows the good shepherd.
comments.author: Ammonius of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The sheep know Christ by virtue as he knows the Father by nature, the first imitating the second.
comments.comment:
Having said that even the sheep know him (John 10:14), and to this he gave the likeness, saying to the sheep that the knowledge toward him is such as his toward the Father.

This indeed is among men the knowledge of the Lord according to virtue, but in the Lord the knowledge of the Father according to nature; for the likeness according to virtue imitates that which is good by nature.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the comparison 'as the Father knoweth me, even so know I the Father'.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: The other sheep are those outside, whom Christ, once the Pharisees were cast out, would bring from all nations to the knowledge of God.
comments.comment:
All are sheep, yet because of difference of mind he says they are not of this fold, which is the world.

He shows that when the Pharisees are cast out he was going as God to rule the nations and lead all into knowledge of God, Jews and Greeks, the one proclaimed beforehand by Moses and many prophets as going to do this.
comments.author: Ammonius of Alexandria
