comments.capsule: The 'fold' is the court of the Jews, and the other sheep from the nations are gathered into the Church, the truly holy court.
comments.comment: The Lord also called the court of the Jews a court when he said, "I have other sheep that are not of this court" (John 10:16), showing clearly that there is also another court, the truly holy one, which was to gather Christ's sheep—those from the nations predestined for salvation. That is, this Church, in which true worshipers worship in spirit and truth.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what 'this fold' and the 'other sheep' are.
comments.author: Basil of Caesarea

comments.capsule: The Father's love and command are spoken in lowly human terms, and the command is to die for the world.
comments.comment:
He says he is loved because of the virtuous deed. Clearly virtue is to die for impiety. He speaks lowly because of the incarnation; for he did not now begin to be loved by the Father.

[John 10:18] The command declares the concord with the Father, even if he speaks lowly. And the command is to die for the world.
comments.selected_reason: Explains 'therefore doth my Father love me' and 'this commandment'.
comments.author: Ammonius of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Jesus gave up his soul by his own authority, dying before the executioners came to break his legs.
comments.comment: Now my Jesus said of his own soul, which was parted from the body not by the necessity common to men but by the extraordinary authority given to him over this also: “No one takes my soul from me, but I lay it down of myself. I have authority to lay it down, and I have authority to take it again” (John 10:18). For since he had “authority to lay it down,” he laid it down when he said, “Father, why have you forsaken me?” (Matthew 27:46; Mark 15:34) and, “crying out with a loud voice, he gave up the spirit” (Matthew 27:50). In this he forestalled the executioners in charge of the crucified, who cut the legs of those crucified, and cut them for this reason, that they may not suffer punishment any longer (compare John 19:31–33).
comments.selected_reason: Shows how the crucifixion bears out 'I have power to lay it down'.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: His words seemed superhuman, and his silence teaches patience under insult.
comments.comment: Since what was said was beyond human, they called him demon-possessed. And by being silent when he heard these things the Lord taught us to bear insults against ourselves gently.
comments.author: Ammonius of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Jesus avoided speaking about himself and showed he was the Christ by deeds, which is why they demand that he say it plainly.
comments.comment: One may see this also in the character of Jesus, who everywhere avoided speaking about himself and for that reason said, “Even if I speak about myself, my testimony is not true” (John 5:31). And since he avoided speaking about himself, and wished to show that he was the Christ by his deeds rather than by his words, for this reason the Jews say to him, “If you are the Christ, tell us plainly” (John 10:24).
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the Jews demand 'tell us plainly'.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: His names light, shepherd and way already declared him the Christ.
comments.comment: Even if he did not say himself plainly Christ, yet by calling himself light, shepherd, way, he signified this; for with these names Scripture is accustomed to call the Christ.
comments.selected_reason: Explains how Jesus had already 'told' them he was the Christ.
comments.author: Ammonius of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Christ's sheep show themselves by obeying and imitating him, and his 'hand' is the power from which no one can snatch them.
comments.comment: Proof of the Lord's sheep is readiness to hear; of strangers, disobedience. For hearing here means obeying what is said, and following means imitation through deeds. He says he gives life, which he also calls eternal: living in cheer and unbroken blessedness. And to perish into the age means to be subject to unceasing torments. By his hand he means the power and authority from which no one can snatch those who follow him.
comments.selected_reason: Explains 'hear', 'follow', 'perish' and 'my hand'.
comments.author: Ammonius of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Death no longer snatches those freed in Christ, whom he made his own again by coming, and he reigns in the flesh as the same King through whom the Father reigns.
comments.comment:
Death was snatching away those still led according to the law, not having perfection in the law, nor being able to remain in the house forever as slaves, as it has been said, not yet having obtained adoption (John 8:35).

But death no longer snatches those who are set free in Christ; for grace already keeps such ones always with God, and the power of God rescues them from death.

[John 10:29] In this way also the Lord acquires us, not as being outside his creative power, since he also 'came to his own' (John 1:11) and all things were naturally his own, but as having fallen away from his holiness because of sin, and being made his own through his coming.

For having acquired a kingdom according to the flesh, he himself is king over those who have fallen, and he is not a different one from the King who is from the beginning and by nature, through whom the Father reigns. Therefore he says that the things given to him and the things reigning through him are being reigned by the Father.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: The Father gives the Son those whom he reveals the Son to, yet Judas, though given, fell by his own change, not by being made evil.
comments.comment:
The Father gives to the Son those having been made according to the good as having an unsurpassed quality; for 'all that the Father gives to me shall come to me' [John 6:37], and 'behold, I and the children whom God has given to me' [Hebrews 2:13]. For just as the Son leads to the Father and hands over to him those to whom he touches himself to provide for understanding according to the one who 'having seen me has seen the Father', so the Father gives these to the Son, whom he makes known to them, just as to Peter; for not 'flesh and blood, but the Father has revealed' the Son. All those having known the Son thus from the Father attain to those things given to the Son through the exceeding perfection of these having such things.

How about Judas? Being one of those given by the Father to the Son according to the ones 'whom I have given', and 'no one was lost of them except the son of perdition' [John 17:12], he fell from such great magnitude as to be called 'a son of perdition'; for there was not yet room in the construction for Judas to be evil, as the heterodox suppose, such a change being found concerning him.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Judas's fall shows humans are not evil by nature.
comments.comment: Since Judas also was one of those given to the Son and fell into wickedness, humans are shown not evil by nature and essence, but [turning willingly].
comments.author: Ammonius of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The hand is one, called now his and now the Father's, so 'I and the Father are one' means one power and essence, while 'I and the Father' keeps them distinct.
comments.comment:
And even if as God by nature he himself gives from himself, yet as man he is also said to receive. He says this not as if through the Father's power alone no one snatches them because he himself is insufficient to keep them, but so they may not call him opposed to God; for he said beforehand that no one snatches them from my hand, and showing that this hand is one, he says it is sometimes his and sometimes the Father's; for he himself is the Father's right hand. Then lest through these words someone think the Son less than the Father, he added next: "I and the Father are one" (John 10:30)—clearly according to the power which he also calls hand.

Signifying that Father and Son are not one according to hypostasis [person], he said "I and the Father"; for they are one in essence, in the power which he also calls hand, sometimes his and sometimes the Father's.
comments.selected_reason: Explains how the 'hand' of the Son and of the Father leads to 'I and my Father are one'.
comments.author: Ammonius of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Father and Son are two distinct realities yet one, as the first believers were of one heart and soul, so Christians worship one God.
comments.comment: … if Celsus had understood the words “I and the Father are one” (John 10:30), and those spoken in prayer by the Son of God, “as I and You are one” (John 17:22), he would not have supposed that we worship any other besides the God who is over all. For “the Father”, He says, “is in me, and I in the Father” (John 10:38). But if anyone is troubled by these words, fearing that we may somehow be going over to those who deny that the Father and the Son are two distinct realities, let him attend to the words “the heart and soul of all who believed were one” (Acts 4:32), so that he may understand “I and the Father are one” (John 10:30). So, as we have explained, we worship one God, the Father and the Son.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Jesus calmly asks for which of his works they stone him, works done to do good and not merely to amaze, which they cannot deny.
comments.comment:
Thus the Jews bore up stones, in order to stone him, bringing upon him this punishment which he himself had appointed from the beginning against the ungodly, and through this alone being able to release those who are now running for his grace through philanthropy.

[John 10:32] Upon these things the Lord was undisturbed, since he himself had the authority to suffer, being unable otherwise unless he himself willed it.

And he asks through what kind of work, which he showed to them from the Father, they are stoning him.

He says he is showing beautiful things [the "good works"], that all the wonders by him happen because of the beautiful, and not for the sake of a wonder alone; for he did not appear to astonish, but to do good.

[John 10:33] The Jews answered him through the wise question, agreeing rightly; for they did not have the power to say that they had not seen good works, but they are slandering the truth of the words, which they ought rather to believe because of the demonstration of the good works.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what Jesus means by 'many good works' and why the Jews answer as they do.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: His works belong to the whole Godhead, and the Jews called his confession blasphemy because they did not know God would come in the flesh.
comments.comment:
The works are not mine alone but of the whole Godhead; for the Father does all things through the Son in the Holy Spirit, and he teaches us to be moderate and not boast if we receive something from God.

[John 10:33] Not knowing that the Son was not going to sojourn with bare Godhead but incarnate "from David's seed" (Romans 1:3), they called the right confession blasphemy.
comments.author: Ammonius of Alexandria

comments.capsule: 'Make yourself God' means 'show yourself to be God' by what he claimed and promised.
comments.comment: You also have in the Gospel what is said by the Jews, that 'being a man, you make yourself God' (John 10:33). For they do not say: 'Being a man, you are preparing yourself to be God', but rather 'From those things which you announce and promise to do, you demonstrate yourself to be God'.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the sense of 'makest thyself God'.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Creatures are called 'gods' only by sharing in the Word, which is why Christ alone can say 'I and the Father are one'.
comments.comment: He calls 'gods' those who were created but became partakers of the Word, as the Lord himself said: 'If he called them gods to whom the Word of God came' (John 10:35). But things that partake cannot be the same as, or like, the thing they partake of. About himself, then, he said, 'I and the Father are one' (John 10:30), because created things are not like that.
comments.selected_reason: Explains how men can be called 'gods' without being like the Son.
comments.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
comments.work: Synodal Letter to the Bishops of Africa

comments.capsule: If men are called gods by grace, the Son by nature is blameless, and 'sanctified' means set apart for sacrifice.
comments.comment:
If Israelites, filthy humans who received this by grace, are not charged, how is the one who has this by nature rebuked?

[John 10:36] The Son is said to be sanctified because he was sent to be slaughtered for the world's salvation; for holy are the things set apart to God for sacrifice.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the argument from 'Ye are gods' and what 'sanctified' means.
comments.author: Ammonius of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Since God's essence cannot be seen, equal works show equal power, and Father and Son are in each other by one nature though distinct.
comments.comment:
Since seeing the essence is impossible, from equality of works he presents the indistinguishability of power, through which he says the Father is known from himself and he himself from the Father.

"I am in the Father and the Father is seen in me" according to identity of nature and essence; for one is the definition of nature, even if we conceive the holy Trinity in distinct existences; for the Father is not Son or Spirit nor the reverse, even if they are not in separation because of their mutual communion and equality; for even among us the begetter's essence is known and in the begotten the father according to the account of essence, yet because we are separated by bodies, we the many are no longer "one."
comments.author: Ammonius of Alexandria

comments.capsule: He slips away so as not to reveal his divinity too plainly.
comments.comment: In order that the divinity might not be made too clearly manifest, joining with those approaching to seize him and not being seized, and that he might not disrupt the rhythm of human order (John 10:39).
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: His easy escape shows he could be taken only if he willed, and he goes to the Jordan to recall John's witness.
comments.comment:
From how easily he escapes them even against their will, it is shown that he would not have been caught unless willing.

[John 10:40] He came there to remind the crowds of what John said about him. Those who cross the mystical Jordan are carried toward God, just as Christ, having crossed the Jordan, came into the church of the nations and remained there.
comments.author: Ammonius of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Mary's anointing outdid Jacob's anointing of a stone, for she anointed the living temple of God the Word and worshiped him.
comments.comment:
…his sisters prayed for him, saying, «Lord, see him whom you love is ill» (John 11:3). Mary, through whom the sister's confession and the brother's faith were united, and the piety of the household was made plain.

For having taken the ointment [John 11:2; told at 12:3], she did not anoint a lifeless stone for the house of God, as Jacob did when he was being wrested away from Esau, but she anointed God, the Creator and Maker of all things, with a living temple united to the Theotokos the Virgin; … Just as he fashioned the shadow, she herself felt the reality and worshiped.

…he learned nothing more than to anoint a stone as a type of the cornerstone, but she not only felt and anointed the holy, living, and God-created temple of the Creator and Eternal God, but also, worshiping the God who is unchangeably in it and through it, she confessed one indivisible Lord, perceiving the invisible glory in the seen beauty, and in the felt flesh, she was discerning the unutterable and untouchable God the Word.
comments.author: Eustathius of Antioch

comments.capsule: This Mary was no prostitute, and Lazarus's sickness led only to a four-day death.
comments.comment:
This is not the woman Matthew and Luke mention; for those were prostitutes, whom Christ endured through goodness.

She did this to wipe a blessing from the holy flesh.

[John 11:4] It is not toward lasting death, but for only four days. …
comments.author: Ammonius of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Jesus waited so that Lazarus would truly die, making the sign greater and undeniable.
comments.comment:
…the illness is not toward death [John 11:4]. Raising Lazarus from sickness was not of such glory and wonder as raising him from the dead.

For this reason he stayed [John 11:6], that Lazarus might die and be buried and the Jews might not say he raised one who had only swooned.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why Jesus stayed two days before going to Lazarus.
comments.author: Ammonius of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Jesus hides his purpose at first, since nothing he does seeks glory.
comments.comment: He does not show immediately that he comes for this [to raise Lazarus]; for all things are unmeasured with him and far from all bulk toward truth, not being accomplished for glory (John 11:7).
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: The twelve hours picture the Jews' shifting opinion, which cannot overcome the one who gives light to all.
comments.comment:
For this reason he foretells [John 11:7], lest when he suddenly goes there they be troubled.

"They are seeking to stone you" and what follows they said as not yet perfected and thinking that he also suffered unwillingly, so that he said this: "Are there not twelve hours" and what follows (John 11:9).

Just as the day is unstable, shifting from hour to hour, so also is human opinion—that is, the Jews'. If the one who walks in day does not stumble, how would I who enlighten all undergo the things of the ill-advised?
comments.author: Ammonius of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The day's twelve hours are the time before the passion, when the Jews cannot harm Jesus until the divine will permits it.
comments.comment:
Jesus answered: are there not twelve hours of the day? (John 11:9).

But the Lord teaches that before the time of the passion he would not suffer anything from the Jews. He teaches by a parable, naming the day the time before the passion, and saying the time of the passion is night, that a man walking in the day does not stumble until the twelve hours of the day are fulfilled. But if he walks at night, he stumbles. He says the reason for not stumbling in the day is that this light is, and the reason for stumbling at night is the absence of the light.

From these things he shows that according to the heavenly will it is that not to suffer or to suffer him happens, and according to the presence or absence of the light it is that men see or do not see, so that until the divine and heavenly will withholds the passion, it is impossible for it to happen; but when it yields and gives way, then it will occur. …
comments.selected_reason: Explains the parable of the twelve hours of the day.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: To God Lazarus was alive, so Jesus speaks of going to him.
comments.comment:
He speaks as to one living when he says "let us go" [John 11:15]; for to him Lazarus lived as God.

Lest we appear without affection, let us hasten to our friend's salvation, overlooking Jewish plots.
comments.author: Ammonius of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The raising of Lazarus was the one miracle the Jews could not slander, because they knew he had been four days dead and buried.
comments.comment:
…Nothing stung the Jews as much as the resurrection of Lazarus. This miracle alone they could not slander. They slandered the healing of the man born blind, saying, "This is he; no, it is not he; it is someone like him" (John 9:9). They slandered the raising of Jairus's daughter, saying that she had merely collapsed and had not been handed over to complete death. They slandered the resurrection of the widow's only son, saying that he had feigned death and had not been swallowed up by the tyranny of death. They slandered the withered fig tree, saying that it had been stripped by birds and not withered by the Lord's word. They slandered the changing of water into wine, saying that the dinner guests were already drunk and did not recognize the jest. Only the resurrection of Lazarus they could not slander.

They knew Lazarus; the man was well known. They had followed the funeral procession, they had seen the tomb being sealed, they had consoled Martha and Mary, the sisters of Lazarus, according to custom, as at a funeral meal for the dead [John 11:19]. They knew that he had lain in the tomb for exactly four days [John 11:17], and that he was a corpse four days dead, completely disjointed, his flesh wasted away, his bones loosened from their sockets, his sinews torn apart, his inward parts scattered, his belly dissolved. Knowing all this, when they suddenly saw the resurrection of Lazarus whole and complete, as from a lathe, gleaming with renewed life, they were thrown into confusion. They nearly fainted, finding no words of pretext for how they might slander the resurrection of Lazarus, since the Lord's strategy had arranged this.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why John stresses the four days and the mourners: they made the miracle undeniable.
comments.author: Amphilochius of Iconium

comments.capsule: Mary stayed home unaware while active Martha went out, and Martha spoke truly from experience.
comments.comment:
Mary was sitting in the house, evidently not knowing; for Martha is active and quick about the table, but Mary is wise and more firm concerning the faith (John 11:20).

For that her brother would not have died had the Lord been present, she [Martha] says truly from experience (John 11:21) …
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: Martha's 'if you had been here' forgot that the Lord, as God, is present everywhere, and he forgave words spoken in grief.
comments.comment:
When Lazarus put off this present life in the natural way, the Lord was not present in Bethany to bodily eyes, though in his divinity he is present everywhere and fills all things. … So when the Lord arrived in Bethany, as soon as Martha, Lazarus' sister, heard of it, she ran, she hurried, she fell before him in supplication, offering a chosen plea. Falling before him, she said to the Lord: "Lord, if you had been here, my brother would not have died (John 11:21). And now I know that whatever you ask of God, God will give you (John 11:22)."

But the Lord, being himself a sea of long-suffering, answered her: "What are you saying, Martha? You call me Lord, and you do not understand what Lord means? Was I not here? Wait a little while; for soon you will learn from your brother. Your brother will rise. I pardon you, Martha; for you are drunk with grief—as he said to her: a person who is drunk makes mistakes—when you sober up, then you will come to your senses. Your brother will rise."
comments.author: Amphilochius of Iconium

comments.capsule: Martha looked to a distant last day, while the resurrection itself stood speaking with her.
comments.comment: But Martha, still caught up in human words, answered the Lord: "I know that he will rise on the last day (John 11:24)." The Lord said to her: "Why do you stammer, Martha? Why do you shrink from the resurrection into distant hopes? The resurrection is speaking with you, and you speak about the resurrection? I am the resurrection and the life; whoever believes in me, even if he dies, will live (John 11:25)."
comments.selected_reason: Shows the force of 'I am the resurrection' against Martha's hope in the last day.
comments.author: Amphilochius of Iconium

comments.capsule: Jesus is not merely living but is life itself, the giver of life.
comments.comment: The Lord called himself life [John 11:25], not a living being; for a living being is receptive of life, but life is what supplies living, as wisdom and the wise: the one receives, the other gives.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why Jesus says 'I am the life' and not merely that he lives.
comments.author: Ammonius of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Christ calls himself the resurrection and the life because, as God, he has life by nature and not by sharing in it.
comments.comment: That incorruption and life are in Christ by nature, and not by participation, you will understand from this as well. For, as one who is God by nature, he said, ‘I am the resurrection and the life’ (John 11:25). But as one who is given life in respect of his humanity, he says, ‘For just as the Father has life in himself, so he has granted the Son also to have life in himself’ (John 5:26).
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 11

comments.capsule: The mourners followed Mary by God's plan, to witness the sign.
comments.comment: If this had not happened by God's economy [God's plan of salvation], the evangelist would not have mentioned it [John 11:31]; it happened so that even unwilling they might come and witness the sign.
comments.author: Ammonius of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Jesus mastered his grief, asked where Lazarus lay in order to gather witnesses, and wept in sympathy with the mourners rather than for Lazarus.
comments.comment:
Christ, grieved and seeing grief moved in himself and the flesh nodding toward tears, rebukes the flesh by the Holy Spirit's power, which, not bearing the movement of the Godhead united to it, trembles and masters the grief; for it was not fitting for the one who brings the hope of resurrection to weep over a dead man [John 11:33].

As one without love of display he said this and pretends not to know, because of the lowliness of human nature—he who knows all as God—that he might draw many to the place [John 11:34].

He asks not as ignorant, he who knew this from a long distance, but so that on the pretext of pointing out the place they may come and see the sign.

Sympathizing with those who wept, he wept—not for the one he was about to raise [John 11:35].
comments.author: Ammonius of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Jesus roused himself like a champion facing his enemies, and his tears showed the compassion of a high priest who shares our weakness.
comments.comment:
…being moved in spirit and by the Spirit usefully, he stirred himself up, like a brave champion seeing the enemies, and prepared himself against the opponents (John 11:33). He does not repeat the likeness toward men, nor does he demonstrate everywhere that which is above man, but he showed the most philanthropic compassion toward those mourning by the tear (John 11:35).

This tear of the Lord is a provision of life for men. This mercy of the Savior overcomes those who are mourning. For this reason the Word descended into a body, so that he might cause those mourning to weep, and that the incorruptible divinity might be brought back toward the life-giving of men. “For we have a high priest able to sympathize with our weaknesses” (Hebrews 4:15).
comments.selected_reason: Explains 'groaned in the spirit' as the Lord rousing himself for battle, and his tears as compassion.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: Jesus knew where Lazarus lay but asked so that the scoffing crowd would follow and become eyewitnesses of the raising.
comments.comment:
While the Lord was saying these things, nearly the whole city of Bethany ran down to the Lord's arrival—not to marvel, but to laugh. For they had no hope that a man four days dead could rise. What then did the Lord do? When he saw such a crowd running down and that they were worthy and sufficient to bear witness to what was about to be raised by him, he answered them: "Where have you laid Lazarus?"

Did the Master of the place not know the place? He knew the place, but he arranged the manner, so that all of them, compelled once again, would follow Jesus, so that receiving the resurrection with their own eyes they might become unambiguous heralds. "Where have you laid him?" Those who were asked said to him: "Come and see (John 11:34)." As the Lord walked and hurried to the tomb, the crowd following behind exchanged words among themselves, saying: "Why does this man want to see Lazarus' tomb? If he is the Son of God, he will raise him."
comments.selected_reason: Explains why Jesus, who knew all things, asked where Lazarus was laid.
comments.author: Amphilochius of Iconium

comments.capsule: The one Christ asked where Lazarus lay as a man and raised him as God.
comments.comment: Therefore there was not one Son of God before Abraham and another after Abraham; nor was there one who raised Lazarus and another who asked about him. The same one spoke in human fashion when he said, “Where does Lazarus lie?” (John 11:34), and raised him in divine fashion. The same one spat bodily as a man, and in divine fashion as Son of God opened the eyes of the man blind from birth (John 9:1).
comments.selected_reason: Explains how the all-knowing Lord could ask a question: he asked as man and raised as God.
comments.author: Athanasius of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Jesus wept not from overwhelming grief but to teach the right measure of mourning, neither unfeeling nor excessive.
comments.comment:
But as for the Lord's weeping over Lazarus [John 11:35] and over the city [Luke 19:41], we have this to say: he also ate and drank, not because he himself needed these things, but to leave you measures and limits for the necessary sufferings of the soul. So too he wept, correcting the excessive passionate and lowly element of those given to wailing and fond of laments. For if anything needs the symmetry that comes from reason, weeping does: on what occasions it should occur, and to what extent, and when, and how.

That the Lord's tears were not passionate but instructive is clear from this: 'Lazarus our friend has fallen asleep, but I am going to wake him' (John 11:11). Who among us mourns a sleeping friend whom he expects to wake a little later? … How then did the One who was about to work such things judge what had happened worthy of tears? Is it not clear that, supporting our weakness from every side, he enclosed the necessary sufferings within measures and limits, avoiding lack of sympathy as beastly, but rejecting the love of grief and much lamenting as ignoble?
comments.selected_reason: Answers why Jesus wept for a friend he was about to raise.
comments.author: Basil of Caesarea

comments.capsule: Christ, who is Life, did not grieve at death, but wept from compassion for our nature enslaved to death.
comments.comment: For the Life would be the last to suffer grief at a death. The Life has nothing at all to do with what is dead; rather, it is itself the undoing of death and the overthrow of corruption. … And if he wept over Lazarus (John 11:35), we say that this was the fruit of his tender love, and the compassion that divine gentleness has toward us. For our nature, under the tyranny of death, was being pitied, and his tear was its release from that suffering.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 12

comments.capsule: Jesus wept to bring the crowd's doubts into the open, and he had let Lazarus die to show his authority over life and death.
comments.comment:
The crowd said among themselves: "For those who had died recently, the ones he raised, we do not know. How then can we know whether they were handed over to a complete death? He will raise this man, and we will know that he truly is the Son of God." … After saying these things, the Lord went to the tomb. And when he drew near the tomb and saw the monument, he immediately wept. What need was there to weep for the one he was about to raise? He wept. Why? Listen carefully. The Lord arranged everything as strategy. He wept at the tomb so that he might make public the opinion of those who followed him, what suspicion they held about him.

So when the crowds following him saw him weeping, they again felt human things and began to exchange words among themselves, saying: "See how he loved him (John 11:36). The one who raised the dead and gave sight to the blind, could not have kept this man from dying, if he loved him so?"

But the Lord, when he saw them still speaking human things, answered them: "It would have been easy for me to preserve the life of Lazarus, as also of Elijah and Enoch, but none of you knew that by my will the life of Lazarus was being preserved. For this reason I allowed him to be swallowed by death, so that you might learn precisely that I have authority over life and death."
comments.author: Amphilochius of Iconium

comments.capsule: Jesus again masters his emotion, and Martha falters before the wonder.
comments.comment:
Again he rebukes the passion [John 11:38], that we may learn that he became man without change as we are.

Because of the excess of the wonder Martha somehow again disbelieves [John 11:39].
comments.author: Ammonius of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The stench proved that Lazarus had truly decayed and that his body had not been stolen.
comments.comment: But as I said before, he was arranging everything wisely, … as strategy for advantage when he said to the Jews: "Roll away the stone," so that from the corpse-bearing stench itself they might learn that he had decayed and was not stolen.
comments.author: Amphilochius of Iconium

comments.capsule: Lazarus, four days dead and stinking, was a sign that Christ will raise all humanity, however corrupted by sin.
comments.comment: …when He raised Lazarus from the tomb, four days dead, a man made up of the four elements, who already stank (John 11:39), who had decayed, who had been mastered by worms, it was made known to the rulers and authorities in heaven and to those on earth (Ephesians 3:10) that He will raise all humanity, made up of the four elements, even if it has stunk in the sin of the transgression, even if it has rotted in the impiety of idolatry, even if, as by worms, it has been mastered by demons and taken captive to do their will (2 Timothy 2:26).
comments.author: Hesychius of Jerusalem
comments.work: On Lazarus and the Palm Branches

comments.capsule: Jesus rebuked Martha's unbelief and had the Jews themselves roll away the stone so that they would be exact witnesses.
comments.comment:
Carried along with these words, Martha herself came to the Lord and said: "Where are you going, Master? Why do you want to see Lazarus' tomb? Why do you stir up our pain again? Why do you rouse our mourning? Why do you want to see the tomb? It will do no good, Master. He already stinks, for he has been four days dead."

But the Lord said to Martha: "Did I not tell you that if you believe you will see the glory of God (John 11:40)? You say to me, 'He already stinks.' Your sister gives off fragrance, and you reek of smoke with unbelief? I want to see the tomb of my friend." …

And immediately the Lord said to them, as you all clearly know: "Roll away the stone (John 11:39)." He commanded the Jews there: "Roll away the stone." See how he arranged everything as strategy, making them precise witnesses of Lazarus' resurrection. "Roll away the stone." He permitted his disciples to move mountains by a word, and did he himself not roll away the stone?
comments.selected_reason: Explains why Jesus told others to roll away the stone, and his answer to Martha.
comments.author: Amphilochius of Iconium

comments.capsule: Jesus speaks of the Father's glory and thanks the Father to teach humility, not because he is lesser.
comments.comment:
In things beyond nature God's glory appears. Because of the hearers' weakness he says the Father's glory; because of freedom from vanity he did not say "you will see my glory" but the Father's [John 11:40].

Being equal to the Father he thanks him [John 11:41], that we may give thanks to the one above ourselves. This is said among friends and equals.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why Jesus says 'the glory of God' and why the Son gives thanks.
comments.author: Ammonius of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Jesus thanks the Father for hearing him even before he asks, because Father and Son share one will.
comments.comment:
The Lord offers indeed the priestly office and prayers on behalf of men, but the Son has a connection and harmony toward the Father regarding his purposes for men, and thus the goodwill of God toward men came to be, after the Christ's sympathy toward fellow-born men had occurred (John 11:41-42). He calls the following of the Father's purpose toward his own purpose the obedience of a father regarding the life of Lazarus, and he gives thanks concerning this.

And he demonstrates such sharpness of the Father's agreement toward his petition, so that even before asking and before uttering the word of my prayer, 'you have heard me,' he says (John 11:41-42), and not as something wonderful or paradoxical for a son to hear a father, nor as if they were separate and becoming something else; for 'I knew,' he says, 'that you always hear me'; for nothing divided what was between, nor are the purposes separated, but whatever is the will of the Son, this is driven from the Father, and the Father's unutterable will is with the Son.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: The loud cry called back a soul far off and foreshadows the trumpet of the general resurrection.
comments.comment:
As if the soul were far off he calls with a cry [John 11:43], not as if it were in the tomb, as the Greeks' children mythologize. The Lord's cry was a type of the "great trumpet" that will sound in the common resurrection. The command is God-befitting and royal.

So also the universal resurrection is going to happen "in a moment, in the twinkling of an eye" (1 Corinthians 15:52). …
comments.selected_reason: Explains why Jesus cried with a loud voice.
comments.author: Ammonius of Alexandria

comments.capsule: One word raised Lazarus whole, and the grave-cloths he walked in were kept as witnesses that he truly rose.
comments.comment:
When those present rolled away the stone with grumbling—for the hard-to-control corpse-bearing stench was stinging them—immediately the Lord cried out: "Lazarus, come out (John 11:43)." The Master is the one calling; no one speaks against him. …

But you, friend, when you hear "Lazarus, come out," do not suppose that the Lord shouted many times. He spoke once and raised the one he had formed. For he did not weep as Elijah did, nor was he at a loss as Elisha was. With a single-sound voice he woke the one sleeping in his presence, saying: "Lazarus, come out." One word, and the wonders were various. The Lord only called out, "Lazarus, come out," and immediately the flesh was being filled out, the hair was being restored, the joints were being bound together, the veins were being refilled with pure blood. Hades, cut off from below, was sending Lazarus onward. The soul of Lazarus, being detained and comforted by the holy angels, was being remolded, the soul into its own body. And the most glorious thing of all was that he was bound everywhere, his feet and his face with burial bands, and he walked without hindrance.

Therefore the Lord also commanded the crowds present more effectively, saying: "Untie him and let him go." See the Lord's strategy and how he arranges everything wisely. For the full assurance of those present he said: "Untie him and let him go. As you rolled away the stone and showed the tomb and shared in the smell, untie the burial wrappings too; preserve the stone as a blessing, keep the burial wrappings as witnesses. If the chief priests and the Pharisees disbelieve that Lazarus has risen, show the burial wrappings; display the burial cloths as the paralytic carried his mat."
comments.selected_reason: Explains the single command and why Jesus had the onlookers untie Lazarus.
comments.author: Amphilochius of Iconium

comments.capsule: Jesus called Lazarus by name as a friend, a sign for all the Lord's friends, and had others loose him so that they could bear witness.
comments.comment:
The calling of the one lying there by name was a symbol of friendship; for he called the youth, whom he raised, 'young man,' saying, 'Young man, I say to you, arise' (Luke 7:14), and the girl likewise 'Talitha koum' [Mark 5:41], but he calls the friend and the familiar one by a more friendly name from the name itself, so that it might be a sign of the resurrection of those called friends by the Lord, whom the apostle says are dead in the Lord, and who will be called to meet him. This is consistent with what he said himself, that 'the dead shall come forth at the voice' (John 5:28-29) having heard 'the Son of God'.

And this exit from the tomb is more fearsome than the wonder according to the resurrection. Uncontradictedly, he also presented to the ignorant the authority of the Benefactor; … Because of this, he also allows them to loose the risen one from the dead, so that they, having surrounded the bonds with their own hands and having freed him from the care, may stand as witnesses of the event to those who are absent. … And 'loose him and let him go', so that being led, he might not be praised with boasting (John 11:44).
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: Jesus told Lazarus to come out before telling him to rise, so that rising and coming out happened at once.
comments.comment:
The command to Lazarus is clear: 'Lazarus, come out' (John 11:43). Before saying 'arise', he commands the exit. First, Lord, raise him, and then, having arisen, command him to run. The one lying down is still being hastened to run, a remarkable transformation. Why do you proclaim the exit to the one lying down before the resurrection?

He says, 'Yes, to the one lying down, I command the run, so that I may not, having been occupied with the dead for two things, delay the exit. I say to him: 'Come out', so that he may run more quickly, having taken one deadline for both resurrection and run.'

Immediately, Lazarus jumps out of the tomb, as if he were a guardian rather than a dead man. … Lazarus was bound with bands and placed with the tomb, but with the same bonds, he was given back to life.
comments.author: Hesychius of Jerusalem

comments.capsule: Loosing Lazarus proved that he was no phantom.
comments.comment: …that with hands and feet and eyes bound he came out walking [John 11:44]. By the loosing they witnessed that it was not a phantom but Lazarus.
comments.author: Ammonius of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The council feared that Rome would destroy them if Jesus were made king, and that very ruin came on them after they killed him.
comments.comment:
…The rest [of the Jews], hearing from those who had seen, went down to the Pharisees, stirring them against him as one who had dared something unholy; for they accused him as having ordered the buried to be dug up. Then he says they gathered a council against him and reasoned, saying: If we leave him thus, all will believe in him and the Romans will come upon us on suspicion of tyranny and will destroy our city. These things, even if they said them from envy, also came out when they did not expect it, when they crucified him.

… After so many proofs they spoke as of a bare man, not knowing that he was the Christ, maker of the signs.

If, they say, those who believe in him make him king, the Romans will come upon us as having tyrannized and will strip us of everything. To avoid undergoing the terrible things they said he should be destroyed. And when they murdered him, the grievous things came out against them.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the council's fear of Rome and its ironic fulfilment.
comments.author: Ammonius of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Caiaphas held a priesthood that Rome now handed out, and his prophecy was given for the office's sake, not because he was holy.
comments.comment:
When priesthoods became purchasable, priests no longer served for their whole lifetime nor by lineage, but the Romans gave it to whom they wished, succeeding them when they wished [John 11:49].

With a mouth speaking only, not with the Holy Spirit's grace touching his heart, the gift of foretelling was given him for the honor of the priesthood, not as to a prophet [John 11:51]. Prophesying benefits no one. It fits against those who do not believe rightly yet foretell some things, who if they say on the day of judgment to the Lord, "Lord, did we not prophesy in your name," will hear that "I never knew you" (Matthew 7:22–23). So one must not be led astray from this; for prophecy is not a fruit of good works by which we recognize the saints, but wholly the Spirit's work, even if it speaks through human instruments—that is, human tongues.
comments.selected_reason: Explains 'high priest that same year' and how a wicked man could prophesy.
comments.author: Ammonius of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Caiaphas foretold Christ's death not by the Spirit but because, as high priest, he was allowed to sense the truth.
comments.comment: It was not spoken by Caiaphas as a prophecy of the Spirit [John 11:51]; for the prophetic Spirit did not devise a plot against Christ, but by some coincidence with the truth and the happening thing, he was granted the opportunity to sense such a thought, because he was high priest, so that he might foretell through his mouth the thing hidden from men until then and unknown.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: The scattered children of God are the Gentile believers gathered into one body under Christ.
comments.comment:
Christ underwent death for the common salvation of all.

The evangelist calls children of God the faithful from the nations who were "far" and have become "near" into "one body," having Christ as one head (Ephesians 2:13–16) [John 11:52]. He [Caiaphas] proclaims beforehand what he does not know, glorifying Christ by necessity as also Balaam did.
comments.selected_reason: Explains who 'the children of God that were scattered abroad' are.
comments.author: Ammonius of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Jesus withdrew not from fear but to await his hour and to teach prudence.
comments.comment: He withdraws for the Jews' condemnation, not from cowardice, and teaches us at the peak of anger not to throw ourselves into dangers [John 11:54]. He fled waiting for the fitting time of the passion and sparing their salvation.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why Jesus withdrew to Ephraim.
comments.author: Ammonius of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Sinners had to be purified before Passover.
comments.comment: Those who had sinned voluntary or involuntary faults did not keep the Passover unless they had been purified [John 11:55] …
comments.author: Ammonius of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Lazarus eating at table proves his resurrection was real, just as the risen Lord ate before his disciples.
comments.comment: “They made a dinner for him,” he says, “and Lazarus was one reclining with him” (John 12:2). This is a magnificent way toward true faith in the invisible resurrection of the saved; for so also the Lord, after his salvific resurrection, manifested himself to his genuine disciples, having taken and eaten in their eyes according to the law of human nature.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why John notes that Lazarus sat at table.
comments.author: Eustathius of Antioch

comments.capsule: Lazarus lived on and ate, and Martha and Mary picture active virtue and contemplation, or the old covenant and the Gospel.
comments.comment:
But Lazarus did not die at once after appearing; he lived on eating and drinking and doing the usual things, which the evangelist said as marveling [John 12:2].

Martha is seen as practical virtue, Mary as spiritual contemplation. Others take Martha as the old covenant, which prepares the Lord's table through the testimony of the old things, established by doctrines concerning Christ, and Mary as evangelical instruction, which anointing the Lord's feet with myrrh—that is, his economy [God's plan of salvation] upon the earth—filled the whole earth with fragrance, which is the house of all humanity. Others understand Martha as the Jews' synagogue wanting to serve God through fleshly things, and Mary as the church from the nations offering spiritual sacrifices and fragrant faith to God and wiping the blessing from his flesh through mystical participation.

For in the rank of fragrance the knowledge of Christ was going to fill the world [John 12:3].
comments.author: Ammonius of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Judas misjudged what is truly good, and Jesus bore his thefts so that Judas could never blame poverty for the betrayal.
comments.comment:
Judas blames that she brought myrrh and not silver, not knowing what is truly good [John 12:5]; for the gift-bearing toward God ought to be preferred to the poor.

The Lord endured him stealing [John 12:6], lest he say that for love of money and want I made the betrayal. Judas was a temple robber, stealing money dedicated to God.
comments.selected_reason: Explains Judas's complaint and why Jesus let a thief keep the money-bag.
comments.author: Ammonius of Alexandria

comments.capsule: By speaking of his burial Jesus defended Mary and shamed Judas, who would sell his teacher for gain.
comments.comment:
Toward conviction of the senseless Judas he mentioned the burial. What he means is this: wait a little and I will go away. He speaks in defense of the woman, lest he seem to prefer himself to the poor.

Saying "leave her" he convicts Judas's hypocrisy as blaming things worthy of praise. And since the myrrh's expense was not for luxury but for mystical need, he apologizes for Mary, even if she did not know the economy [God's plan of salvation] of the mystery. And by mentioning burial he shames Judas, that for shameful gain he was going to betray the teacher.

When there is need of spiritual liturgy or hymnody, one must not leave these and go off about beneficence, but after these liturgies [John 12:8].
comments.selected_reason: Explains Jesus' reply about his burial and about the poor.
comments.author: Ammonius of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The crowds praised Jesus because of Lazarus, but behind their praise lay the coming raising of all human nature, which moved even the angels.
comments.comment:
Come, let us consider why not only men but the angelic powers too hymned Him as King.

The cause of the hymn, then, as it appears outwardly, was the raising of Lazarus, as the Gospel says: “But they took counsel to put Lazarus to death as well, because on account of him many of the Jews were going away and believing in Jesus” (John 12:10–11). This is the outward cause of the believers’ praise; but its hidden and secret cause is the raising of the whole of human nature.

And just as the sign of Lazarus and that raising made men sing hymns to Jesus, so the sign of the raising of the whole of human nature led the holy angels to give glory; and as much greater as the raising of all is than the raising of Lazarus, so much greater was the glory then. The minds of those who shouted, astonished at the miracle, moved them to give glory; but the divine plan, on account of the raising of the whole of human nature, secretly moved not only men but also the holy angels to marvel at Jesus and glorify Him.
comments.author: Hesychius of Jerusalem
comments.work: On Lazarus and the Palm Branches

comments.capsule: Our palm branches should be faith, hope and love, answering to the palm's whiteness, sharpness and sweetness.
comments.comment: …like the branches of the palm trees (John 12:13), and let us follow Him, giving thanks to Him. Instead of their whiteness, let us carry right, undefiled, and simple faith; instead of their sharpness, patient hope, which pierces and slays every thought that rises up to take us captive away from the knowledge of God (2 Corinthians 10:5); and instead of the sweetness of the palm, sweet love, which is made up of the faith and hope already named and the rest, so that what was said may be fulfilled in us: “The righteous will flourish like a palm tree; he will grow like a cedar in Lebanon” (Psalm 92:12).
comments.author: Hesychius of Jerusalem
comments.work: On Lazarus and the Palm Branches

comments.capsule: The palms hailed a conqueror of death, and the donkey and colt picture the nations whom Christ subdues and leads upward.
comments.comment:
As to one who had conquered death they met him with palms; for David's prophecy is fulfilled through this.

The donkey is a type of the nations, whom the Lord, being unclean, made subject. The colt is a type of the nations, whom the Lord, sitting, leads up into the "Jerusalem above," of which the earthly is a type. He calls them a colt because they were untrained in the faith according to piety.
comments.author: Ammonius of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Jesus accepted the crowd's royal welcome yet rode humbly on an unclean donkey, a sign of the Gentile people who would receive him.
comments.comment:
With palms they were escorting his entry and shouting welcome to the coming King of Israel, which is to say, they were bringing in Christ, the promised one, with a conspicuous honor into the city. And he, having received such honor from the people, is shaped into the most moderate state, fulfilling at once also the symbol foretold according to the prophecy.

And thus the seat upon the donkey has a moderate and humble character, having hidden within it the symbol of the not-so-pure people of that time who are to receive the coming of the Lord. But a donkey is not clean according to the law. And the prophet Zechariah cried out, evangelizing Zion indeed, freeing the King of all from fears and redeeming her from mighty enemies, but by the symbol showing him being led by the nations and used by a new people …
comments.selected_reason: Explains the humble donkey of Zechariah's prophecy.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: The disciples were not yet told, lest a suffering king offend them.
comments.comment: For this reason they [the disciples] did not know, lest they take offense if, being king, he is going to suffer such things, and because they could not at once contain the knowledge of the kingdom.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the disciples did not understand these things at first.
comments.author: Ammonius of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The raising of Lazarus won Jesus public honor, which provoked the Pharisees and so led on to the passion.
comments.comment: Therefore, necessarily also in rank, the Lord performed the miracle concerning Lazarus (John 12:17, 19), so that having this happened, he might be honored conspicuously by the multitude, and because of this honor, the Pharisees, having suffered greatly, might counsel against him, and thus the passion might be fulfilled, which indeed happens (John 12:19). They see, therefore, that they argue in vain against the faith toward Christ, they separate the believers in vain, they turn away the rest in vain, some by arguing, others even by threatening.
comments.selected_reason: Explains how the crowd's honor led the Pharisees to say 'ye prevail nothing'.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: The Greeks' coming signals the turn to the nations, and like a grain, Jesus' death will bring a harvest of believers.
comments.comment:
…So then it is time for the disciples to pass over to the nations [John 12:20-22], even if at the beginning they did not do this, so that the Jews might not take offense.

He calls glory the resurrection [John 12:23], after which he was glorified as Son of God.

Do not be troubled if I die; for then the proclamation grows all the more and those from the nations believe. And do not disbelieve; for this also happens in the grain [John 12:24]. When I suffer and die, I rise with greater glory; for all are going to believe in me as God.
comments.author: Ammonius of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Death looks like weakness, but Christ's hour is glory because it ends in a resurrection worthy of God.
comments.comment: And it is not doubtful that the whole world has been saved, Emmanuel having died for it. Yet we say this: how was he glorified by dying? And yet the matter rather has a stigma of weakness — which is why it is also called a despising of shame, having become obedient unto death (Philippians 2:8). But perhaps you will say that he has been glorified through the resurrection. The word holds rightly and is true. Did he then return to life divinely rather than humanly? But I think divinely. So when the Word from God himself is said to suffer in flesh, let us not be ashamed of the suffering; for the end has glory, and this is God-befitting.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On the True Faith, to the Princesses Arcadia and Marina

comments.capsule: Jesus' death did not silence his message but spread it, as a buried grain bears much fruit.
comments.comment: His punishment did not destroy God’s messages but, if it must be put this way, made them known; as Jesus himself taught when he said, “Unless the grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies, it remains alone; but if it dies, it bears much fruit” (John 12:24). So by dying, Jesus, “the grain of wheat,” bore “much fruit,” and the Father always takes care of the fruits that have come, still come, and will yet come from the death of the grain “of wheat.”
comments.selected_reason: Explains the grain of wheat as Jesus' fruitful death.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: To hate one's life means refusing its sinful desires, and that is how it is saved.
comments.comment: The one who has despised life in this world acquires the incorruptible in the age to come [John 12:25]. That one loves his own soul and loses it who does its illicit desires; but the one who hates and saves it is the one who does not obey it when it commands what is illicit.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what it means to love or to hate one's life.
comments.author: Ammonius of Alexandria

comments.capsule: 'My soul is troubled' shows that Christ had a real rational human soul, since neither the Godhead nor a mindless body could feel such dread.
comments.comment: For the divine and highest nature of the Word would reasonably be wholly unreceptive of panic and grief and the causes of cowardice; it will refuse altogether to be in those states at any time, and will not endure our passions at all. And again a body that is soulless and mindless would not admit grief, nor would it conceive any of the gloomy things, nor foresee in advance the fear of what is expected to happen. But a rational soul, examining with the mind both what is already present and also what will follow, would suffer such things, as I suppose seems good to all. How then does Emmanuel say, “Now my soul has been troubled”? (John 12:27)
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On the True Faith, to the Empresses Pulcheria and Eudocia

comments.capsule: Jesus' troubled soul shows real human dread of death, yet he asks not to escape but to be led to the cross.
comments.comment:
Here much of the human is shown, also showing a nature not willing to die, that he was not outside of human sufferings (John 12:27, 28).

For lest some might say that he easily disregards death, he shows by being outside of danger that he spoke these things in a way appropriate to the situation, as a man being troubled and seeking deliverance, if it were not useful. What he says is such: 'Even if I am now troubled, having known death, I do not say so as to flee from it; for it is necessary to bear the burden; for I do not say, deliver me from this hour, but, glorify your name, that is, lead now to the cross' (John 12:28). These things he says, introducing us into a pattern of manliness.
comments.selected_reason: Paraphrases 'Father, save me from this hour' so that its meaning is plain.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: The promised second glory is the immortality given to Christ's risen human nature.
comments.comment: And having said 'I have glorified you' (John 17:4), he brings forth by saying 'and I will glorify again' (John 12:28), so that through an excess of philanthropy, by a second glory after the resurrection of the flesh, he might accomplish making the formerly mortal man immortal, and by such a glory glorifying him, so that not only might he be freed from the former slavery, but also might be worthy of a glory above man.
comments.author: Marcellus of Ancyra

comments.capsule: The heavenly voice was a sound sent for the hearers' sake, and the glory meant is God's glory made known to men.
comments.comment:
There is no dialogue in a voice from the Father to the Son, for the divine is beyond voice; rather, a sound is sent from heaven to the ears of men from the face of the Father toward the Son, so that those hearing might more greatly remember Christ and know his divinity which is above man. Nor is glory attributed to the Father as always having it, except insofar as it shines forth and is known for the recognition of men; nor is the Son to be considered as being glorified from a lack of glory, except insofar as he, formerly unseen according to the flesh, is made manifest in the eyes of men.

… Jesus answered and said: 'This voice did not happen through me' (John 12:30); for even he who knew the Father and the things of the Father was not seen.

… So also is the name of the Father, but a name not that which is composed of syllables nor signified in sounds, but that which makes manifest the identity of the Father [John 12:28].
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: The cross glorifies the Father's name, and the heavenly voice, though heard as thunder, was the Father's real answer.
comments.comment:
And he calls glory the cross [John 12:28], through which human beings came to know the Father’s name.

The Son was always conspicuous in wonders, having the Father as fellow-worker, and he glorifies him again through the sign at his death; for as man he was raised through the Father, even if as God by nature the Son raised himself.

How the voice was arranged is not ours to say; for the Father did not speak as having a body, as some heretics have tried to claim.

To the crowd the voice was indistinct [John 12:29]; but perhaps because it was made known to the disciples through Christ, the Jews ought to have understood that it was the Father who answered back in the way he knows; for Jesus did not ask that thunder happen.
comments.selected_reason: Explains 'I have both glorified it, and will glorify it again' and why some heard thunder.
comments.author: Ammonius of Alexandria

comments.capsule: When Christ was lifted up on the cross, the devil was cast down and death and sin were overthrown.
comments.comment: So he [the devil] perished together with his own shield-bearers, and was driven away from the flock of the godly, though he sprang on it like a savage beast; and he has been cast out of his tyranny over us. The Savior taught us this when he said: “Now is the judgment of this age; now the ruler of this age will be cast out. And I, if I am lifted up on the earth, will draw all to myself” (John 12:31–32). For the passion of Christ became the overthrow of death, the pulling down of the devil, and the destruction of sin: he was lifted up on the cross, and he brought down the devil’s boast and threw it to the ground.
comments.selected_reason: Explains how the cross is the judgment that casts out the ruler of this world.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: In a courtroom against the devil, who killed the sinless Lord, Christ's death frees humanity, and he draws all nations to himself.
comments.comment:
Through faith or unbelief—some being made God’s own, others being set as enemies—all humanity is judged through me [John 12:31], saying to the devil as in a courtroom: granted that you murdered the other human beings as sinners, why also the Lord? The time of the advent is a judgment of the world, since Christ is about to justify human beings and free them from the devil’s greed, not to condemn them now; for Christ’s death justifies all humanity against the devil who wronged the world, when the judgment takes place.

By saying “all,” he also signifies those from the nations [John 12:32]. And he draws them as ones held by a tyrant and unable to flee of themselves—which elsewhere he calls a snatching. And let someone say, How did he also prevail over you? Not only because I rise, but also because I draw all to believe in me, that I am God, not a mere man.

He showed that he suffered willingly and knowing that he was not only dying but also by what manner; the evangelist named the cross death [John 12:33].
comments.author: Ammonius of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Christ dies yet abides forever, and while the light is with them he urges faith, which makes people sons of light.
comments.comment:
The Jews do not understand that Christ is slaughtered as a sheep, yet rising he remains forever, dying no longer [John 12:34].

He calls light the evangelical teaching, and darkness ignorance or the condemnation of the ungodly. He himself is the light. And he speaks of a time both the season before the passion and the whole of the present life, by love of humanity urging them toward faith [John 12:35].

Those who walk in light become sons of light. … The way of salvation is faith into Christ, which makes sons of light—that is, of the Father; for the Son is light and the Father is, as of one nature.

Knowing as God that they were angry, he withdrew, giving time to test what had been spoken to them, not out of fear [John 12:36].
comments.selected_reason: Explains the crowd's puzzle and what 'the light' and 'children of light' mean.
comments.author: Ammonius of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The crowd knew that the Christ abides forever but not that he must first die, and Jesus withdrew so that their deed would be planned malice.
comments.comment:
They are shown to be ignorant regarding the prophets and lacking precise knowledge of the written things; for they have received voices saying that the Christ remains forever, but they did not understand the mystery of death occurring in between and the brief dissolution of the soul from the body (John 12:34).

He does not wish to be seized while wandering in the midst or discussing in between, but withdrawing and overshadowing himself; … for it was not an act of wrath against the Savior that their work had to be, but a plan of malice; for everything done out of wrath is lesser for condemnation, but the extreme is to do evil with a plan.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: Christ came though he knew they would not believe, so that they would have no excuse.
comments.comment: Let no one say: Why then did Christ come, knowing that they would not believe [John 12:37]? For it must be said: so that the Jews might not have a pretext for unbelief, since the prophets also spoke knowing that they were not persuaded.
comments.selected_reason: Answers why Christ came to people he knew would not believe.
comments.author: Ammonius of Alexandria

comments.capsule: 'They could not believe' means they would not: God foresaw and permitted their unbelief but did not cause it.
comments.comment:
…The Jews murdered the Lord through their own ill will, not so that they might fulfill the prophecies; for if it were so they would have been irreligious in that way.

God did not harden them [John 12:40], but allowed them to do what they wished. And they had the hardening from unbelief. Yet it was impossible that God’s foreknowledge, which foresaw the unbelief, not come out—not as compelling. Those unable to believe do not have a nature opposing belief, but a bad choice. Therefore the devil darkens them and God does not hinder.

For this reason the prophets foretell, so that the sober may flee the devil’s pits; for “they could not” stands in place of “they would not” [John 12:39]; and elsewhere too we understand power as choice.
comments.selected_reason: Explains 'they could not believe' and in what sense God hardened them.
comments.author: Ammonius of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The hardening is God's permission and the devil's work, not God's own act.
comments.comment: Let us not think that a hardening and a callousness of heart is brought on by God as the operation of the holy power (John 12:40), but rather a concession to the divine judgment, and the operation of the evil and opposing power.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: The Lord of hosts whom Isaiah saw is the one God in three persons, so John can apply Isaiah's words to the Son.
comments.comment: For Father and Son and Holy Spirit is Lord of hosts. For the deity is one, and one God in three persons. And for this reason, what the Father said in Isaiah [Isaiah 6:1-10], John says that the Son said [John 12:41]; and in Acts Paul says that the Holy Spirit said [Acts 28:25-27]. … But the evangelist John says: “For this reason the Jews could not believe in Jesus, because Isaiah said: ‘He has blinded their eyes and hardened their heart, lest they see with their eyes and understand with their heart and turn, and I heal them’” (John 12:39-40).
comments.author: Marcellus of Ancyra
comments.work: On the Incarnation and against the Arians

comments.capsule: To believe in Jesus is to believe in God, since the Father is seen and received in the Son.
comments.comment:
It is evident that before the fully revealed departure these things were said to the Lord (John 12:44-45), and after these words He withdrew, … He reproved the terrible sin of standing against confession [John 12:42-43]; for he said that those doing this are setting aside faith in God; for one does not believe in something other than God, who is seen in Him, because, he says, the Father is seen in the Son. … but he who, in the vision of the Son, sees the Father, does not turn beyond Jesus to the Father, but remaining in the Son and standing, receives the Father.

… So then, as he was saying, the one believing in me does not believe in a mere human, but in the power of God, in whom the Father is known and believed.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: As the Father's image the Son shows the Father, so honor given to him is given to the Father.
comments.comment:
Being image of the Father he shows the Father through himself [John 12:45]. Through this he signifies the indistinguishability of essence, showing the consubstantial; for the divine is incorporeal. These things signify likeness.

Because of the hearers’ weakness he speaks as man [John 12:44]. When I am honored, do not think you honor a man; for through me the Father is honored.
comments.author: Ammonius of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Seeing the Father in Jesus means spiritual sight, not looking at his body, or else even his crucifiers would have seen God.
comments.comment: As for “the maker and father of the universe”, we say that to see him is “a hard task”. Yet he is seen, not only in keeping with the words, “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matthew 5:8), but also in keeping with what is said by the image “of the invisible God” (Colossians 1:15): “He who has seen me has seen the Father who sent me” (John 14:9; John 12:45). For no one with any sense would say that in these words Jesus was referring to his body, which could be perceived by the senses and was visible to men, when he said, “He who has seen me has seen the Father who sent me.” For on that reading all who said, “Crucify, crucify him” (Luke 23:21), would have seen God the Father, and so would Pilate, who received authority over his human nature; and that is absurd.
comments.selected_reason: Explains in what sense whoever sees Jesus sees the Father.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: As light the Son reveals himself and the Father; he came now to save, and his rejected word will stand as judge.
comments.comment:
As the Father is light, so also the Son [John 12:46]. Therefore Paul, wanting to show the great resemblance, calls the Son “radiance” of the Father (Hebrews 1:3): just as light appearing makes both itself clear and the things seen, so the Son, being light and having come, made both himself and the Father known to us.

The aim of the present coming was not to judge but to save the faithful [John 12:47]. And so as not to give them occasion for unbelief, he refers the cause of unbelief toward him up to the Father.

For the word of his humility condemns them [John 12:48]. The Son himself is going to judge the disobedient, not the word; for he speaks enigmatically. On the day of judgment the word that called us to salvation punishes those who disobeyed.
comments.selected_reason: Explains 'I am come a light' and how 'the word ... shall judge him'.
comments.author: Ammonius of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Though he speaks of a commandment from the Father, the Son speaks with the Creator's own authority, not as a servant.
comments.comment: His words are spoken with authority [John 12:49], because he is both Creator and the lawgiver to his own creatures, according to the word of God, through whom all things came into being (John 1:3), who came to his own (John 1:11) and converses with authority, not as if he were any servant of the words given from God. … Nor is the lawgiving foreign to the Savior, nor does he speak from revelation, nor does he converse as if things were commanded, if we think according to divinity his own nature and his eternal existence.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: As the Word who expresses the Father's mind, the Son speaks of a commandment, meaning that his words are the Father's too.
comments.comment:
Being Word of the Father he himself interprets what is in the Father and makes it manifest. Therefore he also says he has received a commandment [John 12:49]; for so among us too word publishes what is in the mind.

He says he does these things as from the Father, since the Jews saw him reshaping the shadow of the law toward the more spiritual.

Saying this he did not abolish his own authority, but shows that nothing alien to the Father is in the Son. I utter nothing contrary to the Father, nor as mine alone, but as common.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the Son speaks of receiving a commandment.
comments.author: Ammonius of Alexandria

comments.capsule: John says the supper was before the feast of the Passover, so Matthew's 'first day of unleavened bread' must mean the day before it.
comments.comment: It was the custom of those eating the Passover, and they were dining. And John has said nothing of a remembrance of the Passover, having made it by saying: 'Before the feast of the Passover, Jesus knowing that his hour had come to pass from this world to the Father, having loved his own who were in the world, loved them unto the end' (John 13:1) and the following. 'Before the feast of the Passover' he says, not in the feast of the Passover, so that we also received 'the first of the unleavened' (Matthew 26:17) naturally, having understood it as before the unleavened.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: Knowing his hour, Jesus went willingly to the death he calls a passing, and there showed his love perfectly to all his own.
comments.comment:
He foreknew the passion; therefore it must be said that he came willingly to suffer; for he would not unwillingly have endured so insulting a death. He calls hour the Passover feast at which he suffered; he calls his death a passing.

He loved them even before the Passover, having become man; but when he also handed himself over to die, then he perfectly showed his love toward human beings. Not only Jews but also others he has as his own as Creator. He calls his own all who are in the world.
comments.selected_reason: Explains 'his hour', 'depart' and 'his own', and how he loved them to the end.
comments.author: Ammonius of Alexandria

comments.capsule: John marvels that Jesus washed his betrayer's feet; 'already' means Judas had agreed the day before.
comments.comment: As astonished the evangelist says that he washed the feet of the one who had set himself to hand him over to death. On the fifth day the supper; on the fourth Judas agreed to betray Christ; therefore he said the devil had already cast into the heart that Judas should betray him.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why John names Judas's plan before the foot-washing.
comments.author: Ammonius of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The washing readied them for the gospel and taught humility, the Spirit would explain it later, and only Christ's cleansing grace gives a share in him.
comments.comment:
Through the touch he was cleansing their feet for readiness of the gospel [Ephesians 6:15]. And he also leads them into humility.

[John 13:7] When I am taken up, he says, then from the Spirit’s grace you will learn what is happening.

[John 13:8] If you do not accept the lesson of humility, you have no share with me—that is, unless someone washes off the filth of sin through Christ’s grace …
comments.author: Ammonius of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The foot-washing signifies that Jesus must wash away the soul's defilement for us to walk his way and have a part with him.
comments.comment:
And just as holy Moses and his successor Joshua are commanded by God to loose the sandals when stepping upon a holy place—it not being fitting for the feet to wear dead hide in a holy place—so if someone is going to walk unimpeded, perhaps he ought not only to loose but also to wash off the uncleanness that has come about from the dust around the feet. And we suppose a symbol of this to be that the Savior, having put water into the basin, washed the feet of the disciples, saying to Peter who did not yet understand the mystery and for this reason was hindering: “If I do not wash you, you have no part with me,” (John 13:8) and “What I am doing you do not know now, but you will know after these things.” (John 13:7)

Therefore it will be necessary for the uncleanness around the feet of the soul, so to speak, also to need Jesus, so that he may wash it off and we may be able to have a part with him. For if this remains, it is an obstacle to our walking the road according to the sound word—the Savior who said: “I am the way.” (John 14:6)
comments.selected_reason: Explains 'If I wash thee not, thou hast no part with me'.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Both of Peter's replies came from love, and the disciples were clean through Christ's teaching, except Judas.
comments.comment:
Having at first spoken against it through humility, now through excess of reverence Peter says something superfluous—both from fierce love [John 13:9].

They were clean, enlightened by the teaching and freed from Jewish error and having cast off all wickedness by being with Christ [John 13:10]. And by witnessing purity to the others he proves unclean the one who is not clean [John 13:11].
comments.selected_reason: Explains Peter's 'not my feet only' and 'ye are clean, but not all'.
comments.author: Ammonius of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Jesus washed their feet not because they were dirty but to give an example of humility in deed.
comments.comment:
By saying “I am” he showed that he is God by nature and teacher [John 13:13].

Not because they were filthy did he wash them, but to teach them to be moderate. The basin does not hold the rank of a bath nor lighten sins, but leads toward perfect virtue.
