Not only in word but also in deed he gave the example of perfect humility [John 13:15].
comments.selected_reason: Explains the purpose of the foot-washing as an example of humility.
comments.author: Ammonius of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Only God is master and sender by nature, so no servant or apostle can surpass him.
comments.comment: No slave of any nature exists among men, nor does anyone naturally possess the power to send or to be sent (John 13:14, 16), but God alone is master by nature, being beyond the nature of his own works, and He alone is the apostle of nature, being above the being sent. Here it is impossible for slaves to surpass the master, or apostles the sender; for that which is greater by nature is not surpassed.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: Blessing comes from doing what we know, and Judas was not forced by prophecy to betray but freely turned from good.
comments.comment:
It is not knowing virtue that is to be emulated, but working it; for knowing and not doing brings greater punishment. Knowing happens to belong to many; doing does not belong to all. Therefore he said: blessed are you if you do them [John 13:17].

Judas was not compelled to betray so that the Spirit’s words might come out—which is full of every blasphemy—but so that we may know that Scripture spoke about that one whom we see having done what was foretold. And if the Lord chose Judas and he transgressed, nothing follows from this; for he chose him while he was good, and he was changed like Adam and Saul; for God does not abolish free will, but allows each to act as he wishes, so that the wicked may be punished and the virtuous crowned.

Through the morsel the Lord fulfilled the prophecy that says: “He who eats my bread has lifted up his heel against me” (Psalm 41:9; John 13:18).
comments.selected_reason: Explains 'happy are ye if ye do them' and 'that the scripture may be fulfilled'.
comments.author: Ammonius of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The psalm's table-companion who lifts his heel is Judas, a trusted friend who struck like a serpent at the heel.
comments.comment: The resurrection, he says, will dissolve the conspiracy of the enemies against us and the betrayal of friends (Psalm 41:9). For already a disciple has risen up against me—one deemed worthy of peace from me, counted among those entrusted to me, and sharing my food—but he was exposed as a serpent, wanting to seize my heel. The Lord himself remembered this as spoken about him, saying, “But so that the Scripture may be fulfilled, the one who eats my bread has lifted up his heel against me” (John 13:18) (Psalm 41:9).
comments.selected_reason: Explains the image 'lifted up his heel against me'.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: In foretelling the betrayal Jesus showed divine knowledge of hearts and divine goodness, still honoring Judas while turning his evil to good.
comments.comment:
In these things, the Lord showed both the knowing and the non-evil [freedom from malice] to be divine from Himself (John 13:21): the knowing by seeing the traitor and separating him by the word from those being saved, since He did not wish to separate him by the deed until even washing the feet like the others. But it is God's to examine hearts and to foresee what comes from them.

And the non-evil is divine, not in the sense of dishonoring the plotter, but in honoring him equally by using his evil for the common good; for God provides the gifts from Himself to both the evil and the good, just as the Lord Himself has said: raising the sun upon the evil and the good (Matthew 5:45), and raining upon the just and the unjust. And He acts by permitting the evil of the wicked for some useful purpose, … just as those who plotted against Joseph helped Joseph to glory through their plotting, and the salvation lying through him in famine for many (Genesis 50:20).
comments.selected_reason: Explains why Jesus named the betrayer only in word and still treated him as one of the twelve.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: Jesus shared the secret quietly with the beloved disciple, and the morsel, given as to a friend, exposed Judas, after which Satan took hold of him.
comments.comment:
Having leaned upon the chest of Jesus so as not to cry out loudly to the others (John 13:25-26), he [John] was eager, … Thus Jesus grants to the beloved the sharing of the mysteries; for he says that to know and to make manifest what is hidden with him is to be a friend. Therefore he is judged by word and shows by deed the one he is signaling. And this is not in vain; for the movement through deed is more manifest and more able to be remembered. And he wanted him to be remembered, because he had foretold the betrayer, so that no one would think him to be acting without knowing.

And the sign for the signaling is wonderful; for through this unthinking gathering, he signals him by giving the morsel, and by this, having shown him, he will be a betrayer, whom he honored as a friend. Therefore the betrayer can no longer hold himself, but from the point where the Lord pointed him out, the devil prevails over his thoughts and leads him toward the evil outcome, having him through wickedness and the condemnation toward this, which he proved worthy of himself. Since it seemed to him to hide it, he was exposed by the glory of the morsel; not being able to bear the exposure, he hastened to go to the end. The evangelist called this the entrance of Satan [John 13:27], the condemnation of the passions by the devilish thoughts.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the beloved disciple's quiet question and the sign of the morsel.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: Satan 'enters' a careless soul not by dwelling in it but by deceiving it and working his malice through it.
comments.comment: But they again raise objections, saying: “It is written, allegedly, concerning Ananias: ‘Why has Satan filled your heart?’ (Acts 5:3); and concerning Judas, that ‘Satan entered into him’ (John 13:27).” To them it must be said that he fills the one who does not attend to “Do not let your foot be moved, and he who keeps you will not slumber” (Psalm 121:3; LXX 120:3) — not by being partaken of, nor by riding upon the soul as it were, but by deceiving, and working in the treacherous manner of malice, and making his own wickedness a mere side-show.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Satan first prompted Judas and then entered him once he was set on betrayal, and Jesus' 'do quickly' was a reproach, not a command.
comments.comment:
On the fourth day Satan cast into Judas that he should betray the Lord [John 13:2], and he spoke this to the Jews on the fifth toward evening. When he saw Judas wanting to betray the Lord in deed and hurrying to it, then he entered into him [John 13:27]. So casting in is one thing and entering into him another, just as striking someone with the hand from outside is one thing and giving him an opening and thrusting the sword in is another.

The evangelist calls the devil’s entrance the confirming of Judas to do what is pleasing to the devil. When God made him plain and set him apart, then the devil sprang upon him because of his measureless shamelessness.

He does not say this [“do quickly”] as commanding, but as reproaching the one he let do what he wished, since he did not want to be corrected. Since this is settled for you, hasten to the plot against me; for suffering does not grieve me.

The morsel given him in the order of a blessing was not the cause of Judas’s apostasy, but the unchangeable wickedness after the exposure. Therefore the enemy also sprang in as into an ungated city.

Since perhaps John said it to him secretly and he heard, no one knew [John 13:28]; for if they had known, perhaps they would even have killed him—or because they were in turmoil, not knowing what was in Judas’s heart, they did not understand what was said.

If someone says how the one fed from others’ means, who did not allow the disciples to carry a bag or purse, had a money-box [John 13:29], it must be said that this happened only for the sake of the poor.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the difference between 13:2 and 13:27 and 'That thou doest, do quickly'.
comments.author: Ammonius of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Christ is glorified by conquering death through death, and Father and Son glorify each other, as the cross and Pentecost revealed.
comments.comment:
Even if the Son does all things, yet through what he does he ascribes them to the Father and glorifies the Father [John 13:31].

Christ, as having put death to death through his own death, was glorified; he teaches that enduring what is shameful for God’s sake is glory.

The Father was glorified in the Son, since it became known whose Father he is. So also the Son is glorified as having such a begetter.

Through himself the Father will glorify the Son, and at once—that is, on the cross, when the sun was darkened, the rocks were split, and after fifty days the Spirit descending made the Son plain to all [John 13:32].

They were seeking him as one who loves and as a teacher [John 13:33].
comments.selected_reason: Explains how Father and Son glorify each other in 13:31-32.
comments.author: Ammonius of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Love as Christ commands it fulfills the whole law, so Paul calls it the law's fullness.
comments.comment: From here I think also the apostle, having learned the power of love (John 13:34-35), names it 'fullness' and 'law' [Romans 13:10; Galatians 6:2]; for it is evident that he who grants even of his own soul to his friends will stand away from all other pleasures and much more will forgive; and this being accomplished, there is no pretext or need for any of the partial commands, all of which are briefly contained in this.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: The commandment is new because it asks love beyond the law, even for those we owe nothing, as Christ died for us.
comments.comment:
New is the form of this commandment, and beyond the law is loving the neighbor more than oneself [John 13:34]. I do not want you to love those to whom you owe, but those to whom you do not owe; for I too die for you, to whom I owe nothing.

Not from the signs you do will you be known as my disciples—for that belongs wholly to grace from above—but from loving one another and having concord and giving yourselves [John 13:35].

Christ is a son of love, who is love according to nature, being love itself by nature and fruit of love, not having the good of love as something acquired.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what is new in the new commandment and why love, not signs, marks a disciple.
comments.author: Ammonius of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Christ makes love, not even martyrdom, the mark of his disciples.
comments.comment: For Paul knows—Paul knows clearly—that of love nothing is either greater or equal, not even martyrdom itself, which is the chief point of all good things. And how is this so? Listen. Love, even without martyrdom, makes disciples of Christ, but martyrdom without love would not be able to accomplish this. From where is this clear? From the very words of Christ. For he said to his disciples, “By this everyone will know that you are my disciples, if you love one another” (John 13:35). See, love without martyrdom makes disciples. And that martyrdom without love not only does not make disciples but does not even benefit the one enduring it, listen to Paul saying, “If I hand over my body to be burned, but do not have love, I gain nothing” (1 Corinthians 13:3).
comments.author: John Chrysostom

comments.capsule: The disciples cannot follow yet because their race is unfinished, but souls later follow Christ into heaven.
comments.comment: [John 13:36: “you cannot follow me now”] Only because they cannot walk into heaven in the body, and also because they have not yet completed the 'race' of the apostolate, which made them worthy of following the Lord. But the saying shows that the souls follow the Lord into heaven, becoming no longer below or under the earth as captives (John 13:36).
comments.selected_reason: Explains why Peter cannot follow 'now' but will follow afterward.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: Peter could not follow yet but would later die as Christ did, and Jesus foretold his denial without causing it.
comments.comment:
Because of weakness he forbids Peter to follow him, yet later promises because of boldness [John 13:36]. Since he too was going to be crucified as Christ was, he foretells what will happen to him alone.

Peter has become a type for us of asking teachers what we do not know.

Disbelieving somewhat what was said, Peter inquires, and so also promises to die for him [John 13:37].

Since you do not want to be persuaded that what I say cannot fail to happen, you will know it in the denial [John 13:38]. And he underwent this not because Christ led him into it, but because he left him bare, so that he might not be lifted into arrogance.

Let no one say that Peter denied because Christ said so; for he did not lay necessity on him so that he should come to denial, but as God he foretells to the disciple what was altogether going to be. And the denial did not come from an unbelieving soul, but from weakness.

Not all of you are going to deny, he says; Peter’s denial will be wiped out through repentance and confession.
comments.selected_reason: Explains 'thou shalt follow me afterwards' and that the prediction did not force the denial.
comments.author: Ammonius of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Peter's boast trusted his own strength instead of asking for Christ's help, yet his fall was a slip of the tongue, not Judas's sin of the heart.
comments.comment:
Did Judas and Peter not fall together—the one as having said, “What will you give me, and I will hand him over to you?” (Matthew 26:15), the other as having said, “I will lay down my soul for you” (John 13:37)? For he should have known that a mortal does not give his soul for immortality. And again: “Even if I must die with you, I will never deny you” (Matthew 26:35). He could have said: “If you strengthen me, I will never deny you. If you make me secure, I who am weak do not fear shipwreck. If you share in the battle, I do not shrink from death.”

But the one was a matter of the tongue, and the other a sin of the heart. Therefore Peter fell and rose again, and became a guide for others who had fallen; but the other, led from the depths to the pit, threw away the silver, took the rope, and hanged himself.
comments.selected_reason: Shows what was wrong in Peter's promise to lay down his life.
comments.author: Hesychius of Jerusalem

comments.capsule: Since saving faith is directed to God, Christ's command to believe in him shows that he is God.
comments.comment:
That faith toward Christ is as toward God (John 14:1). From Peter’s first letter: “So that,” he says, “your faith and hope may be in God” (1 Peter 1:21) — and yet Christ is proclaimed through the holy apostles. And he himself says somewhere: “Truly, truly I say to you, the one who believes in me has eternal life.” (John 6:47)

So when faith is toward God, and Christ says “Believe in me,” how would he not be God clearly?
comments.selected_reason: Explains what 'believe also in me' implies: Christ asks for the faith owed to God.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On the True Faith, to the Princesses Arcadia and Marina

comments.capsule: The place was prepared long ago; Christ ascends to open heaven, once closed to all flesh, and will come back to take his own there.
comments.comment:
If the place in which you are going to be with me had not long ago been prepared for you, I would have gone away and prepared a place for you.

[John 14:3] There is no need to ascend for the sake of preparing a place for you, but so that I may make you a pasture of ascent where the angels’ dwelling is, which was impassable to all flesh. When therefore I do this, coming “in the regeneration” (Matthew 19:28) I take you with myself, that you may be where I am.
comments.selected_reason: Explains 'I go to prepare a place for you'.
comments.author: Ammonius of Alexandria

comments.capsule: 'Way' names Christ's visible humanity, which leads us into righteousness, while 'truth' and 'life' name the invisible divine nature.
comments.comment:
For the manhood of Christ has become for us the starting point of the fairest ways of righteousness, leading us to better pursuits. It fittingly joins us to the Spirit, guides us into paradise, and restores us to our proper pasture. Therefore Christ said, “I am the way and the truth and the life” (John 14:6).

By the name “way” he indicates the covering according to the manhood, which belongs to bodily and visible things; for a way is a portion of earth and a perceptible ground. But the name “truth” and “life” indicates the nature of the Father; for truth is an intelligible thing that falls under neither sight nor touch.
comments.selected_reason: Explains each of the three words in 'the way, the truth, and the life'.
comments.author: Eustathius of Antioch

comments.capsule: Christ is truth as perfect virtue and life as eternal existence, and he both walked the road of virtue as a man and is himself the way to God.
comments.comment:
He calls Himself Truth because of the perfection and precision of virtue, and Life because of the lasting and eternal nature of existence; and He makes manifest those who are established in virtue and attain eternal life, showing them to be traveling toward God and that this is the way.

He has also said that He is both traveling and being the way; traveling indeed according to the earthly citizenship, in which He fulfilled every virtue and brought life as if a crown to the citizenship, but being the way because He Himself is the living virtue and the eternal life… And through incarnation He also took up the earthly energies and good works, through which He leads all toward God and toward His own divinity.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: Christ is the way that leads to the Father, the truth whose promises cannot fail, and the life that even death cannot stop.
comments.comment:
He is way because through him they were coming and he himself was Lord of leading up to the Father. Truth because of truthfulness, that these things will altogether be. And life, because not even death itself, he says, will be able to hinder you from coming.

He is way through the practical, truth as true definition of the faith, life as raising us and leading into incorruption and freeing from the ancient curse.
comments.author: Ammonius of Alexandria

comments.capsule: To 'see' the Father is to know him with the mind through the incarnate Son; Philip hoped to see God with his eyes.
comments.comment:
Here he calls sight the knowledge according to mind. Therefore the one who contemplates the Son not in bare essence but clothed in flesh knows his equal Father in all things. Knowledge shows contemplation through notions; vision shows assurance through God-befitting works.

[John 14:8] As knowing the Son exactly he [Philip] said this, thinking perhaps he could see God with the eyes.
comments.author: Ammonius of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Seeing the Father in Christ cannot mean seeing his body, or Pilate and the crowd would have seen God; it means knowing the Son as the image of the invisible God.
comments.comment:
As for “the maker and father of the universe”, we say that to see him is “a hard task”. Yet he is seen, not only in keeping with the words, “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matthew 5:8), but also in keeping with what is said by the image “of the invisible God” (Colossians 1:15): “He who has seen me has seen the Father who sent me” (John 14:9; John 12:45).

For no one with any sense would say that in these words Jesus was referring to his body, which could be perceived by the senses and was visible to men, when he said, “He who has seen me has seen the Father who sent me.” For on that reading all who said, “Crucify, crucify him” (Luke 23:21), would have seen God the Father, and so would Pilate, who received authority over his human nature; and that is absurd.

That the words “He who has seen me has seen the Father who sent me” are not to be taken in the commoner sense is clear from what was said to Philip: “Have I been with you so long, and you have not known me, Philip?” (John 14:9). He said this to him when he made the request, “Show us the Father, and it is enough for us” (John 14:8). Whoever, then, has understood how we must take what is said about the only-begotten God (John 1:18), the Son of God, “the firstborn of all creation” (Colossians 1:15), inasmuch as “the Word” became “flesh” (John 1:14), will see how anyone who has seen the image “of the invisible God” (Colossians 1:15) will know “the Father and maker of this universe”.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what 'he who has seen me has seen the Father' can and cannot mean, in plain terms.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Man images God only as a product images its maker, but the Son bears the Father's very form, so that seeing him is seeing the Father.
comments.comment:
…concerning man, he says, it has been written, that he is ‘an image and glory of God’ [1 Corinthians 11:7]. But nowhere, O you ones, has it been written that man or any other creature is to be ‘an emanation of the glory of God and a character of the hypostasis’ [Hebrews 1:3]. It is something else to be a man as an image of God, that is, the thing made of the maker, just as Solomon says concerning the product of a carpenter: ‘The maker is perceived in a likeness to the things created’; but it is something else to be, according to the same form and identical and co-ruling, an emanation of glory and a character of hypostasis, in-dwelling and unerring.

For he says: ‘He who has seen me has seen the Father’ (John 14:9). But he who has seen a man has not seen God, just as he who has seen the product has not seen the carpenter.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Whoever sees the Son sees the Father, not because they are one person, but because the Son is the Father's exact likeness.
comments.comment:
Nothing else, he says, is the Son except what the Father is while remaining Son; for even if you happen to say, Philip, that I know you, that you are Son, yet you have not recognized me, that having the whole Father in myself I remain again being Son.

From what the Son has done both before incarnation and after incarnation, his infinite strength appears to the mind as “in a mirror” (1 Corinthians 13:12).

The wording signifies the extreme resemblance and equality. Therefore, lest someone fall into Sabellius’s heresy by dividing the hypostases [the distinct persons], he adds saying: the one who has seen me has seen the Father. And this he makes clear through knowledge. He says these things about the invisible essence of himself and of the Father; for it is not possible to see the divine with fleshly eyes. Therefore he said: the one who has seen me has seen the Father—not that he himself is the Father, but that through the extreme resemblance the one who sees the Son sees the Father; for each is self-subsistent.
comments.author: Ammonius of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The Son is in the Father by sharing his very nature.
comments.comment: Having by nature in his own nature the Father’s own things through the consubstantial [the shared essence]; for the Son essentially encompasses the Father and is in him through the consubstantial. …
comments.author: Ammonius of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Christ credits his words and works to the Father not as a servant would, but because he is so united to the Father by nature that he does nothing without him.
comments.comment: [Christ speaking:] …I attributed my words to him [the Father] and said, “The words I speak to you I do not speak of myself; the Father who remains in me does the works” (John 14:10). I attributed the works and the words to him, not to show that I fulfill a service, but to show that I have been united to the Father in nature in such a way that I have neither word nor work without him. That is why I went on to say, “Believe me that I am in the Father and the Father is in me; but if not, believe because of the works” (John 14:11; John 5:36).
comments.selected_reason: Explains why Christ says his words are 'not of myself' without making himself a mere servant.
comments.author: Amphilochius of Iconium

comments.capsule: The disciples' 'greater works' are spiritual healings, opening blind souls and deaf ears, which surpass the bodily miracles Jesus did.
comments.comment: For my part I would say that, in keeping with Jesus’ promise, the disciples have done even “greater” works (John 14:12) than the visible works that Jesus did. For the eyes of those blind in soul are always being opened, and the ears of those who had been deaf to words of virtue hear eagerly about God and the blessed life with him. Many, too, who were lame in the feet of what Scripture calls the “inner” man (Romans 7:22; Ephesians 3:16), now that the Word has healed them, do not merely leap but leap “like a deer” (Isaiah 35:6)…
comments.selected_reason: Gives a clear answer to how disciples could do 'greater works' than Jesus.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The apostles never did bodily wonders greater than raising Lazarus; their works are called greater only because their power came from Christ, whose works include creation itself.
comments.comment:
When I was speaking concerning the Gospel, concerning that place: ‘He who believes in me, the works that I do, he will do, and greater than these he will do’ (John 14:12), to others this interpretation was also given: if you consider the one who does, the great things are small; as compared to God they are small. For the apostles did not perform sensible works greater than those of the Savior. The Savior raised Lazarus, already on the fourth day being in death and near to decomposing and already having reached the point of stinking. The apostles did not do anything of this kind. Jesus brought the blind from birth to sight.

If, however, you consider these works of the Savior, they are small compared to having performed the rational essence, the heavens, the souls. And the works of the apostles, even if they were greater than those of the Savior, since their power is from Him, are rather called greater than those which the Savior did; for they were not able to do greater than these. But Jesus both did and always does.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Christ is one with the Father by nature, the apostles only by grace through faith, so their works are really the Lord's and they do nothing greater than he.
comments.comment: He was currently exercising His natural unity toward the Father (John 14:12), and He freely offers also a union toward the apostles according to His grace; for this is the likeness and imitation of that which is natural according to grace; and indeed this happens through faith, but that the former is not through faith, but according to natural power; for Christ does not work the wonders toward the Father by faith, but the apostles perform the things of the Son by faith in the Son, and the works are not the apostles' own, but the Lord's own, and those things being done through them. Therefore, reverence is indeed offered to the Son, but reverence is owed to the apostles in no way, nor would they do anything greater than the Lord.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: By saying 'I' both of going to the Father and of answering prayer, Christ shows that one person speaks in both his human and his divine nature.
comments.comment: …“I am going to my Father; and whatever you ask in my name, this I will do, so that the Father may be glorified in the Son” (John 14:12–13). In the statements made about both his divinity and his humanity, he places the “I,” so that the meaning of the words is shown by their sequence, while the discernment of the natures is shown by the difference in what is said. And because he speaks in both cases as though about one person, he signifies the union of the person.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the one 'I' says both 'I go to my Father' and 'this I will do'.
comments.author: Cyril of Jerusalem

comments.capsule: When Christ answers prayer the work is his own, and through it the Father is shown and glorified, since the Father is always approached through the Son.
comments.comment:
Christ does whatever the apostles ask (John 14:13); for He said, 'I will do whatever you ask in my name.' And His own work is thus demonstrated.

In this he says that the Father is glorified in himself, the Father working, while the Father is being manifested through the energy of the Son; for there is no other approach to the Father or through the Son, neither of old nor now nor again, but the approach through the Son is more intimate, and it has come to be now, because having been made flesh, he has become nearer to us.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: Keeping the commandments is our part and proves our love; sharing the divine nature is Christ's gift, asked of the Father for us.
comments.comment: Regarding John 14:15-16, … the keeping of the commandments is ours, and this is the proof of the love toward the Lord; but from him to us the participation in the divine nature is granted to those who are suitable for becoming participants through obedience; and he says to ask the Father as a brotherly embassy on our behalf…
comments.selected_reason: Shows how 'if you love me, keep my commandments' and the promised gift fit together.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: 'Another' shows the Spirit is a distinct person, yet of Christ's own kind; Christ 'asks' as man; and the world cannot receive the Spirit because it knows only what it sees.
comments.comment:
…By saying “another” he shows the difference of the hypostases [the distinct persons], and by saying “as me” the kinship of essence. … Nor is the Spirit sent as if displaced, but he who is everywhere stands over them with authority; yet he said this showing the time of the presence; for unless Christ were sacrificed and sin loosed, the Spirit would not have come upon the faithful.

And by economy [his plan of salvation], as man giving reverence to the Father, he said “I will ask.” And he called him another because he is self-subsistent, not because he is alien to the Father or the Son; for he works those things which the Son does, so that the Spirit seems to be the Son himself. Therefore he is also called Spirit of truth, which is Christ.

Paraclete is the name of both the Son and the Spirit as giving us comfort and as interceding for us with the Father; for this name produces comfort and does not signify a different essence of Spirit and Father.

By saying “remains” he taught that not even after death does the Spirit depart, just as a quality of the Godhead comes to be in you and remains always in the saints, whenever through virtue and purity they are eager to keep the grace in themselves.

That is: the worldly, who conceive nothing outside what is seen, cannot receive what is incorporeal and invisible; “receive” he said—that is, they can neither contemplate nor so know.
comments.selected_reason: Explains 'another Comforter', 'I will pray the Father', and why the world cannot receive the Spirit.
comments.author: Ammonius of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The Father sends the bodiless Spirit, whose presence is invisible, so those who count only visible things real cannot grasp him.
comments.comment: Regarding John 14:16-17, the Spirit indeed of truth, the incorporeal, is being sent from the incorporeal. Therefore also he has said the Father sends it, revealing his incorporeal presence, since he himself is seen in a body. But the presence of the incorporeal is invisible. Therefore also to those who think that only the visible things are real, this presence of his is ungraspable; for indeed he is also unfeeling and because of this unknown; for what they do not behold with eyes, this they neither know nor think to be…
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: Christ says 'orphans' because he is leaving those he had called 'little children.'
comments.comment: He never left them empty of his providence, yet he also appeared to them after the resurrection. Since when he came he called them “little children,” [John 13:33] when about to depart he said orphans.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why Jesus uses the word 'orphans'.
comments.author: Ammonius of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The 'little while' runs until the second coming, and Christ's resurrection is the pledge that his disciples will share the life to come.
comments.comment:
Because he was going to appear only to them after the resurrection, he said “a little” to all. He calls a little time the span until the second coming; for even a long time is little to God. But you the saints will know me through the Spirit’s indwelling, not those who love the world’s things.

An earnest of the coming life, which you are to receive, is my resurrection. He says the disciples live not only the present life but the coming one.
comments.selected_reason: Explains 'yet a little while' and 'because I live, ye shall live also'.
comments.author: Ammonius of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Christ is in the Father by nature, believers are in Christ because he became man, and he is in them by the Spirit dwelling within.
comments.comment:
When he rose from the dead and they obtained the Holy Spirit, they received knowledge that the Son, having the same power as the Father, is not split from him because of the unity of essence, and is always with them helping them.

[Christ means:] I, being life by nature, joined myself to the Father who is by nature and life itself. And I also joined you to the Father through the co-dwelling of the Holy Spirit, making you “partakers of the divine nature” (2 Peter 1:4); for I am in the Father naturally as his fruit, and you in me inasmuch as I became man, and I in you through the Spirit’s indwelling.

After the resurrection those who believe rightly will know perfectly; for now “we know in part” (1 Corinthians 13:9), that just as the Son is consubstantial with the Father, so also there is one will of both.
comments.selected_reason: Explains clearly the three 'in' phrases of the verse.
comments.author: Ammonius of Alexandria

comments.capsule: By naming those who keep his commandments, Christ shows that only the good will be loved by Father and Son and see God's glory.
comments.comment: …by having and keeping his commandments he shows that not all may obtain such a gift, but the good; for after the resurrection those who believed rightly and lived perfectly will know perfectly the glory of the Godhead. Such people, he says, the Father will love, and the Son also will love, to whom the authority and power of the Godhead will be perfectly manifested.
comments.author: Ammonius of Alexandria

comments.capsule: God dwells in believers by grace through faith and the Spirit, not by nature as the Father is in the Son, and the plural 'we' shows Father and Son are two persons.
comments.comment:
As a lover of the good, Judas wanted all the good to enjoy the vision of God.

[John 14:23] The Father is in the Son naturally, but in us relatively; and when we hear of union of Father and Son we understand the natural, but when union of God and human beings, we understand the relative that comes to the saints from faith and the communion from partaking of the Spirit. And by speaking in the plural he destroys Sabellius’s heresy that says one hypostasis and one person of Father and Son.

He teaches that only to the disciples exceptionally and beyond reason will the illumination be, for those who keep the commandments.
comments.selected_reason: Explains 'we will come unto him, and make our abode with him', including the plural.
comments.author: Ammonius of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The word is both Christ's and the Father's, being common to both.
comments.comment: He seems to say the word is his and not his, because he speaks nothing outside the Father as his own, but what seems good to him—my word and the Father’s is common.
comments.selected_reason: Resolves the paradox of 'the word which ye hear is not mine'.
comments.author: Ammonius of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The Spirit reminds the disciples of what Christ taught, so no later prophet can claim a new revelation, and his coming will make up for Christ's absence.
comments.comment:
Therefore those around Montanus [a second-century prophet] who came after two hundred years were not the first to obtain the Spirit; for what could the Spirit remind them of that they had not heard at all from Christ?

[Christ means:] Do not take my absence hard; for when the Spirit comes he will be a provider of great goods to you, teaching you the security of my words and comforting you from the afflictions that press you. When the Spirit comes you will learn many things you do not know, and he will recall what I said.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what 'bring all things to your remembrance' implies about the Spirit's teaching.
comments.author: Ammonius of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The world's peace can exist even among the wicked, but Christ's peace brings harmony with others and within ourselves.
comments.comment:
[Christ means:] Do not be troubled hearing that I am about to suffer; for there is much gain from this.

The world’s peace is where it also happens for evil; but Christ’s peace persuades not only to be at peace with those outside but also with yourselves, so that the flesh may not rebel against the soul.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the contrast between the world's peace and Christ's.
comments.author: Ammonius of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Christ's bequest of peace is an inheritance that does not shrink however many share it; only division makes it narrow.
comments.comment: …that inheritance is not the land that was given to the sons of Jacob. The land was given to the sons of Israel; the more people possessed it, the more crowded it became. Our inheritance is called peace. I read the testament: My peace I give to you, my peace I leave with you (John 14:27). Let us hold together what cannot be divided. Many possessors do not crowd it… Our possession does not become narrow; only dissension makes narrowness.
comments.selected_reason: Reads 'peace I leave with you' as a bequest in Christ's will, and explains what kind of inheritance it is.
comments.author: Augustine of Hippo
comments.work: Sermon to the People of the Church of Caesarea

comments.capsule: Christ added 'not as the world gives' because he knew the world would make war on his followers, yet they still have his peace.
comments.comment: Jesus, then, is the founder not of faction but of all peace. He said to the disciples, “Peace I leave with you; my peace I give to you” (John 14:27). Then, since He knew that men of the world and not of God would make war on us, He added to those words, “Not as the world gives peace do I give you peace” (John 14:27). And even if we are afflicted in the world, we take courage because of Him who said, “In the world you have affliction; but take courage, I have overcome the world” (John 16:33).
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Christ made peace by breaking the power of the hostile forces, so his own, freed from captivity and fear, have a peace of soul that cannot be shaken.
comments.comment: Regarding John 14:27, Christ came to those being at war, and he worked peace, pulling down the strength of those warring; for there is no longer power for the opposing powers against those belonging to Christ; for they have come out of captivity, having known the Redeemer. Therefore peace is motionless for them, because it is a peace of the soul toward freedom being attained and fear being cast off and turmoil being expelled. Since therefore the good things of the soul are certain and unshakeable, the peace of the soul is certain.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: Christ called the Father greater as a man on earth, not because he is of another essence, for as God he is not less than the Father.
comments.comment:
You ought, hearing that I go to the Father, to take courage and not be grieved.

He calls return the time of the resurrection. The Father’s being greater does not make him of another essence, as the heretics say. When he was on earth as man he said the Father is greater. He says this because of the appearing body, since insofar as he is God he is not less than the Father, nor is he led up into the heavens—he who fills all things and is inseparable from the Father.
comments.selected_reason: Explains 'my Father is greater than I' and why it does not make the Son unequal.
comments.author: Ammonius of Alexandria

comments.capsule: 'The Father is greater' does not mean an unequal nature: it is said partly because the Son became man and partly because the Son has his being from the Father.
comments.comment:
…insofar as he is the Son, he received from the Father that he exists, while the Father did not receive this from the Son. And insofar as he took up a changeable human being—a creature that was to be changed for the better—through his ineffable mercy in his earthly mission, many things are found said about him in the Scriptures in such a way that they have driven the impious minds of heretics, who wanted to teach before they learned, into error. They have made the heretics think that he is not equal to the Father and not of the same substance as him. Such statements are these: “The Father is greater than I” (John 14:28)…

All of these were set down not to signify an inequality of nature and substance—otherwise these would be false: “I and the Father are one” (John 10:30), and “Whoever has seen me has seen my Father” (John 14:9)… Rather, those statements were set down partly because of the administration of the man he took up, which is why it says: “He emptied himself” (Philippians 2:7)—not because that wisdom was changed, since it is entirely unchangeable, but because he willed to become known to human beings in such a lowly way.

So partly because of this administration those things were written about which the heretics make false accusations, and partly because the Son owes to the Father that he exists, and in owing this he also owes to the Father that he is equal to or on a par with the Father. But the Father owes nothing of what he is to anyone.
comments.selected_reason: Gives the two classic reasons why the Father is called 'greater' while the Son remains equal.
comments.author: Augustine of Hippo

comments.capsule: The devil found nothing in Christ because Christ defeated every temptation he brought, from the wilderness to the persecutors.
comments.comment: The Lord says in the Gospel: “See, the ruler of this world is coming, and he finds nothing in me” (John 14:30). The devil certainly encountered no sin in him, because he was defeated in every temptation he brought against him, whether when he hungered or afterward when he preached, through his persecutors (compare Matthew 4:1–11; Luke 4:1–13). The Savior therefore declares that the devil detected no sin in him.
comments.author: Julian of Eclanum

comments.capsule: The ruler of this world has nothing in Christ because Christ, who did no sin, owed no debt, unlike the rest of us.
comments.comment: It can be referred both to the prophet, according to one narrative, and to the Savior. … 'I owed nothing, and no one owed me.' (Jeremiah 15:10 or John 14:30) 'The ruler of this world comes, and he has nothing in me.' (John 14:30) And truly he owed nothing. But each of us is a debtor by sins and a debtor holding a certificate of debt. After his certificate has been wiped out, how many certificates have they made again? 'He who did no sin, and no deceit was found in his mouth,' (1 Peter 2:22 or Isa 53:9) made no certificate of debt.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The devil holds only those under sin, so Christ dies not as his captive but freely, out of love for the Father who wills to save the world.
comments.comment:
…because of the love, he says, which is toward the Father, I endure death (John 14:30-31).

The ruler of evil prevails through the evil in man, taking as his own the one found under evil. Therefore, he says, it shall not happen to me as it does to certain men lying under sin, but as one voluntarily handing himself over and showing to the world the love which I have toward the Father, because, the Father willing to save the world, I work this.

The matter seems to be a departure, but it is a voluntary issuing forth, because he pursues such a place, in which he shall be known by the betrayer and shall be betrayed (John 14:31).
comments.selected_reason: Explains 'the prince of this world hath nothing in me' and 'Arise, let us go hence'.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: Christ stops talking as his passion nears and dies willingly from love.
comments.comment:
With the passion standing there is no longer need of words.

[John 14:31] Dying willingly for love toward God—which has no harm—since the Father who loves him would not have wanted this otherwise.
comments.author: Ammonius of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The Father tends the branches, the faithful made alive in Christ by the Spirit, while Christ the root needs no tending.
comments.comment: [Christ is the root,] …which the Father does not cultivate as needing no care, but the branches. And branches of Christ are the faithful united to him through the Holy Spirit’s indwelling and become “partakers of the divine nature” (2 Peter 1:4), who also receive care from the Father. And Christ as root holds the faithful together and makes them alive through the Holy Spirit; for salvation did not come from one person but from the divine Trinity.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what it means that the Father is the husbandman and the faithful are branches.
comments.author: Ammonius of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The vine teaches believers to bear fruit, to cling to neighbors in love, and to be dug around by casting off worldly cares.
comments.comment:
For you remember clearly the image of the Lord, that he calls himself the vine, and the Father the vinedresser, and he called each one of us, having been grafted into the Church through faith, branches (John 15:1-2). And he summons us to abundant fruit, so that we may not be condemned for uselessness and handed over to the fire. …

He also wants us to hold fast to our neighbors by the twining of love, as if by tendrils, and to rest upon them, so that always having our impulse toward what is above, like some climbing vines we may set ourselves beside the tops of the highest things.

He also requires us to accept being dug around. And the soul is dug around in the putting away of the cares of the world, which are a weight on our hearts. So the one who has put away fleshly love, and the friendship toward money, or has considered the anxiety for this wretched little glory to be spit upon and contemptible, has been dug around, as it were, and has breathed again, having put off the vain weight of the earthly mind. But it is necessary, according to the word of the proverb, not to grow wild like wood—that is, not to live ostentatiously, nor to hunt for praise from outsiders—but to be fruitful, storing up the display of works for the true vinedresser.
comments.selected_reason: Draws out the vine image in terms any reader can follow.
comments.author: Basil of Caesarea
comments.work: Homilies on the Six Days of Creation

comments.capsule: Faith alone does not save a branch: fruitless ones are cut off, while fruitful ones are cleansed by trials.
comments.comment:
The believer is a branch of the intelligible vine, which is Christ, and gains nothing from faith alone, but there is need also of virtuous works which come through cleansings.

Those who cling “to the Lord” and do not live worthily of him are punished, but the pious living bear much fruit. If we have faith but not works, he casts out as dead and fruitless branches, cutting. Or fruitless branches are the Jews.

He says these things about the trials they were going to endure, which made them more proven. …
comments.selected_reason: Explains the two actions of the verse: taking away and purging.
comments.author: Ammonius of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Union with Christ needs perfect love as well, since no one cut off from the vine can do good.
comments.comment:
Even if someone is united to Christ through sanctification in the Spirit, still he needs also to hold to perfect love and follow him; for the one cut off from Christ through not having perfect sanctification and love cannot do any good.

Because fruit-bearing is impossible except for those fixed to him alone, he calls himself vine …
comments.selected_reason: Explains 'without me ye can do nothing' and why Christ calls himself the vine.
comments.author: Ammonius of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Turning to fleshly things cuts one off from the vine, to dry up and await judgment.
comments.comment: Whoever therefore separates himself from the Lord toward fleshly matters, has driven himself away from the vine and becomes dry, no longer receiving the life-giving cluster (John 15:6). And such a one shall be kept for the eternal judgment just as the dry branches are for the fire (John 15:6).
comments.selected_reason: Explains the withering and burning of the branch in plain terms.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: Those who remain in Christ receive not only virtue's fruit but powers from God given in answer to prayer.
comments.comment: Remaining in me, he says, you shall not only have the things of virtue bearing fruit from yourselves, but also the greater things of virtue, I mean indeed the powers from God, which you shall receive through asking (John 15:7); for whatever you shall wish to ask, and it shall happen to you, is the power surpassing the extraordinary (John 15:7).
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the promise 'ye shall ask what ye will' gives.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: The Father is glorified when disciples remain in Christ and serve God in spirit.
comments.comment:
And he himself, not less than the Father, contributes to the disciples’ care.

[John 15:8] That is: the Father rejoices when you remain in me. Through what you do the Father is praised. This makes Christ’s disciples and bears much fruit: serving God spiritually, passing by the letter.
comments.selected_reason: Explains how the Father is glorified by the disciples' fruit.
comments.author: Ammonius of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Love for God is free and shown by obedience.
comments.comment: It is in us to love God; for he does not force our free will. For one must not only believe but also do the commandments.
comments.author: Ammonius of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Christ loved the disciples as the Father loved him, yet our love and obedience come by toil and hope of reward, his by nature.
comments.comment:
Just as I, he says, fittingly loved by him according to divinity and not having risen from men, so also you, fittingly toward me in the flesh, were loved by me (John 15:9-10). Therefore, the love which you have received, guard it. And guard it, if you keep the things commanded by me, preserving in this the imitation and the likeness toward me; for I also, thinking and doing in agreement with the Father, precisely guarded the love toward the Father (John 15:10).

And you, likewise, fulfilling the commands of mine through work, will demonstrate the love toward the Master; for neither is the love shown by you toward the Lord in the same way as the Lord toward the Father, nor is the keeping of the commandments given in equal measure by servants toward a Master and by a son toward a father. For it was by nature for the Lord to fulfill all things that are pleasing to the Father, without any toil, nor any care, nor any discipline regarding this, but for us, the achievement is through toil. And one keeps the decrees of the Father without hope of a reward, but we endure toil for the sake of reward and we practice the keeping of the commandments. Thus, there is one way of the love of the Lord toward the Father, and another way for us toward Him.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the 'as … so' comparison in the verses and where it stops.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: Love sums up the virtues, and Christ's death shows his going away was love, not hatred.
comments.comment:
As teacher of the inhabited world Christ hands these things to them: that love is the sum of the virtues, his commandment is to die for friends and to love friends more than yourselves.

He shows that his departure was not of hatred but of love; for I die for you.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what 'greater love' means and how it applies to Christ's death.
comments.author: Ammonius of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Virtue lifts servants to be Christ's friends, told as much as they needed to hear.
comments.comment:
Through virtue, having surpassed the measure of slaves, they became friends. And he raises slaves up to glory beyond nature if they willingly do what is pleasing to God.

[John 15:15] That is: as much as they needed to hear…
comments.selected_reason: Explains how servants become friends and what 'all things' means.
comments.author: Ammonius of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Christ's 'hearing' from the Father is not a human hearing in time but an eternal knowing, put in human words for us.
comments.comment: In John 15:15, he does not speak of such a hearing as that of men, just as he does not speak of such a love nor of a similar keeping of commandments; for a word brought from the Father to the ears is not intended to inform of the decrees of the Father, but he has spoken of a hearing that is not received by him at a certain time, but is always present. …through common and human words, the divine excellence must be sealed for us to perceive familiarly as God, and not according to human lowliness, since even the Word concerning God has taken on the form of a human shape and our names of passions, interpreting the incorporeal, formless, and impassible God.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: The Son grants prayers too, being equal to the Father.
comments.comment: The Son gives what is asked in place of the Father, so that we may know that the Son was not less than the Father.
comments.author: Ammonius of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Saying the Father gives what is asked in Christ's name shows that Father and Son give as one God, not two.
comments.comment: “You did not choose me, but I chose you, that you should go and bear fruit, and that your fruit should remain, so that whatever you ask the Father in my name he will give you.” (John 15:16) See how everywhere he shows that he works the same things with authority as God the Father. For he had said, “If you ask in my name, I will do it” (John 14:13–14); but now he says, “Whatever you ask the Father in my name he will give you.” (John 16:23–26) So then — does the Father give on his own apart from the Son, and the Son separately give his share apart from the Father? Would the saints’ prayer-requests then come from two gods? Not so — God forbid. For there is one God, the Father, and one Lord Jesus Christ (1 Corinthians 8:6). The Father distributes the good things in the Son, in the Spirit. …
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the asking is 'of the Father in my name'.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On the True Faith, to the Princesses Arcadia and Marina

comments.capsule: We were chosen not because we pleased God but so that we might, and the apostles' lasting fruit is the Church.
comments.comment:
…For we were not chosen because we were pleasing, but so that we might be pleasing. Therefore, he says, having chosen them, he set them for fruit-bearing, so that, even if we were not previously made precious to God, we might become so through the latter things.

What is this incorruptible fruit of the apostles that remains forever? It is the Church. And it is not possible for God to hear the one who does not hear, nor for one to receive blessing who does not bear fruit.
comments.selected_reason: Explains 'Ye have not chosen me' and what the fruit that remains is.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: Prayers offered in Christ's name are granted because through him we have access to God, and facing the world's hatred they must love one another.
comments.comment: …so that if you hear the commandments, he says, and bring forth fruit, and your requests will be fulfilled. And requests are granted to you from God, those being offered through my name; for through me you have access to God by my name and with boldness (John 15:16). As they are about to hate you by all, he commands them to love one another.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: The world's hatred should not grieve the disciples, since it hated Christ and only loves its own.
comments.comment:
This is for us; for you suffer this because of me. Therefore do not ache or take it hard; for you are not better than I.

If the wicked loved you—that is, the world—clearly you too would be wicked.

The one who despises the world’s things, even if he is from the world, is said not to be from the world.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what 'not of the world' means and why the hatred should not distress them.
comments.author: Ammonius of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Servants who suffer like their Master share his sufferings, and insult to him reaches the Father.
comments.comment: If I suffered all things for slaves, when you the slaves suffer the like for the Master, you ought not to take it heavily. If you suffer things like mine, do not be troubled; for so you become sharers of my sufferings. Even if they do this toward my insult, yet through me they also insult the Father.
comments.selected_reason: Explains 'The servant is not greater than his lord' as a comfort.
comments.author: Ammonius of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Sin is worse in those who drew near to God and then threw off the reins, as Christ's coming made his hearers answerable.
comments.comment: …For what sin is like that of the one far from God and of the one who after drawing near has thrown off the reins? For “if I had not come,” (John 15:22) he says, “and spoken to them, they would not have sin.” (John 15:22) For which reason also “among those who draw near to me I will be sanctified” (Leviticus 10:3); because the one who does not know the will of the Lord and does not do it will be beaten with few blows; but the one who knows and does not do it will be beaten with many. [Luke 12:47–48] …
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Christ left nothing undone for them.
comments.comment: I omitted nothing, he says, of what tends to the Jews’ benefit, neither in words nor in works, of which no one saw the like.
comments.author: Ammonius of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Their hatred was groundless, as the prophet foretold.
comments.comment: And through the prophet he showed that the hatred against him was irrational. The Jews’ wickedness fulfilled what was prophesied.
comments.author: Ammonius of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Christ says the Spirit proceeds from the Father, not that he was created, to show the Spirit shares the Father's divinity.
comments.comment: In order that no one might suspect his being a beginning or an end, but might truly believe that it is the Spirit of God, proceeding according to his nature, breathed uncaused and not becoming, as one of the other functional spirits, the Lord teaches in the Gospel according to John, saying: 'the Spirit of truth, which proceeds from the Father' (John 15:26). And he did not say 'is created.' For every birth and procession is accomplished through equal and similar things; but most distinctly is the birth and procession from the one Father through the union of his own divinity.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the verse says 'proceedeth' and what that word implies.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Christ foretells persecution to show he knows all as God and can rescue them, for their killers will think murder is worship.
comments.comment:
So that you may know that as God by nature I know all things, I foretell what will be, and so that you may believe that I can free you from the dangers brought upon you.

[John 16:2] So great will be the madness of those who kill you—not only Jews but also Gentiles and heretics—that they think slaughtering you is a power of God-loving worship.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why Jesus foretold persecution and the killers' warped piety.
comments.author: Ammonius of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Unless Christ suffers, the Spirit does not come.
comments.comment:
Under fear and grief they were beside themselves and silent.

[John 16:7] Unless I suffer, the Spirit who is cause of every good gift does not come upon you.
comments.author: Ammonius of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The Spirit's presence in believers convicts unbelievers of sin, since being without the gift proves them unfit for it.
comments.comment: He will convict the world as having been condemned under sin because of unbelief; for faith has loosed sin, but unbelief has bound it, and appearing among those believing, the Spirit was a condemnation of those unbelieving; for being deprived of the gift, they were convicted of the one present to those having believed, and this showed them to be vessels unfit for the Spirit (John 16:8).
comments.selected_reason: Explains how the Spirit convicts the world 'of sin, because they believe not'.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: After the Spirit came, unbelief stood exposed as sin, the devil was condemned, and the unbelieving were shown unjust.
comments.comment:
So great is the power of the Holy Spirit’s descent that then the sin of those who have offended against me will be made plain. As many as after the Holy Spirit’s descent did not believe in Christ remained in their own sins; the one who did not believe in the sinless one is condemned as a sinner.

[John 16:11] He was condemned as having killed through the Jews the Christ who is sinless, since he was making excuses saying that Adam did not die through me but because he sinned. And since after the passion healings happen through the Holy Spirit, through the deeds the devil’s overthrow is shown.

[John 16:10] Unjust is the one who did not believe in the righteous one taken up into the heavens for his righteousness and become unseen to human beings. …
comments.author: Ammonius of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The Spirit shows the righteousness of faith, kindled by Christ's ascension, and the condemnation of the devil whom he trod down.
comments.comment: He also showed the righteousness in the believers, and this was not for the sake of anyone else, except for the ascent of Christ; for this kindled the men, that the flesh from us and a human appearance might ascend the heavenly throne and sit beside the Father. And this itself had the condemnation of the world, when, having been seized by man and having fallen under his feet, he trod upon the head of him. So it is rightly said that the presence of the Spirit in us has a demonstration of these three: the sin of the world, the righteousness of faith, and the condemnation of the devil.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the 'righteousness' and 'judgment' of which the Spirit convicts the world.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: The Spirit says only what the Son says, not from weakness but because the Trinity is in perfect harmony.
comments.comment:
That is: he speaks in agreement with me; for the Spirit is not lacking; being self-subsistent as consubstantial with Father and Son he knows all things and has power of himself to act.

[John 16:12] When the Spirit teaches you, then you will be able to leave the legal types and make the worship “in spirit and truth” (John 4:23–24). The Spirit is not greater than the Son, he says. Therefore he will speak nothing from himself, but what he hears; for what I say, that one also will say. The Spirit will teach human beings the things of the Son’s Godhead and glory and of equality with the Father. He does not fail to speak from weakness; he said this because of the exact harmony of the Trinity.
comments.selected_reason: Explains 'he shall not speak of himself' and what the disciples could not yet bear.
comments.author: Ammonius of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The Spirit's 'hearing' and 'receiving' from Christ are human words for divine sharing, not a gaining of knowledge he lacked.
comments.comment:
…the energy and teaching of the Spirit will be directed toward me, for even by me the Spirit moves (John 16:14). And that which is saying 'by me' is clear, and that which is 'from the Father'; for the Father's things are mine. Therefore, that which is from me shall be received, according to the same manner again heard, not as some knowledge being added to the Spirit in this present time; for that would be troubling and raise doubts, if the Spirit then receives the learning whenever it is about to bring it to men.

And it is terrible if someone should set it as being entirely taught; for it will no longer be believed, dwelling in men and bringing all wisdom into them, if it is not some natural wisdom, but he himself needs to be taught.

So, instead of saying that the Spirit moves entirely from himself, he said, 'he will receive from mine and will announce to you' (John 16:14). For voices are smaller toward a more known man, but the glory of the Spirit is greater toward that which is more at home with divinity.

And it is said that God hears the words of man, and it is clear that not only at a certain time does knowledge of God approach, but also before our words, he knew our prayers and the whole according to thought from the beginning from the creation; knowing also the movements of his own creatures that are changing, and yet it was said, 'hear, O Lord' and 'the Lord heard.' … the words are human, as I said, while they are understood divinely by the pious; and the unchangeable and unwavering glory of God shall not be shaken in your suspicions because of Him hearing men speaking.

So then, neither in the Spirit is hearing and receiving an addition of some knowledge, nor a change upon the unchangeable essence of the Spirit.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: The Spirit glorifies Christ by making believers wise and by making Christ dwell in them.
comments.comment: Our Lord Jesus Christ promised that when He had gone away He would send us the Comforter (John 16:7), and to this He added, “He will glorify Me” (John 16:14). And we understand, quite rightly, that His Spirit glorifies Christ both by making wise those in whom He comes to dwell and by making Christ dwell in the saints through Himself; for Christ is in us through the Holy Spirit. …
comments.selected_reason: Explains in plain terms how the Spirit 'shall glorify me'.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: All the Trinity's things are common, so the Spirit's are Christ's.
comments.comment: As the Son naturally has the Father’s things through the consubstantial, he said that the Spirit’s own things are also his, as the things of the Trinity are common.
comments.author: Ammonius of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Since the Father's own attributes, such as creating and eternity, belong to the Son, the Son shares the Father's very substance.
comments.comment: Again, let them say whether created things can say, 'All things that the Father has are mine' (John 16:15). The Father has the creating, the fashioning, the eternal, the being almighty, the unchangeable. But created things cannot have the fashioning, for they are created; nor the eternal, for they have a beginning of being; nor the almighty and unchangeable, for they are ruled and of a changeable nature, as the Scriptures say. Therefore, if these things belong to the Son, they are his not from virtue, as we said, but clearly from his substance, as the council said: he is not from another substance, but from the Father's, whose own these things also are. And what belongs to the Father's substance, and is offspring from it—what could it be, or how could anyone name it, except consubstantial? For what one sees in the Father, one sees also in the Son; and in the Son not by participation, but according to substance. …
comments.selected_reason: Explains what 'All things that the Father hath are mine' implies about the Son.
comments.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
comments.work: Synodal Letter to the Bishops of Africa

comments.capsule: Christ said 'ye shall not see me,' not 'I die,' to spare the grieving disciples.
comments.comment:
So as not to grieve the disciples, he also did not say “I die,” but “you do not see me.”

[John 16:17-18] Under grief they did not understand, and that he was departing they knew, but how he would come they did not know; for they were ignorant of the resurrection before the outcome.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why Jesus speaks of 'a little while' and not seeing him, and why the disciples were puzzled.
comments.author: Ammonius of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Christ answered the disciples' unspoken question because he knew their hearts, a sign of his divinity.
comments.comment: Alluding to the ascension into the heavens to the others, to whom the said thing was not yet clear, they hesitate to ask. Therefore they observe for themselves and speak quietly. And it was not necessary to inquire by word, since he knew the seeking in their hearts even before the question (and Christ hears the thoughts in the heart before the words on the lips), and how they would ask them and how to propose the seeking to them; he answers by indicating to them and through this the divinity for the confirmation of faith: 'for you seek,' he says, concerning the word which soon declares my departure, and soon again there shall be the return (John 16:16-20).
comments.selected_reason: Explains why Jesus answers a question the disciples had not asked aloud.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: The world's joy at the passion is brief, and the disciples' sorrow will soon turn to joy.
comments.comment: This shall be so. It is also said that through sorrow it is necessary for joy to appear to you, and injustice shall rejoice for a little while as if it had prevailed, but when I have passed over the passion: but you shall be grieved as if you no longer had the Savior. But change shall follow quickly the matter…
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: Grief over his death will give way to lasting joy, like a mother's after childbirth.
comments.comment:
Since being deeply grieved they did not want to hear about his death, wanting to fix this doctrine in them he said “you will weep”; after the grief there will be joy.

The reward of your grief will be joy, as also for the woman in labor the joy from childbirth after the grief. Since when he died it appeared to them to pass from grief into joy, he used the example of the woman giving birth.

[John 16:22] Since you will be persuaded that as God I rose and die no longer, even if with the flesh I go up into heaven.
comments.author: Ammonius of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The disciples' pangs at the passion will end in a joy no one can take away, the birth of the new man in the resurrection.
comments.comment:
You will be brought to the joy of the resurrection (John 16:22).

His departing will be sorrowful for the disciples, but the resurrection a delight; and each occurs in a short time.

The matter will appear similar to the pangs of women; for just as a woman labors before the birth, but from the pangs the birth and the after-birth end in delight, and the delight destroys the memory of the sorrow, so it will happen to you regarding this new and wonderful birth; for now, as truly a man is born into the world from extraordinary pangs,

so pangs concerning the passion will come to you, but a joy through the resurrection after the passion, a joy that is by no means again being cast away or removed by man or anyone else, when, through the resurrection of the new man, having newly stood forth, you will arrive at boldness toward God; for you will rejoice when you see a child produced, strange to the world,

both incorruptible and undying, …
comments.selected_reason: Explains the woman in labor as a picture of passion and resurrection.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: Christ teaches prayer to the Father in his name, not to himself nor to the Father apart from him.
comments.comment: So when the saints give thanks in their prayers, they confess their thanks to God through Christ Jesus. And as the one who is exact about praying must not pray to the one who prays, but to him whom our Lord Jesus taught us to call Father over our prayers — so no prayer at all is to be offered to the Father apart from him, as he himself shows this plainly, saying: 'Amen, amen, I say to you: whatever you ask my Father, he will give you in my name. Until now you have asked nothing in my name; ask, and you shall receive, that your joy may be full.'
comments.selected_reason: Explains the wording 'ask the Father … in my name' and 'hitherto have ye asked nothing'.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Because Christ is the one Mediator, every prayer reaches the Father through him, which is why prayers close in his name.
comments.comment: …For since He is the Mediator (1 Timothy 2:5), through whom alone the Father can be approached, and in whom is every spiritual gift, surely through Him every prayer will also reach its fulfillment; … The Son Himself has taught us this, saying to the holy apostles, “In that day you will ask Me nothing. Truly, truly, I say to you, if you ask the Father anything, He will give it to you in My name. Until now you have asked nothing in My name; ask, and you will receive, that your joy may be full” (John 16:23–24). Through Him, then, is the Amen to God the Father, for glory through us. For it is our custom to close every prayer in the name of Christ.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: 'Proverbs' means veiled speech, used for disciples still infants, to be made plain after the resurrection and the Spirit's coming.
comments.comment:
[“In that day”] He means the time of the resurrection.

For as in proverbs Christ speaks these things as one going on to say; for it cannot be understood according to the letter. And that one asks and receives who asks what is profitable for bettering souls.

He calls proverb the unclear and veiled word. Because of their infancy he speaks in a shaded way. But when you advance, then I unveil to you the Father’s glory. After the resurrection I will speak clearly to you the things about the Father. When you receive the Spirit, then you will receive clear knowledge about Son and Father.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what 'proverbs' means and when Christ will speak plainly.
comments.author: Ammonius of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Talk of God speaking and hearing is figurative, the only way people can now hear, but the perfected will know him without veils.
comments.comment:
The sayings concerning God are parabolic and through likenesses (John 16:25), in which God is compared to a man speaking and the Son to one listening, and the Spirit likewise as one listening and receiving words.

Father and Son are made similar as those coming to a man and dwelling in men; for speech and hearing and going and dwelling, and as many such things as have bodily similarities.

It is not possible for men to hear otherwise than thus.

And there will be, he says, a time when not through visible likenesses, but through the invisible glory of God, you will hear and know, when, having been perfected in the Spirit, you will be familiarly disposed toward the knowledge of God, and then some divine conversation of the Lord toward you will become clear, and not the teaching concerning the Father being done through some veil.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: Christ came from the Father without leaving him and leaves the world without forsaking it, since as God he fills all things.
comments.comment:
He can as God give, yet as already saying “I ask” he stayed with the word by economy as man.

[John 16:28] From the essence, he says, I came out from the Father, being indivisibly in the Father and having the Father self-subsistently in myself. Neither when he became man, left behind by the Father, is he said to have come into the world, nor when he was taken up with the flesh was he left behind by the world; for he is God filling all things.
comments.selected_reason: Explains in what sense the Son 'came forth' from the Father and 'leaves' the world.
comments.author: Ammonius of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Christ spoke of their belief humanly, stooping to what they wished to hear.
comments.comment: The “now you believe” he says more humanly; for insofar as I am God, I am in God and Father naturally and without interval. He said this by condescension, since the disciples wanted to hear this.
comments.author: Ammonius of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The disciples' faith will soon be shaken and they will flee, but Christ is never alone, for nothing separates him from the Father.
comments.comment:
But even that which is now credible, he says, will immediately be shaken (John 16:32), and you who say you believe will flee a little later, once your faith has been shaken by fear.

And this, he says, is not difficult for me, but for you; for you will be left alone by the teacher and will leave the Savior, but I will not be left alone by the Father; for there is nothing separating me and the Father.
comments.selected_reason: Explains 'yet I am not alone' against the disciples' coming flight.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: Christ conquered as man so that his victory over sin and death passes to us.
comments.comment: Christ appeared better and more powerful than every worldly sin and also gives the faithful to conquer. Or that Christ, having come to be from us insofar as man, appeared better than death and corruption and the grace passes over to us. And so we ought to take courage that we will receive, since as man he conquered and we seem in him to have conquered; for if as God he conquered, it is nothing toward us.
comments.author: Ammonius of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Christ steadies the disciples' souls, for courage comes not from human strength but from his unconquered power.
comments.comment:
In the world you will have tribulation; but take courage, I have conquered the world (John 16:33).
