About to depart, he says, I establish your souls by necessity through the things now spoken, so that they may not be troubled, but to hold fast by faith against circumstances; for many are the things troubling among men, but great is the help for courage from the one who has conquered; for your courage will never be firmly established from your own manliness,

since there is nothing in man hard and unshakable and good, but from my unassailable power, the confidence will be secure for my partakers.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: Christ's victory over the world is that of his own flesh over suffering, death and corruption, undoing sin through the same flesh by which it entered.
comments.comment: That is why he says, “Take courage; I have overcome the world” (John 16:33). He did not put forward a divine struggle, but showed his own flesh victorious over suffering, death and corruption, so that through the very flesh by which sin entered into the world, and through sin death reigned in all men (Romans 5:12–14), through that same flesh, in its likeness, sin might be condemned in the flesh (Romans 8:3); the ruler of sin, the tempter, might be overcome; death might be undone, so that it would not reign; corruption might vanish in the burial of the body; the first fruits of the resurrection might be shown; the beginning of righteousness might be set to work in the world through faith; the kingdom of heaven might be proclaimed to men; and communion between God and men might be entered into.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what Christ's 'overcoming the world' accomplished.
comments.author: Gregory Thaumaturgus

comments.capsule: Because Christ overcame the world, it has power over believers only as far as he allows.
comments.comment: We too, when God allows the tempter and gives him authority to persecute us, are persecuted; but when God does not wish us to suffer this, even in a world that hates us (compare John 15:18) we live in peace, against all expectation, and take courage from Him who said: “Take courage, I have overcome the world” (John 16:33). And truly He has overcome “the world”; therefore the world has power only so far as He who overcame it wills, since He received from the Father the power to overcome “the world.” And we take courage from His victory.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Christ asks the Father to glorify the flesh his enemies insulted, giving his human body the glory he had by nature.
comments.comment: Christ says: He sent me because of the flesh, not so that I would be insulted, but so that I would be glorified. Therefore, since you were disposed toward me without gratitude, through the very flesh that had been sent I kept saying to the Father, “Father, glorify your Son” (John 17:1). Glorify the one these people insult. Glorify also the flesh they reject, so that they may learn that, as Father, you will glorify the man from Mary without distinction, because of his communion with your only-begotten Son. You will give now to the temple assumed by me, my human body, the glory that I myself had from nature with you before the ages.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what 'glorify thy Son' asks for.
comments.author: Amphilochius of Iconium

comments.capsule: The 'hour' is the time Christ chose to suffer, not blind fate, and his prayer teaches us to flee to God in trials.
comments.comment:
He calls hour the fitting time of the passion, at which he judged to suffer—as also he said about the wine—not the hypostasis-less fate. [impersonal fate]

Through the form of prayer he trains us in trials to pray and take refuge in God.

[John 17:2] So that the hearers may not take offense, by economy he says “what you have given me.”
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the 'hour' is and why the Son prays.
comments.author: Ammonius of Alexandria

comments.capsule: 'The only true God' leads believers to the one rule of God and away from the scattering of many gods.
comments.comment: And this was the life that the only Son gave to his own disciples when he said that they might have life in themselves, to know the only true God and Jesus Christ whom he sent (John 17:3). So by saying "the only true God," he led us to the one rule of God, so that we would no longer be enslaved under the elements of the world, so that polytheism would no longer be in us and human thoughts would no longer be scattered toward such fornication, but toward the unity of the only true God. For Scripture says, "The invention of idols is the first fornication" (Wisdom of Solomon 14:12).
comments.selected_reason: Explains why eternal life is knowing 'the only true God'.
comments.author: Epiphanius of Salamis

comments.capsule: Since knowing Christ is joined to knowing the only true God, Christ is true God.
comments.comment: “And this is eternal life, that they know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you sent.” (John 17:3) If knowledge of Jesus Christ is necessarily joined to, and enters together with, knowledge of the only true God, and this procures eternal life, how is it not clear to all that Christ is true God? For the Word became flesh, and remained Word.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On the True Faith, to the Princesses Arcadia and Marina

comments.capsule: Right faith is the true life.
comments.comment: It must be noted that right faith is the true life that grants its own goods to those who believe. …
comments.author: Ammonius of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Christ glorified the Father by completing the incarnation's work.
comments.comment: He is said to glorify the Father having done all things unto incarnation, or that the Father’s power is made known through his Son, if he speaks as man; for through what the saints accomplish, God is glorified.
comments.author: Ammonius of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Christ glorified the Father by finishing the work of abolishing death, making us a new creation.
comments.comment: Having perfected us thus, he was saying to the Father and God in the heavens: “I glorified you on the earth, having perfected the work that you have given me to do.” (John 17:4) For it is truly glory to God and Father to abolish death through his own offspring. So the perfecting is his through sufferings, but for us what has happened is an addition of what was lacking; for the things in Christ are a new creation (2 Corinthians 5:17). …
comments.selected_reason: Explains what 'the work' was and how it glorified the Father.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On the True Faith, to the Empresses Pulcheria and Eudocia

comments.capsule: Christ asks glory as man and on our behalf, for his humiliation becomes our glory.
comments.comment: So whenever Scripture says that the Son received something, or that the Son was glorified, it says this because of his humanity, not because of his divinity. … For the immortal God did not come to save himself, but those who had been put to death; and he did not suffer for himself, but for us. For this reason he took on our lowliness and our poverty, so that he might grant us his riches. His suffering is our freedom from suffering; his death is our immortality; his tears are our joy; his burial is our resurrection; his baptism is our sanctification. … And his dishonor is our glory. That is why he asks for glory on our behalf, saying, "Glorify me, Father, with yourself, with the glory I had before the world existed, with you" (John 17:5). For we are the ones glorified in him.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the eternal Son asks to be glorified.
comments.author: Marcellus of Ancyra
comments.work: On the Incarnation and against the Arians

comments.capsule: Leaving the world in the flesh, Christ asks the Father's unseen care for the disciples, now sons, who till then needed only to see and hear him.
comments.comment:
Why does he say he asks about them, and what is the asking?

Already, he says, they need the spiritual perception of the invisible working in souls, because I no longer walk among them according to the flesh, nor will I discourse with them; for I am already leaving the world, passing into the heavens.

But set over them the invisible oversight, keeping them as sons, since they have become sons, having received from me the name of sonship.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why Christ now prays for the disciples to be kept.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: Christ came in a body to extend heaven's glory to earth, to be glorified in those being sanctified there.
comments.comment: He has sanctified all things both divinely and carnally. Therefore, he is glorified not only in those currently possessed under his kingdom, but also in those who remained from the beginning under the kingdom; for this is the 'let your will be done on earth as in heaven' (Matt 6:10). Such also is that which is said by the angels: 'glory to God in the highest and on earth peace among men of good will' (Luke 2:14). Because of this, the Son of God came through a body, in order to extend the glory that is in heaven onto the earth, and to be glorified not only in the holy ones according to heaven, but also in those being sanctified according to the earth.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: All the Father's is the Son's; as man he speaks of receiving the name.
comments.comment:
Nothing is the Father’s that is not the Son’s and the reverse. Through my equality with you I am glorified by everyone.

[John 17:11] By economy as man he speaks of God’s name having been given him, having it by nature as God and Son.
comments.author: Ammonius of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Judas perished by his own stubbornness, since Christ keeps the good but forces no one, and Scripture names as cause what was only foretold.
comments.comment:
He did not drag them by necessity. Therefore Judas also perished through voluntary obstinacy; not only Judas but many others also perished, not with Christ; for as far as it lay with him, no one perished. He was called son of perdition as awaiting like a birth the day of perdition.

According to idiom Scripture sets as a cause things that happen from the outcome. Judas, having learned what was foretold, ought not to have betrayed Christ. And if someone says how he perished while Christ was keeping them, it must be said that he does not keep the base but lets them free to do what they wish, yet keeps and empowers the good because human choice is not enough to keep a person.
comments.selected_reason: Explains how Judas was lost while Christ kept the disciples, and the sense of 'that the scripture might be fulfilled'.
comments.author: Ammonius of Alexandria

comments.capsule: 'Son of perdition' names a person by the habit that bore his deeds.
comments.comment: …And again, habits — the worse and the better — are called mothers of the things done according to them. So too one is called “son of perdition” (John 17:12), “son of vipers” (Matt 3:7), “of death,” “son of light” (Luke 16:8), and another “son of peace” (Luke 10:6).
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: While present Christ guarded them and none fell but the one who chose destruction; returning to the Father he asks for them.
comments.comment:
While I was indeed present, it sufficed for them to see me and to hear me, and this was sufficient for them to guard the faith.

Therefore they were guarded, and no one of the salvation in me fell away, except the one who having offered himself to destruction alone, concerning whom also the prophetic Spirit is filled that his 'memorial from the earth' should be destroyed.

But now, returning already to you, I ask for your invisible perception for them.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: The disciples are 'of the world' by nature but not by their guileless life, and the 'as' does not make them equal to Christ.
comments.comment:
He says these things so they may not lose heart but rather rejoice that he goes to the Father.

[John 17:14-16] When he says they are “from the world,” he means nature. When he says they are not, he says it because of guilelessness, as he also was. And the “as” here is not of exact indistinguishability. What he says is this: they have become heaven-citizens and have nothing in common with the earth; for the difference of natures is great, that he is God by nature and they are human beings.
comments.author: Ammonius of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Christ is not of the world by nature, the apostles by likeness to him, and for that strangeness the world hates them.
comments.comment: Clearly in this he divides that which is according to nature and that which is according to likeness (John 17:16); for he says that he himself is not from the world, and likewise the disciples are not from the world. It is evident, however, that Christ indeed was not from the world according to truth, until he had descended from heaven, but the apostles, according to the likeness, have descended from the world after having become like Christ. He says, moreover, that they have become men who are strangers, because of the virtue which is above man, and that they are appropriately hated by those thinking the opposite. They indeed now have with me, through the intimacy toward me, the estrangement toward the world, and no longer are bound to it. But they are anxious for the confirmation in this good thing, lest they be harmed by the evil malice of the devil and be estranged again from this divine intimacy.
comments.selected_reason: Explains how both Christ and the disciples are 'not of the world', yet differently.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: Christ prays that their holiness be real, not ending in the flesh.
comments.comment: Let the good be in them truly and the sanctification be real (John 17:17), lest, 'beginning in spirit, in flesh,' they should ever be accomplished, or even live according to carnal irrationality, but according to the virtue of this word, in which is again true virtue.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: Sent like Christ, the disciples need the Spirit's sanctification.
comments.comment: Since the disciples were going to do something like what Christ did, he says they need sanctification through the Spirit, so that they may be able to run through the inhabited world unhindered by the evil one.
comments.author: Ammonius of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The 'as' does not make the disciples' mission equal to his: he came from heaven as teacher by nature, they teach by gift and imitation.
comments.comment: Much there is in this of inequality (John 17:18); for he says that he sends the disciples just as he himself is sent from the Father. There is no equality between the presence from heaven into the earth and the mission of the disciples occurring in the earth; for they are not sent as teachers by nature just as the Lord is, but having received the teaching power and wisdom, and thus through imitation, the good enters into the world, and that which was sent from heaven from the Father passes through all via the disciples sent by him.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the limits of 'As thou hast sent me … so have I also sent them'.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: Sacrifices are called holy as offered to God, so Christ 'sanctifies' himself and his disciples as an offering.
comments.comment: All sacrifices are called holy as brought to God. And he said “in truth” because sanctification through the sheep was in type—or that I also dedicate them to you as an offering—or that when the head was sacrificed this happened—or that they also presented “their bodies” as a “living sacrifice” (Romans 12:1)—or also that without death he made them a sacrifice by being slaughtered for them.
comments.author: Ammonius of Alexandria

comments.capsule: 'I sanctify myself' means Christ dedicates himself as a spotless offering to the Father for the Church.
comments.comment: …so Christ, as it were, did not refuse to suffer for the holy tent, that is, the Church, and was dedicated for her as a fragrant aroma to God the Father (Ephesians 5:2). That is why he said, ‘For their sake I sanctify myself’ (John 17:19). By ‘I sanctify’ he means ‘I bring and dedicate an unblemished offering to God the Father.’ For whatever is dedicated to God is said to be sanctified, as in the saying somewhere in Scripture: ‘It is a snare to a man to sanctify hastily something of his own, for after he has made the vow he comes to regret it’ (Proverbs 20:25).
comments.selected_reason: Explains the meaning of 'sanctify' in 'I sanctify myself'.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 10

comments.capsule: Christ is sanctified as man and sanctifies as God by his own Spirit.
comments.comment: “And for them I sanctify myself, so that they also may be sanctified in truth.” (John 17:19) Christ sanctifies himself. Is it as a human, or rather because he is God by nature, having as his own the Holy Spirit, which is also true? Since no human sanctifies himself, Christ sanctifies himself; so there is one Son and Lord, being sanctified humanly, yet sanctifying divinely by his own Spirit his own temple.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On the True Faith, to the Princesses Arcadia and Marina

comments.capsule: Christ prays for all believers to be reshaped into God's image, a union by agreement of faith, not of essence.
comments.comment:
Not only for the disciples but also for all the faithful Christ asks that the grace given through the Holy Spirit be given—the grace that reshapes the human being into the divine image. And this union does not happen according to essence or according to hypostasis, but according to the agreement of faith, by which the faithful knew that the Son was incarnate by the Father’s good pleasure; for this is being sent. …

When they are counted worthy of the unity spoken of, then they know that you sent me.
comments.author: Ammonius of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The Word is one with the Father by nature and became man to be one with us, so that we too are perfected into one.
comments.comment: “That the world may believe that you sent me; and the glory that you have given me I have given them, that they may be one as we are one; I in them and you in me, that they may be perfected into one.” (John 17:21–23) Setting the eye of understanding carefully on the force of what is before us, let us consider what is in it. What glory does the Son say he has received from the Father and given to us? He himself will free us from searching this out when he says “that they may be one as we are one.” For in natural identity the Word from God is one with his own Father, even if each is understood in his own hypostasis. And how has he also come to be in us? In the same way — I mean essentially and naturally? Yet God’s nature would be wholly incompatible with creation, I mean in identity according to essence. How then has the One above creation come to be in us naturally? He became human, so that just as he is one with the Father in the nature of the deity, so he may also become one with us in the relation according to humanity; for in this way we too are perfected into one.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what 'that they may be one, even as we are one' means and how it can be true.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On the True Faith, to the Princesses Arcadia and Marina

comments.capsule: The glory given is the Spirit's grace, which Christ, its giver, asks for as man.
comments.comment: He calls glory that of signs and doctrines and like-mindedness. Being himself the giver, because of the hearers he shapes the request. And as man he is said to receive what belongs to him by nature; and he means the Spirit’s grace.
comments.author: Ammonius of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Christ's 'as I and you are one' is to be read like the one heart of the believers, so Christians worship one God.
comments.comment: To this too we must reply that, if Celsus had understood the words “I and the Father are one” (John 10:30), and those spoken in prayer by the Son of God, “as I and You are one” (John 17:22), he would not have supposed that we worship any other besides the God who is over all. For “the Father”, He says, “is in me, and I in the Father” (John 10:38). But if anyone is troubled by these words, fearing that we may somehow be going over to those who deny that the Father and the Son are two distinct realities, let him attend to the words “the heart and soul of all who believed were one” (Acts 4:32), so that he may understand “I and the Father are one” (John 10:30). So, as we have explained, we worship one God, the Father and the Son.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The verse shows Father and Son as distinct persons and Christ's glory before creation, which the faithful are to behold.
comments.comment: Through what he says—the one who gave and the one who received—he shows the hypostases of Father and Son. And again by saying he himself was before the world he refutes the heretics who say that from Mary’s times Christ had his beginning, as having the glory before the world. He said before the foundation of the world; for “you have given me” is of condescension. And he did not say that they may share his glory, but that they may behold it, which is the faithful’s greatest rest and glory.
comments.selected_reason: Explains 'before the foundation of the world' and why the faithful 'behold' his glory.
comments.author: Ammonius of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Christ asks that disciples who share his sufferings share his rest, and even now they are with him by living spiritually.
comments.comment: …If indeed someone should wish to be my disciple, let him come eagerly through the equal sufferings with me, and as it were go and love the same path; for this one will rest together and live together. And this he himself was seeking for us from beside the God and Father, saying: ‘I wish that where I am, there they also may be with me.’ (John 17:24) And otherwise we are with Christ, walking upon earth, yet no longer fleshly, but living as citizens spiritually, and being eager to make lodging and rest what seems good to him. …
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 5

comments.capsule: John's account leans toward showing Christ's divinity, since his humanity was already well known.
comments.comment: One must pay attention to John presenting the history concerning the distress and grief of the Lord (John 18:1), which the others do not omit. But, as I have said, his writing leans more toward the manifestation of divinity, since the humanity was sufficiently foreknown; he speaks of human things more from an attack, but the proofs of divinity are clearer because of the folly.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: Christ went where Judas knew, to show he suffered willingly.
comments.comment: To persuade the disciples that he came willingly to the passion, he went away to a place known to Judas, so that he might not escape notice and did not shut himself in as in a prison.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why John notes that Judas knew the place.
comments.author: Ammonius of Alexandria

comments.capsule: His captors could not have taken him unless he gave himself up, as their falling back at 'I am' showed.
comments.comment: …If he himself does not give himself, they were not able to do this. For they came greedily to seize him, he says: 'Whom are you seeking?' (John 18:4) and he says: 'Jesus the Nazarene' (John 18:5). 'I am,' as he said, 'they went backward and fell to the ground' (John 18:6). And again a second time: 'Whom are you seeking?' and he said the same to them, and they fell to the ground again. …
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the soldiers fell to the ground.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Christ was recognized only when he willed.
comments.comment: He asks not as not knowing, but so that we may know that even when present he was not seen or recognized except when he wished. …
comments.author: Ammonius of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Christ shields the weak disciples; only Judas is lost.
comments.comment: Because of the disciples’ weaknesses he puts them outside trials as God; he always keeps the disciples, only letting Judas perish by preferential wickedness.
comments.author: Ammonius of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The cut ear signals Israel's deafness, and its healing a later restoring of Israel's understanding.
comments.comment: …The cutting off of a servant-priest's ear was thus a sign of the darkness of deafness cast upon them; and regarding the restoration of the ear, one might say it signifies the later restoration of the understanding of Israel which is now spoken of, when they will understand the one they ignored and may perhaps hear the one preaching, Elijah; for then the hearts of the fathers will be restored to the sons according to Micah (Malachi 4:6).
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: Peter struck in defense of his teacher, not himself, and the cut ear signals that the Jews will lose all right hearing.
comments.comment: [Peter,] …as he wished to die for the teacher, he did this. Peter, taking courage from what Jesus did, himself also did this. And let no one accuse Peter as a murderer, since he did this not defending himself but the teacher; yet they were still incomplete. Through the type he shows that the Jews will be empty of every right hearing.
comments.selected_reason: Explains Peter's motive in drawing the sword and the meaning of the severed ear.
comments.author: Ammonius of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The Lord let the sword be drawn to fulfil his word, then stopped it and healed the ear, harming no one.
comments.comment: It also seems there was a forgiveness from the Lord regarding their use of the sword then. For Luke recorded this as the Savior manifesting the impending war by saying, 'let someone sell his garment and buy a sword' (Luke 22:36), while the disciples said, 'look, two swords are here' (Luke 22:38), to which he replied, 'it is enough' (Luke 22:38). This was not a mindless thing being forgiven by the Lord, who commanded not to resist 'the evil one,' but also for the sake of what was said, so that he might show by deed what he had foretold by word, and since they were using the righteous sword, he stood and prevented them, so that they would no longer use it; as he himself, having said these things, recorded that after saying this, the Lord said, 'let it be until this,' and this 'until' has a limit and a prohibition of the use of the sword according to the law. And Luke adds to the history, 'and having touched the ear, he healed him' (Luke 22:51), which was the most manifest work toward harming no human being. …
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: Christ was bound to free us from the devil's bonds.
comments.comment: Binding him they fulfilled Isaiah’s word: “Let us bind the righteous” (Isaiah 3:10 LXX sense). The Lord was bound so that he might free us from devilish bonds.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the binding of Jesus matters.
comments.author: Ammonius of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The 'other disciple' is John.
comments.comment: John went in with Jesus among the crowd unrecognized, and then as known he spoke to the doorkeeper and brought Peter in.
comments.selected_reason: Identifies the 'other disciple' and explains how Peter got in.
comments.author: Ammonius of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The high priest probed whether Christ opposed Moses, but Christ exposed his feigned ignorance of teaching given openly.
comments.comment:
He asked what he taught his own disciples, asked him whether he agrees with what is through Moses or introduces another teaching and what his disciples are persuaded of, so that if he finds him opposing Moses’ things he may hand them also over to the Jews as God-fighters.

[John 18:20-21] He exposes him pretending not to know things spoken in the open. And if he taught all things openly, the secret things said about him by some are not acceptable. Ask the servants who earlier marveled at the teaching and now are arresting me.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the high priest's question and Jesus' reply about teaching openly.
comments.author: Ammonius of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The servant struck Christ unbidden to clear himself of having admired him, and Christ rebukes the insult without cause.
comments.comment: And without being ordered the servant struck Christ, since Christ himself hinted saying “see, these know”—those who once heard and praised—and wanting to free himself from the suspicion that he was among those not marveling, he himself did this; for he would not have spoken something fitting so as to be moved from this to strike him. He exposes the servant wronging him not only because he simply struck him, but because having earlier marveled he now without finding fault dishonored him.
comments.author: Ammonius of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Satan defeated Peter's promise.
comments.comment: When the evil one shook Peter he was defeated of his promise.
comments.author: Ammonius of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The leaders kept out of the hall to honor the Passover type, though the law no longer had force among them.
comments.comment:
They did not kill him themselves as being under Romans, so that they might not be punished by Pilate.

Honoring the type they did not enter—that is, a sheep; for they were going to sacrifice the Passover according to the law that had no force among them. Or he calls Passover the whole feast, or that it was preparation day, when also the old Passover happened.
comments.author: Ammonius of Alexandria

comments.capsule: John dates the passion so that Christ the true Lamb died on the day and hour the Passover lamb was slain, and the other Gospels agree.
comments.comment:
It seems John clearly intends to demonstrate what has been clearly revealed by the other evangelists regarding the day of the passion; for he has related that the supper was before the Passover feast, from which time after rising he was handed over, lest the Passover be eaten, at the very moment when the time of the slaughter of the lamb and the death of Christ was being drawn together. For the time was evening, in which 'the Spirit delivered over' (John 19:30) the true Lamb at the ninth hour of the day, and the slaughter of the lamb is also in the evening according to the law, so that by the same day and hour the event was prefigured to be fulfilled.

And the Jews were not able to escape, not that they would fulfill the event during the feast, even though they were keeping watch and saying, 'Not during the feast, lest there be a disturbance' among the people. Therefore, it is possible to understand also regarding the other evangelists that they call the first of the Unleavened Bread the one before the Unleavened Bread, that is, the thirteenth, and that a Passover was prepared for them by the disciples in this way, but the supper was not the eating of the Passover; for in this they coincide with John, and most especially the voice of Matthew coincides, whom he remembered after the Lord said: 'Know that in two days the Passover takes place, and the Son of Man is handed over to be crucified' (Matthew 26:2), as regarding this day both the Passover would be offered and he would be crucified.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why John notes they had not yet eaten the Passover.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: The leaders had no charge, and their refusal to judge him themselves fulfilled Christ's word that he would die at Gentile hands.
comments.comment:
Without cause they declared that he had justly been handed over; they call a reasonable cause their arresting him, as if they err in doing nothing unjust. If your law also punishes the guiltless, judge him yourselves.

[John 18:32] Clear proof that the Lord suffered willingly: from what, knowing, he foretold that he was going to be handed over to the nations to be crucified.

[John 18:31] As having fallen from rule—for they were under Romans—they said this. Or it is not permitted to crucify him; for so they wished, that they might also parade the manner of his end. Or that he calls himself king and the charge is public and it belongs to you to put him to death.
comments.selected_reason: Explains 'It is not lawful for us to put any man to death' and how it fulfilled Jesus' word.
comments.author: Ammonius of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Christ calmed Pilate by showing he was no rebel but king of heaven and earth, while the angels kept silent.
comments.comment:
He says these things wanting to free him.

[John 18:36] The angels were quiet while their king was insulted, understanding the economy of Christ’s presence.

He looses Pilate’s anxiety persuading that he is not a rebel but king of heaven and earth. Therefore Pilate is without defense, not as killing him as a blasphemer but as a favor to the Jews.
comments.author: Ammonius of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Jesus denied being a king in the common sense but taught a kingdom given by God for the good of its subjects.
comments.comment: …He was to be a king, not as Herod supposed, but as it befitted God to give a kingdom, for the good of those who are ruled, to one who would do his subjects no middling or indifferent good, if I may so call it, but would train them and bring them under laws that are truly God's. Jesus knew this; and while he denied that he was a king in the sense in which most people understand it, he taught what sets his own kingdom apart when he said: “If my kingdom were of this world, my servants would be fighting, so that I would not be handed over to the Jews; but as it is, my kingdom is not of this world” (John 18:36).
comments.selected_reason: Explains what 'My kingdom is not of this world' means.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Christ was born to banish falsehood and show God's reign.
comments.comment: For this I became man and was born from Mary, that driving falsehood and the devil from the world I may show the divine nature reigning over all.
comments.selected_reason: Explains 'To this end was I born … that I should bear witness unto the truth'.
comments.author: Ammonius of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Christ proves the truth, but his hearers stand at the threshold.
comments.comment: He says he himself will prove the Truth to men and through his own knowledge grant salvation to them, but they stand only at the threshold of the matter…
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: God's Son made himself man.
comments.comment: He did not make himself Son of God, but as Son of God he made himself man, remaining unchangeably as…
comments.author: Ammonius of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Pilate feared superstitiously.
comments.comment: …Therefore also as a light idolater Pilate, seized without discernment, was afraid.
comments.author: Ammonius of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Pilate had power only because Christ chose to suffer.
comments.comment: Even if you are a ruler, yet finding no fault against me you could not condemn me, unless I willingly by the Father’s good pleasure led myself to suffer.
comments.selected_reason: Explains 'Thou couldest have no power at all against me, except it were given thee from above'.
comments.author: Ammonius of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The Father allowed the Son, who chose it, to suffer, and this is the sense of power 'given from above'.
comments.comment: …Yet this did not happen entirely and wholly by the Father’s will; he wanted him not to suffer, if the Jews had accepted him. But since they did not receive him, the Father consented to the Son who chose to suffer this. That is why it is also said that the Father struck “the shepherd,” since he allowed him to suffer though able to prevent his suffering. The word said to Pilate by Christ is also to be understood thus: “You would have no authority at all against me unless it had been given you from above” (John 19:11) — instead of “the Father did not consent to me who chose to suffer.”
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The betrayer's sin is greater because he added pain to the innocent one who was to suffer, setting himself against God.
comments.comment: He says that the sin of the betrayer is greater (John 19:11) because, according to the prophet, 'those whom you struck down, they themselves persecuted' and as it is elsewhere foretold concerning the betrayer, 'instead of which he did not remember to do mercy, but persecuted a man, poor and wretched, and whose heart was set on killing.' For it is a terrible thing to impose a burden of pain and tribulation in time upon one who does no wrong, instead of the righteous and good; for he to whom it was necessary to suffer, to him, having added pains, stands against God.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: John's 'sixth hour' differs from the third hour in Mark through a copyist who mistook the Greek sign for three for that for six.
comments.comment:
For in that very feast they killed him.

The evangelist marked the hour because of the resurrection that happened on the third day. The fine scribe, instead of the gamma letter which signifies the third, wrote the marked sign which the Alexandrians call Gabex, which shows the sixth, having much likeness to each other. And through the scribal error the disagreement happened; for instead of third hour he wrote sixth.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the 'sixth hour' and why it seems to clash with the other Gospels.
comments.author: Ammonius of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Led away as if beaten, Christ conquers, bearing on his shoulder the rule and the chastisement Isaiah foretold.
comments.comment: They lead him away as if they had conquered, but the Lord, being led, conquers, carrying upon his shoulder the beginning or the instruction, as one might interpret the prophecy of Isaiah saying, 'whose beginning was upon his shoulder' (Isaiah 9:6). It is instruction, because he bore the instruction on our behalf, according to: 'the instruction of our peace is upon him' (Isaiah 53:5); and it is the beginning, because he reigns over the captives under death and under sin, enduring on the wood the death on the wood instead of them (John 19:16). …
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: Crucified between robbers, Christ fulfilled Isaiah, and the two robbers picture two peoples or our own dying to the old life.
comments.comment: Through being crucified in the midst of two robbers the Scripture was fulfilled that says “and he was numbered with the lawless” (Isaiah 53:12). These are a type of the two peoples who are condemned through their sins—or that those who cling to Christ ought to crucify themselves as dying to the former way of life, yet living in newness according to the gospel.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the meaning of Jesus being crucified between two others.
comments.author: Ammonius of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Pilate's title mocked the Jews by proclaiming Christ their king, and it was the 'handwriting' against Adam that Christ nailed to the cross.
comments.comment: Not finding what to say against him Pilate wrote this, so that he too might not be thought a robber. He publicly proclaimed him king and that the Jews killed their king, writing to mock the Jews. This is “the handwriting” [Colossians 2:14] which the sentence against Adam nailed to the cross, which the devil holding led all human beings into death as none wholly doing what seems good to God—and dying for us on the wood he freed us.
comments.author: Ammonius of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The seamless tunic that was not torn is a sign of the unity of the Church, which no one can divide and still possess Christ.
comments.comment: This sacred sign of unity, this bond of harmony holding inseparably together, is shown in the Gospel when the tunic of the Lord Jesus Christ is not divided or torn at all. Instead, as they cast lots for Christ's clothing to see who would rather put on Christ, the garment is received whole, and the tunic is possessed undamaged and undivided. Divine Scripture speaks and says: "Now the tunic was seamless, woven in one piece from the top, so they said to one another, 'Let us not tear it, but cast lots for it to see whose it will be'" (John 19:23-24). He bore the unity that comes from above—that is, from heaven and from the Father—which could not be torn at all by the one who received and possessed it, but held its whole and solid firmness once for all, inseparably. Whoever tears and divides the Church of Christ cannot possess Christ's garment. … But because the people of Christ cannot be divided, his tunic, woven throughout and holding together, was not divided by those who possessed it. Undivided, joined, connected, it shows the cohering harmony of our people who have put on Christ. By the sacred sign of the garment and its meaning, he declared the unity of the Church.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why John records that the tunic was seamless and not torn.
comments.author: Cyprian of Carthage
comments.work: On the Unity of the Catholic Church

comments.capsule: Heretics who tear the Church act like the soldiers, but Christ's true garment stays whole and untorn.
comments.comment: Many still dare to do the same as the soldiers, those scattering the church of Christ and seeking each one his own profit, doing whatever he might take (John 19:23). This was the work of the heresies of the impious. The antichrist will desire to tear apart the whole church just like the tunic; for indeed a people is depicted as being around the stumbling block of God, which is made manifest in those regarding Jeremiah where it was said, 'just as the girdle clings to the waist of a man, so I joined the house of Israel and all the house of Judah' (Jeremiah 13:11); but the true girdle of Christ remains, being neither torn apart nor alienated (John 19:23).
comments.selected_reason: Explains the soldiers' treatment of the tunic as a picture of the Church.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: Christ bowed his head before expiring, against the usual order, because he died willingly as Lord of all.
comments.comment:
The Jews’ impiety reached its end, and he willingly endured the death according to the flesh and bowed the head because the flesh’s tones were dissolving.

He bowed the head; for it was not nailed, and then he expired; for he was Lord of all, though custom has first expiring and then bowing the head. … The end shows the separation of the soul from the body.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why John says he bowed his head and then gave up the ghost.
comments.author: Ammonius of Alexandria

comments.capsule: 'It is finished' declares the purpose of his coming: prophecy, human virtue and God's providence all reach completion in salvation through Christ.
comments.comment: He who accepted all unmercilessness on our behalf and, drinking vinegar, says 'it is finished' (John 19:30), was demonstrating the intention of the visitation and the purpose of all things occurring therein; for on account of completion, all these things occur, for I speak not only of the completion of the prophetic words, but also of all virtue practiced among men remaining incomplete without Christ, and of all the providence which comes from God concerning men, enjoying its completion in the salvation through Christ (John 19:30). …
comments.selected_reason: Explains what 'It is finished' means.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: Feigning piety, they fulfilled the Scripture that no bone would be broken.
comments.comment: They pretend to honor the day and ask a favor so that the men may die more quickly. They ask so that another Scripture may again be fulfilled that says a bone of him will not be crushed.
comments.author: Ammonius of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Christ laid down his life before the soldiers came, so that his legs were not broken.
comments.comment: John records Jesus as having said something of this kind in the words: “No one takes my soul from me, but I lay it down of myself. I have authority to lay it down, and I have authority to take it again” (John 10:18). And perhaps this is why he went out of the body beforehand: to preserve it, and so that his legs would not be broken like those of the robbers crucified with him. “For the soldiers broke the legs of the first, and of the other who was crucified with him; but when they came to Jesus and saw that he had breathed his last, they did not break his legs” (John 19:32–33).
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The blood means redemption; the water, sanctification and rebirth.
comments.comment:
One of the soldiers, disbelieving whether he had died, pierced his side.

The blood shows redemption and the water sanctification. Through water the church is born again and through blood and flesh she is fed.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the meaning of the blood and water.
comments.author: Ammonius of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Eve's side brought ruin, but from Christ's side flowed water and blood that cleanse the world, as the law's sprinklings and washings foreshadowed.
comments.comment: A side had to be struck, and this is excused for the soldiers; for the Lord provided one side instead of another. The woman's side and that which is evil from her releases the Lord from suffering; for from her side there proceeded a disastrous counsel for man. But from the holy side water and blood flow, through which the world is cleansed, having its sins removed by the joining of those who were divided according to the law; for there were blood sprinkleings for cleansing and water baptisms for purification. Since all things pertaining to Him were pre-arranged for Christ, the Lord's body provided both to the world: sacred blood and holy water, and already existing as dead according to the human manner; for it holds within itself a great power of life.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: The blood and water gushed out to sprinkle and so baptize the believing thief.
comments.comment: The Savior finds a way even in a desperate way. Since the one aged by sins had believed in the Savior, and he needed to be cleansed, Christ manages, after the passion, that the soldier pierce the side of the Lord with a spear, and blood and water gush out; for from his side, the Evangelist says, 'Blood and water came out' (John 19:34), in the truth of the one fallen, as a type of the mysteries. And the blood and water did not come out simply flowing, but in a torrent, so that it might sprinkle the body of the thief; for that which is sent in a torrent sprinkles, but that which flows simply flows calmly, as it comes. But in a torrent blood and water came out from the side, so that, having sprinkled the thief, it might baptize him, as the Apostle says: 'We have come to Zion with the blood of sprinkling, speaking better than Abel' (Hebrews 12:24).
comments.author: Severianus of Gabala

comments.capsule: The events match the Scriptures, and the unbroken bone stands for the firm mystery of Christ that true believers keep whole.
comments.comment: The evangelist confirms that he himself is the Christ proclaimed beforehand through the Scriptures; for the deeds came out in agreement with what was said about him. Bone is understood as the taut and unbreakable of the mystical word. And since the sheep bore the image of the Lamb of God, one is fed the head of Christ by taking the things about his theology, the feet by being taught the things about his incarnate economy, and the inwards the hidden doctrines; for each of the doctrines about Christ has a hidden and mystical word. Since therefore bone is understood as the taut of the mystery, those who fittingly and harmoniously hold the mystery about Christ—a bone of him will not be crushed. When he comes to judge, then they will see him and mourn.
comments.author: Ammonius of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The unbroken bones show that his death was not like ours and that his suffering did not master the strength of his body.
comments.comment: The bones of the lamb are not broken (John 19:36), showing by the type that the suffering does not belong to the power of the body; for the power of the body is such that our bones were being said to be broken by men near Hades. But that He did not die in the same way for all men, He showed the change in this, in that the harmony of His bones was not scattered.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: Joseph, one of the seventy, came openly once the Jews' rage had cooled.
comments.comment: Those who feared to approach Jesus openly now, with Jews watching, ask for the body. This one was not of the Twelve but of the seventy, and as the Jews’ rage was quenched he approached without fear. …
comments.author: Ammonius of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Christ's body was truly dead, since it could be wrapped, anointed and buried, which a spiritual body cannot suffer.
comments.comment: …Christ the firstfruits: for this reason his body became a dead body. For if his body had not become dead — able to be wrapped in linen, to receive myrrh and whatever else belongs to the dead, and to be laid in a tomb — a spiritual body cannot suffer these things. …
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Christ, a new kind of corpse, was laid in a new tomb, so that his burial was as pure as his virgin birth.
comments.comment: For he was not like the rest of the dead: even in death he showed signs of life, the water and the blood (John 19:34), and was, if I may call him so, a new kind of corpse. It was right, then, that he should be placed in a new and clean tomb, so that, just as his birth was purer than every birth, because he was born not from intercourse but from a virgin, so his burial too might have purity. This purity is shown through the symbol of his body being laid in a new tomb, one not built of gathered stones with no natural unity, but standing in a single rock, united throughout, quarried and hewn.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the tomb was new, one where no one had been laid.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Joseph, a stranger, buried him in a new tomb nearby so that no one could say another body rose or that it was stolen.
comments.comment: …And if he had been with others, some of the unbelievers were going to say that it was not Jesus’ body that rose but another’s. He was laid in a new tomb because of the strangeness of the run back from death into life and the novelty devised against corruption. It was arranged that the place be near, so that the story about theft might also be shown false.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why John notes the tomb was new and near.
comments.author: Ammonius of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The evangelists' times for the resurrection meet at midnight, and Christ rose while the stone and seals were still in place.
comments.comment:
Though Matthew said the resurrection happened in deep evening, and John early while it was still dark, they do not disagree about the time of the resurrection, but ran together into the same time of hours; for one moves from the end and the other from the beginning into the very middle of the night.

Christ rose while the stone still lay and the seals. And the tomb is opened toward faith in the signs that happened. Unclear is the time of the resurrection as also that of the second coming.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the timing 'when it was yet dark' and why the stone was taken away.
comments.author: Ammonius of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Small differences over hours, amid full agreement on what matters, show the evangelists were not colluding to lie.
comments.comment:
What those trying to show them disagreeing want, I do not find; for if about the resurrection they had not brought out the same judgment, or had not said the same day on which the resurrection happened to occur, or had not all alike reported the women first come for honor of the dead, they would have some pardon for this absurd and foolish censure; but if in the things aforesaid they showed much agreement—alike announcing the resurrection, saying the day is the same, the women alike come—what ever does their exactness about the hours want? I at least do not understand, and yet I think nothing else so tends to establish the truth of what was said as that those who showed much agreement in the most crucial things are found disagreeing in some very small things and in what it was likely that being human they would err, showing the exchange of words by brief hours; for if wanting to lie they had chosen an agreeing judgment about this, nothing would have hindered. Having once chosen to lie about this, keeping much and exact agreement in all, it lay before them to lie and each by himself would fulfill his own aim. Necessity surely was that they vary a little, many things being what forced them to suffer these things.

And if Luke says that the disciples disbelieved those about Joanna, nothing contrary; for they had not yet gone away to the tomb and did not believe as it happened, as going to bear witness as eyewitnesses to the resurrection. Or they disbelieved those about Joanna as having heard from the two men, but were persuaded by Mary saying that they took the body.
comments.author: Ammonius of Alexandria

comments.capsule: No one saw the resurrection itself, a hidden mystery, and Mary first reported only that the body was gone.
comments.comment:
After the Sabbath evening (John 20:1), the Lord raised the one previously foretold by Him, bypassing the three days, as it was said that the first day had suffered, but immediately the third was beginning to rise. And the three days seem to endure instead of all the time of the then-past and the then-future, delivering Himself to death instead of all those who were finishing.

Thus, rising to reach those arriving at the tomb, and no one stood by for the resurrection to be happening; for it was a mystery, if indeed something else of those administered by God, which is not manifest to men and does not lie before the eyes. A woman first stands at the tomb and at first announces to the disciples that the Lord is not in the tomb, not implying the resurrection, but thinking that He had been carried away from the tomb by the adversaries and as if calling them to a search.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: Peter went to the tomb twice, which fits Luke's account.
comments.comment: This is not contrary to Luke also that Peter alone went away to the tomb; for when after seeing the linen cloths he went away, later those about Joanna came saying that the Lord rose, and Peter alone ran again to the tomb hoping perhaps himself also to see some vision.
comments.author: Ammonius of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The grave cloths left folded apart proved neither friends nor foes had taken the body, and the disciples believed.
comments.comment: This was a mark of the resurrection; for if enemies stole it, they would not have left the garments for profit, and if they were friends they would not have endured to insult the body naked; for if the disciples had seized it, they fled because of the guarding soldiers and Jews and would not have stood stripping the body and setting the cloths apart and the napkin apart. And it shows that a body that has passed into incorruption has no further need of garments. They did not see him risen, but from the gathering of the garments they conceive the resurrection and believe this, holy Scripture crying it. When the angel appeared, the guards fled terrified and therefore those around Peter came to the tomb without fear.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the linen clothes and napkin led the disciple to believe.
comments.author: Ammonius of Alexandria

comments.capsule: They grasped the resurrection only after the event.
comments.comment: They understood and believed the word of the resurrection which earlier they did not know. Before the experience the disciples did not know the word about resurrection.
comments.author: Ammonius of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Mary stayed weeping at the tomb, thinking the body moved, and her love earned her the sight of angels who prompted her to ask.
comments.comment:
The disciples also fled to themselves by God’s economy, so that they might not suffer something before the proclamation, but Mary, conceiving nothing perfect, remained weeping at the tomb not only because he had died but also because she thought the Lord’s body had been moved.

[John 20:11-13] So that she might weep more, she stooped into the tomb, to whom the angels speaking guidingly say “why do you weep,” urging her to ask something and learn about the resurrection, for which also they appeared clothed in white.

Remaining through affection she was counted worthy also of the angels’ vision.
comments.author: Ammonius of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The Gospels' one angel and two angels do not conflict: one rolled away the stone, the two stood by or sat in the tomb.
comments.comment: …Matthew and Mark reported one (Matthew 28:2–5; Mark 16:5), and Luke and John two (Luke 24:4; John 20:12). These accounts were not contradictory. For those who recorded one say that this was the one who rolled away “the stone” from the tomb (Matthew 28:2); while the others say that the two are those who, “in dazzling clothing” (Luke 24:4), stood by the women who had come to the tomb, or those who were seen inside “sitting in white” (John 20:12).
comments.selected_reason: Explains why John has two angels where Matthew and Mark have one.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Christ came to Mary in humble form so as not to frighten her, and then named her so she would know he was risen.
comments.comment:
To those he appeared more wondrous, but to the woman in a humble form, so as not to frighten her. Therefore she also thought him to be a gardener. She sees the Lord and did not recognize him either because of the darkness or because by God's fitting power he concealed himself. By economy she turned and saw the Lord yet did not recognize, so that she might not be troubled as seeing a demonic fantasy; for she still suspected that he was dead.

Swallowed by grief she still doubted about the resurrection.

[John 20:16] With a certain manner the Lord names her, so that even so she may come to perception that he both rose and was present.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why Mary took Jesus for the gardener and knew him when he spoke her name.
comments.author: Ammonius of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Good news came through a woman so that the evil a woman brought might be undone, and Christ eased the disciples into faith in his rising.
comments.comment:
After these things, seeing the Lord, she announces the blessed sight to the disciples (John 20:18). For it was necessary that the good thing be known and announced through a woman, so that the evil caused by a woman might be undone by the good knowledge which the woman brought. Not being overwhelmed by the brightness of the angels, but being surprised at the sight, she turned back and saw Jesus standing, this being the result of Him having been seen by her.

The Savior wants to show the resurrection and persuade (John 20:17), but he approaches those who have not yet heard of the resurrection in a similar way to how he approached those before the resurrection, not knowing how to fit them, unless he leads them into the same living way, so that having a familiar relationship with him, they might approach him familiarly. He says it is necessary to ascend to the Father, and after doing this second appearance, to receive the known friends and new men already approaching in the time. Do not, he says, grasp me now; for there is another great and salutary work remaining for you which I must fulfill, to ascend to the Father, who will indeed be your Father through me, and especially when I ascend the firstfruits rising from among you. This indeed she, having gone, has made good news to the brothers (John 20:18). …
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: Christ calls his Father 'God' as man, and gives us his Father as ours by adoption, without ceasing to be Son by nature.
comments.comment: When Jesus said to his apostles, 'I am going to my Father and your Father, and to my God and your God' (John 20:17), he clearly referred to his own Father as God, speaking from his human perspective. Through him, we have been called to adoption, and he has given us his Father as our own. Just as we, though called sons of the Father, are still human and have not forgotten the grace of the one who honored us, so too the natural Son and Lord, though he recognized God as his Father through his flesh and his likeness to us, did not cease to be what he is.
comments.selected_reason: Explains 'my Father, and your Father; and … my God, and your God'.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: God is Christ's Father by nature and ours by grace, and his God by the plan of salvation because he became man.
comments.comment: So the Son of God also tastes death because of his fleshly father, so that the sons of man might share in the life of God because of their Father according to the Spirit, God. He is therefore Son of God by nature, but we are sons by grace. And again, he became a son of Adam by the plan of salvation and for our sake, while we are sons of Adam by nature. Therefore he says, “I am going to my Father and your Father, to my God and your God” (John 20:17). For God is his Father, as I said before, by nature, but ours by grace; and God became his God by the plan of salvation, because he is man, but for us he is by nature Master and God.
comments.author: Marcellus of Ancyra
comments.work: On the Incarnation and against the Arians

comments.capsule: 'Touch me not' corrects Mary's view of him as a mere man returning to his old life, and 'my God' is said as man, 'my Father' as Son by nature.
comments.comment:
Since as far as it concerns you I am not God but a mere man about to be again with human beings according to the way of life before the passion and you do not think I will be with the Father, do not touch me.

[John 20:18] As more intimate he grants this one the boast of the good news, as returning more than the others at the tomb and going about the tomb.

[John 20:17] Since according to the essence of flesh the Son became our brother, as God by nature existing as the Father’s Son he says his Father; and God, as man according to us, he names God his God.
comments.selected_reason: Explains 'Touch me not' and why Mary was the one sent with the news.
comments.author: Ammonius of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Christ came through locked doors by divine power, for after the resurrection he showed himself through divine authority.
comments.comment: Someone might reasonably raise this puzzle: if the Word was in a body even after the resurrection, as also before the precious cross, how did he appear unexpectedly in the midst of the disciples when the doors were locked? To this we say: by divine power. One must remember Paul saying that “from now on we know no one according to the flesh; even if we have known Christ according to the flesh, yet now we know him so no longer.” (2 Corinthians 5:16) For after the rising from the dead, since the economy on which the taking of flesh was done as needed is already finished, he uses authority and power befitting God, wanting to be recognized rather through these than through the measures of the emptying, as at the fitting time.
comments.selected_reason: Explains how Jesus came in when the doors were shut.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On the True Faith, to the Princesses Arcadia and Marina

comments.capsule: Christ greeted the women with 'Rejoice' to undo sorrow and the apostles with 'Peace' to end the enmity of the devil.
comments.comment: …See him, then, appearing early to the women and late to the apostles. Early, here, he greeted the women with 'Rejoice' (Matthew 28:9); late, in Zion, he greeted the disciples with 'Peace' (John 20:19). 'Rejoice' to the women, to undo the sentence of sorrow; 'Peace' to the disciples, to put an end to the enmity the dragon had planted. That is why he spoke to them with this distinction: 'Peace be with you; for the war is with the devil, and the enmity against him remains. His horn must be broken, his venom poured out, his sting trampled. Now I will forge the weapons with which war will be waged against him.'
comments.author: Hesychius of Jerusalem

comments.capsule: Coming through shut doors showed his divinity, the wounds proved the same body, and his word of peace calmed their fear as he sent them out.
comments.comment:
Since entering with the doors shut he made the disciples doubt whether perhaps what appeared was not a body but only a type, Luke clarifying the mind said: “Handle me and see, that a spirit does not have flesh and bones” (Luke 24:39) and he ate and showed the flesh’s wounds.

Through this he showed the Godhead’s strength. He did not present himself by day, so that all might be gathered; on the day he spoke with Mary he also appeared to the disciples by God-befitting power and with the doors shut, wondrously and unexpectedly appearing to them; for he was God, even if he had the thick body.

He showed the marks of the passion so that they might be assured that it was the same that had suffered, even if it had become spiritual and they had passed into incorruption. For this he showed them, to put all their turmoil to sleep.

Through this the word was fulfilled which the Lord said: “a little and you will see me,” “and your heart will rejoice” (John 16:16–22). Through the word of peace he looses their cowardice. “He himself is” Christ “our peace” (Ephesians 2:14). Yet through this we also were taught in the mystical assemblies to say to ourselves the word of peace.

[John 20:21] Since through the cross all things have become easy, I send you to do the work which I did.
comments.author: Ammonius of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Coming through shut doors and giving the Spirit showed his power beyond the flesh, renewing the breath God first gave Adam.
comments.comment:
Falling in through the closed doors by the power of divinity, performing a transgression, he gave them the beginning to understand the power and the authority of Christ not according to the flesh nor yet according to the human manner, but beyond the nature of the flesh. And that it might be certain to appear more divine to them, it is clear from the fact that he immediately showed them only those things pertaining to the faith of the resurrection and granted the divinity of the Spirit (John 20:22). For these things were not done while walking with them and eating with them and resting with them and walking along with them, but he begins to accommodate himself similarly to being higher than the human way of life.

We see an inspiration in the first breathing of the soul of man being made with sanctification. For the mission was not of soul alone, even if the thing breathed in is called the spirit of life; it is clear from the prophecy of him who is immediately prophesied by the one who was breathed in; for without the divine Spirit it is not possible for prophecy to exist, as Paul testifies. Therefore, he who from the beginning breathed in, after the soul, gave the Holy Spirit himself to the soul.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: By breathing the Spirit Christ showed the Spirit is his own and renewed the image Adam had before the fall.
comments.comment: Through what he breathed and gave spirit, he showed that it is consubstantial with him and not alien and proceeding through him from the Father, which nerved them to do what is pleasing to God and to know the power of the mystery according to God. And the breathing made the renewal for humanity and taking again the “according to the image” which Adam had before the transgression. And saying he sends, he sent ahead of time to confirm that this will be for all at the appointed time.
comments.author: Ammonius of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Christ breathed the Spirit on the disciples to restore what Adam received by God's breath and lost by sin.
comments.comment: …God, giving nature its most complete beauty, makes him sharer of his own Spirit. For “he breathed into his face a breath of life” (Genesis 2:7); for what truly gives life is the Spirit of life, that is, of Christ. But since he slipped from deceit into sin, the Spirit was removed. When God and Father was pleased “to recapitulate all things in Christ” (Ephesians 1:10) and to bring human nature back up into its ancient beauty, we received back through grace what the intrusion of sin had damaged in us. For Christ breathed into us after the resurrection, renewing us into the ancient beauty: “Receive,” (John 20:22) he says, “holy Spirit.” So the Spirit is united to us; for “the one cleaving to the Lord is one spirit.” (1 Corinthians 6:17) …
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: He gave power over sins, or readied them for the Spirit, saying 'receive', not 'you have received'.
comments.comment: He gave them a spiritual gift of loosing sins and condemning. And others say that he made them fit for reception of the Spirit which they were going to receive after the ascent. For which reason he did not say “you have received Holy Spirit,” but “receive.” …
comments.selected_reason: Explains 'Receive ye the Holy Ghost' and the power over sins.
comments.author: Ammonius of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Giving the Spirit and authority over sins is God's work, done through a bodily breath because the flesh is the Word's own.
comments.comment: The whole deed is God-befitting and worthy of every word. First, breathing on the apostles and giving the Spirit is not a human act. Then it is great and above creation to grant such authority that they may retain the sins of those they choose, and also forgive those they may wish. And why does he give the Spirit also through a fleshly breath? Because his flesh has not become alien to the Word, but is his own in a proper sense. The breathing through flesh is human; but it is the work of divine power to make those who are counted worthy sharers of the Spirit.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why Jesus breathed on them and what the gift shows about him.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On the True Faith, to the Princesses Arcadia and Marina

comments.capsule: Thomas doubted out of grief at missing the sight, and God allowed it so that all might know the crucified body rose.
comments.comment:
And Thomas, though absent, obtained the Spirit’s grace through the breathing; for upon the whole choir of the apostles the Lord poured out the grace.

[John 20:25] Beyond measure Thomas, busying himself through thinking it impossible, is charged. Therefore he did not say only “unless I see,” but “unless I handle,” lest what is seen be a phantom. Hearing then from the disciples that he took a lance wound, he was persuaded even without seeing, but as beyond reason he disbelieved the resurrection. He said it not so much as disbelieving as grieving that he too was not counted worthy of the sight. And by economy Thomas disbelieved, so that through him we all may know that the crucified body rose; for by seeking to see the wounds about the flesh, he was seeking whether that very flesh rose.
comments.selected_reason: Explains Thomas's demand to touch and why his doubt helps us.
comments.author: Ammonius of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Thomas allowed that a dead man's soul might be seen, but not that Jesus rose in a solid body, so he asked to touch.
comments.comment: …Jesus called to himself one of the disciples who disbelieved and thought the wonder impossible. For that disciple had agreed with the woman who said she had seen him, on the view that it is not impossible for the soul of one who has died to be seen; but he did not go on to think it true that he had been raised in a solid body. That is why he said: “Unless I see,” “I will not believe”; and he added: “Unless I put my hand into the mark of the nails and touch his side, I will not believe” (John 20:25).
comments.selected_reason: Explains exactly what Thomas doubted.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Christ kept and showed his wounds out of condescension, so that no room for unbelief would remain.
comments.comment:
For the shock of the signs almost draws even the unwilling who see toward faith.

[John 20:27] He shows himself having wounds and allows him to handle him; for by condescension he so appeared to Thomas though freed of every thickness of body and become light, so that he might be persuaded that it was the same crucified body. And from using Thomas’s words he shows that even when Thomas was saying these things he was present. And even if bodies are raised incorruptible and lacking nothing in the new resurrection, yet so that no word of unbelief may remain, as Thomas sought to see, so he showed; and not only Thomas but also the angels ignorant of the economy of the incarnation and saying: “Who is this who comes from Edom” [Isaiah 63:1] and again: “What are these wounds in the midst of your hands?” teaching he says: “with which I was struck in the house of my beloved” (Zechariah 13:6).
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the risen body still bore wounds.
comments.author: Ammonius of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Touching Christ's flesh, Thomas confessed the whole Christ, flesh and Word together, as God.
comments.comment: He was always, it says, God the Word, and this same God became flesh, so that his flesh might become God the Word (John 1:14). Just as Thomas, having touched his flesh, cried out, "My Lord and my God" (John 20:28), declaring the whole together as God.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what Thomas confessed in 'My Lord and my God'.
comments.author: Marcellus of Ancyra
comments.work: On the Incarnation and against the Arians

comments.capsule: John wrote not to amaze or entertain but so that readers might believe and have eternal life.
comments.comment:
Many indeed and other signs Jesus performed in the presence of his disciples. Many indeed things left behind by John have been written alongside the other evangelists, and many also are left there; for not one single book can contain all things accomplished concerning the Savior.

And John also teaches us, for which reason of scripture he was worthy to recount the recollections of the presence of Christ, that it is for the greatest benefit of those hearing; for it is neither for the purpose of striking wonder at the miracles nor for the purpose of delight in the narrative, but so that we might believe by the power through his works, and believing, we might bring to ourselves the only true benefit, which is unto eternal life.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the purpose of John's Gospel stated in these verses.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: The empty night pictures the fruitless times before Christ, and the great catch at his word the gospel drawing in the nations.
comments.comment: The whole contemplation of this section is as follows. Those before the disciples passing the time in darkness of demonic error caught nothing or very few, which is in place of nothing; nor those worshipping in types and shadow, where they themselves despising the law obeyed human commandments; but also the throng of the nations was un-netted, not receiving the divine lessons. But when the “sun of righteousness” (Malachi 4:2) came, hungering for humans’ salvation, he found nothing edible among humans and says to cast the evangelical word, which is the right teaching, compared with which the law and the prophets are understood as left; and by the grace of the one who commanded they drew many; for the wonder upon this surpasses the apostles’ strength.
comments.author: Ammonius of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The 153 fish stand for the fullness of the nations, the saved of Israel, and the Trinity.
comments.comment: Peter draws the spiritual net with the others, bringing the catch to Christ. And the hundred are understood as the fullness of the nations, the fifty as the race from Israel saved according to election, and the three invent the showing of the holy Trinity, to whose glory the life of the faithful caught is understood conjoined.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the number of fish.
comments.author: Ammonius of Alexandria

comments.capsule: 'Come and dine' hints at the saints' rest.
comments.comment: “Come, breakfast” has a riddle in the word: that after the toils rest and food and enjoyment will succeed the saints.
comments.author: Ammonius of Alexandria

comments.capsule: He ate to prove the resurrection, not from need.
comments.comment: …And he does the human things before the passion. And if Luke said that he also “ate,” not as still needing the flesh but for demonstration of the resurrection.
comments.author: Ammonius of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Christ's three questions let Peter undo his three denials with three confessions and showed Christ's care for the flock.
comments.comment:
Wanting to rekindle him from the despondency after the denial he asks him, and through the three questions and confessions he wipes out the three voices of the denial and through words he sets right the faults that happened in words. And from this a custom has come that three confessions be required of those about to be baptized.

He asks him a third time not as not knowing—for how, also the one who foretold his passion?—but to show that he cares greatly for the oversight of his sheep and that Peter loved him greatly.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why Jesus asks Peter three times.
comments.author: Ammonius of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Peter, kept by Christ's help through his fall, must show the same care by strengthening and feeding the brothers.
comments.comment:
For this very thing was foretold even before the denial (Luke 22:31-32), showing indeed that he will be tested by the devil when he turns away from the confession into Christ, but by the help from Him, he remains upon the faith.

And it is necessary for the one receiving this help to show similar sparing and care toward the brothers. For 'Simon,' He says, 'Simon, behold, Satan has asked you to sift you like wheat (Luke 22:31). But I have prayed for you, so that your faith may not fail. And you, when you have turned back, strengthen your brothers' (Luke 22:32).'

The Lord repeats those words and says that, if you love the Teacher and Savior who kept you even until now in love, you must imitate my care toward you, strengthening the brothers and feeding them just as a shepherd feeds a flock, calling the sheep his own.

And if he was shepherding through Peter, it is because he is the true shepherd and teacher. …
comments.selected_reason: Links 'Feed my sheep' to Jesus' earlier word 'strengthen thy brethren'.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: The triple confession answers the triple denial, and martyrdom by the cross will be Peter's greater proof of love.
comments.comment:
