Regarding the third of those questions, he is simultaneously making an exhortation to him that reminds him; at the same time, he is reminding him of the third denial that had occurred, and opposing the triple confession of love against the triple denial and demanding the readiness of service, so that he might confess Christ in works,

whom he denied by words while taking care of his own salvation (John 21:18-19).

He says that he will make an even greater proof of love through martyrdom, and prepares him to have this readiness, so that, opposing need with courage, he might remove the martyrdom unto death concerning the Lord, which previously had become a denial through fear of death.

And ‘to be girded,’ he says, means to be bound.

And the following path will be especially through the cross, because he suffers the same things as the Savior …
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: Peter wished to die for Christ but not by the cross, lest he seem to share his Master's honor, so the form of death was laid on him.
comments.comment: This signifies the death through the cross, which he underwent unwillingly, even if for the hoped-for things he was put to death willingly. Some from this thought that Peter suffered unwillingly, but it is not so; rather he wanted to suffer, yet did not want to be crucified, lest he seem among the simpler to have been counted worthy of the same honor as the Master. Therefore he teaches him not to be troubled; for this form is not of choice but brought on by others.
comments.selected_reason: Explains 'carry thee whither thou wouldest not'.
comments.author: Ammonius of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Every death for Christ glorifies God, whatever its manner, since the willingness is ours.
comments.comment: Know this too: the word spoken through John we learned, saying, 'These things said he, signifying by what death he shall glorify God.' (John 21:19) Every death for Christ glorifies the Father — whether by sword or fire or beasts or bonds. Let the manner be what God wills; ours is the willingness. For the confession hallows every manner, and every manner perfects the confessor.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Christ parted Peter and John for the world's good, and 'if I will that he tarry' was not a promise that John would not die.
comments.comment:
He said this wanting to cut off the untimely sympathy they had toward each other; for if they were not separated from each other, the inhabited world would have suffered the greatest loss. And he did not say “he does not die,” but “if I want him to remain”—that is: a work was entrusted to you, do this, care for your own; for what do you want, if I do not wish to send him with you but that he remain here?

[John 21:23] The disciples received the Lord’s word as a decision that he will not die, which he did not say. But what he said, speaking in riddle, he said the long-livedness of his life; for in the times he died without punishment.
comments.selected_reason: Explains 'what is that to thee?' and the rumor that John would not die.
comments.author: Ammonius of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The Lord's word concerned those who never truly die, believers, and John shows he himself had no promise of escaping death.
comments.comment:
…Thus, therefore, the word of the Lord was about those who in the end do not die. And this was made manifest by saying: 'He who believes in me, even if he dies, shall live, and everyone living and believing in me shall not die for ever' (John 11:25-26).

Because of this, they were making it without hopelessness to live and not to die. But it was laid up for those left behind until the presence of Christ, for those being born in the last generation, just as Paul taught.

And John points out that he himself did not have the promise of not dying, but the brothers, hearing this word, took this from ignorance (John 21:23).
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: The disciple who bears witness is John himself, the Gospel's writer, and one loved by the Truth cannot lie.
comments.comment: As having spoken without falsehood he bears witness to himself the truth. Therefore in many places naming himself indefinitely here he plainly signifies himself; for he himself is the one who wrote the gospel. One loved by God would not have been able to lie, therefore do not doubt; for the truth would not have loved him loosening the truth.
comments.selected_reason: Identifies the disciple who 'testifieth of these things'.
comments.author: Ammonius of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The world could not hold the books, whether for their number, the greatness of the deeds, or the worldly minds unable to receive them.
comments.comment:
One must refuse to speak the things better than all writing in books, which not even the world itself can contain because of the greatness of contemplations. If all were written, no human would suffice for acquiring the books. For this it was not written, so as not to overpass the memory of the hearers. Or if all were written, the books would be numberless and no one could know all. Or if someone wants to present the greatness of what happened, neither the world nor human hearing contains them. Some say that those living worldly cannot contain hearing the God-signs according to what was said in the beginning: “and the world did not know him” (John 1:10), as also the Lord himself said that “not all contain this word” (Matthew 19:11).

Many and numberless are the God-signs and from many these were taken that can perfectly benefit.

So many are the things done and said by the Savior that all libraries would be full, he says I think, of books containing the histories of the Lord’s works and the words upon them, if one were going to write all according to each.

We understand the name of the world differently. And it is possible according to one meaning to present the truthfulness of the word and to refute the rashness of those who mindlessly mock the God-breathed words of the evangelists.
comments.author: Ammonius of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The world could not hold the books because of the greatness of Christ's deeds, not their number.
comments.comment: …But of the more divine and greater things that might be said about him and that he himself declared, John says that “not even the world, I suppose, could contain the books that would be written” (John 21:25). For the saying that “the world could not contain the books that would be written” is to be understood not, as some take it, of the number of the writings, but of the greatness of the matters; for the greatness of the matters not only cannot be written down, but cannot even be told by a tongue of flesh, nor expressed in human languages and sounds.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what 'the world itself could not contain the books' means.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria
